Algeria.d:
In Algeria two outside forces show in the record today, one that reached into the security state from below and one that reached across the border from a neighbour.

The first is drug money at the top of the police. When customs found 701 kilograms of cocaine at the port of Oran in May 2018, the seizure exposed a network that reached Abdelghani Hamel, the Director-General of National Security, who ran the national police, the force meant to stop such shipments. He was removed, and military and civilian courts later convicted him and several generals. The convictions were for corruption and illicit enrichment rather than trafficking, and Algeria has published little about the drug case itself, so how far the network reached into the police and army is still not public.

The second is Morocco, Algeria's neighbour and rival. The 2021 Pegasus Project, a group of journalists working with Amnesty International, reported that Morocco had picked more than 6,000 Algerian phones, among them politicians and senior military officers, as targets for Pegasus, spyware sold by the Israeli firm NSO Group that can read everything on a phone. Morocco denies using it. Algeria cut diplomatic relations in August 2021 and named the spying among its reasons.

The Muslim Brotherhood, the Islamist movement founded in Egypt, is also recorded as present. What the record leaves today is a security state that handles its own failures in closed military and civilian courts, so the public record is mostly the verdicts.
Algeria.imp: Algerians know their police chief was removed over a cocaine network, but not who else in the police or army was part of it, because the trafficking evidence was never published. If the Pegasus reporting is right, the private calls of their generals and politicians may have been read by a neighbouring government, and that suspicion helped end diplomatic relations with Morocco. Watch for any release of the Oran files and for any official finding on the phones.

Angola.d:
In Angola outside money and outside churches reach into the state through the oil business and the pulpit, and the record also shows the Davos network at the finance ministry.

Oil is where foreign money lands. Sonangol is the state oil company. Trafigura, one of the world's largest oil and metals traders, was convicted by the Swiss Federal Criminal Court in January 2025 over €4.3 million in bribes paid in 2009–11 to an Angolan official tied to a Sonangol subsidiary; it was ordered to pay $145.6 million and has appealed, so the ruling is not final. The Brazilian builder Odebrecht is also recorded as present, and Iceland's Samherji fishing company and the Portuguese Espírito Santo banking group are judged likely but not documented.

Religion is the second route. The Universal Church of the Kingdom of God, a Brazilian-run Pentecostal church, built a large following in Angola. After Angolan pastors accused its Brazilian leaders of racial discrimination and of pressing pastors into vasectomies, the government in June 2020 dissolved the church's board and removed Bishop Honorilton Gonçalves. It had already been suspended for 60 days in 2013 after a deadly crush at a Luanda stadium event.

The third is the World Economic Forum, the Davos forum. Finance minister Vera Daves de Sousa, in office since October 2019, is an alumna of its Young Global Leaders, a five-year programme of meetings and courses for people under about 40. That is a lawful programme, not wrongdoing. The Gülen movement and the Order of Malta are also present.
Angola.imp: Angola's oil money passes through state companies, and the Trafigura case shows a foreign trader paying an official to get at it, which means some of the value of Angolan oil went to private pockets. Angolan churchgoers found their large church run from Brazil until the government stepped in. Watch the Trafigura appeal, whether the official who took the money is ever named and tried in Angola, and how Sonangol's trading contracts are awarded now.

Benin.d: This is an estimate. Nothing is documented on the map for Benin yet. The only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status. Two French Masonic bodies, the Grand Orient de France and the Grande Loge Nationale Française, are judged likely but not documented. The conditions scores show a moderate chance of powerful groups inside the state and weak checks. As a best guess, the most likely route in is the one seen in French-speaking neighbours such as Burkina Faso, Niger and Côte d'Ivoire, where presidents and ministers have been reported as members of lodges tied to France.
Benin.imp: No case means nothing has been found, not that nothing is happening. With weak checks, influence could sit inside the state without anyone recording it. For people in Benin, the thing to watch is who holds the top offices and what networks they belong to, especially lodges tied to France, which have reached presidencies across the region, and whether the cocaine trade on the West African coast starts to show up in its ports.

Botswana.d: This is an estimate. Nothing is documented on the map for Botswana yet, and no organisation from the map's list is recorded as present or even judged likely. The conditions scores are among the better ones in Africa on this map: a lower chance of powerful outside groups sitting inside the state, and checks on power, such as courts and a free press, that are fairly strong. As a best guess, if an outside force did reach in, the most likely route would be the one most common across southern Africa on this map: a foreign company paying officials for licences or contracts, as Samherji is accused of doing for fishing quotas in neighbouring Namibia.
Botswana.imp: Botswana's empty record fits its fairly strong checks, but an empty record can also mean no one has looked. For people living there, the thing to watch is how big state contracts and mining or other licences are awarded, and whether foreign courts or regulators ever name Botswana officials in bribery cases, which is how most such cases in the region have come to light.

Burkina Faso.d:
Burkina Faso's military government now leans on Russia for its security, and the record shows how that came about and what older network it replaced.

Captain Ibrahim Traoré's government ordered French troops out in early 2023. Africa Corps, the Russian defence ministry unit that took over most of the Wagner Group's work in Africa, arrived on 24 January 2024, an initial 100 people to be expanded to 300, and set up its first African base at Loumbila, north-east of the capital Ouagadougou. Wagner itself, the Russian private military company tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, is recorded as present. Ghana's president had earlier claimed a mine was handed to Wagner as payment; Burkina's mines minister denied it, so how Russia is paid is not on the record. The country also sits on the Sahel cocaine route: UN figures put seizures across Burkina Faso, Chad, Mali, Mauritania and Niger at 1,466 kilograms in 2022, against an average of 13 a year in 2015–2020, with the money moving into gold and property.

The network it replaced ran through the lodges. Under Blaise Compaoré, president from 1987 to 2014, the Grande Loge du Burkina, the national Masonic lodge, was led from the top of the state: Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that Compaoré was a former grand master and that his foreign minister, Djibrill Bassolé, had succeeded him. Being a Mason is lawful; what the reporting shows is a private circle at the head of government. The French Grand Orient and Grande Loge Nationale Française are judged likely present.
Burkina Faso.imp: People in Burkina Faso now depend for their security on foreign soldiers whose terms have never been published; the claim that a mine changed hands was denied but never cleared up. Decisions about the war are taken by a military government with Russian partners at a base outside the capital, beyond reach of a parliament or press. Watch for any published agreement with Russia, for mining titles going to Russian-linked firms, and for cocaine money showing up in the gold trade.

Burundi.d:
In Burundi the documented outside force is the tobacco industry, working on the officials who write health law. Leaked records from British American Tobacco (BAT), the world's second-largest listed tobacco company, reported by BBC Panorama in 2015, name payments to officials in Burundi. A 2021 University of Bath study of those and other leaked papers counted 236 payments worth $601,502 across ten African countries from 2008 to 2013, and said the payments in Burundi, Comoros, Rwanda and Uganda were aimed at frustrating tobacco control laws modelled on the WHO's tobacco treaty. Burundi is one of four neighbouring states in East and Central Africa where that same effort shows up. The UK Serious Fraud Office closed its investigation in 2021 without charges, and BAT denies the allegations, so this remains reported, not proven.

Also recorded as present are the Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, and the Atlas Network, a US-based network of free-market think tanks. Burundi's conditions scores are among the harsher on the map: a high chance of powerful groups sitting inside the state and very weak checks, such as courts and a free press. That combination means much of what goes on is likely unrecorded, and the tobacco case came to light only because of leaks in Britain.
Burundi.imp: If the payments did what the Bath researchers say, Burundians live with weaker tobacco rules than their government signed up to under the WHO treaty, which means fewer limits on how cigarettes are sold and advertised. With no charges in Britain and no inquiry recorded in Burundi, nobody has had to answer. Watch whether Burundi's tobacco law catches up with the treaty, and whether health officials' dealings with the industry are ever examined.

Cabo Verde.d: This is an estimate. Nothing is documented on the map for Cabo Verde, and the only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status. The conditions scores are among the best in Africa on this map: a lower chance of powerful groups inside the state and fairly strong checks. As a best guess, the risk comes by sea. West African states such as Guinea-Bissau, Senegal and Sierra Leone sit on the route South American cocaine takes to Europe, and there the trade has reached ports, airports and security officials.
Cabo Verde.imp: An empty record here fits Cabo Verde's fairly strong checks, but it can also mean no one has looked. For people on the islands, the thing to watch is whether drug seizures reach court, and whether port, airport and coast guard officials are ever named in trafficking cases, since those are the offices the trade has bought elsewhere on this coast.

Cameroon.d:
Cameroon's record points to two outside forces with long reach into the state, both tied to France, alongside foreign traders and influence networks.

The first is money. Yaoundé, the capital, is home to the Bank of Central African States (BEAC), the central bank that issues the CFA franc for six countries: Cameroon, the Central African Republic, Chad, the Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea and Gabon. The French Treasury guarantees the currency's fixed rate against the euro, and in return the six must still deposit half their foreign-exchange reserves with it. West Africa's CFA zone dropped that rule from 2021; Central Africa's has not, and a French Senate report in December 2024 called the reform incomplete.

The second is a private order around the president. Le Monde reported in 1999 that President Paul Biya gave tens of millions of francs between 1988 and 1992 to Raymond Bernard's OSTI, a Templar order, and its sister body CIRCES, 40 million francs of it from Biya personally, and that 11.2 million francs moved from SNH, the state oil company, to Bernard's own account. The presidency called Bernard an 'old friend' and would not comment. Bernard was questioned in the Solar Temple inquiry but not charged.

Foreign traders have paid their way in too: Glencore, the Swiss commodity trader, admitted in a British court in 2022 that bribes were paid in Cameroon among five African states. Facebook in 2019 removed fake accounts run by Prigozhin's Russian network that targeted Cameroon. Opus Dei and the Gülen movement are present, and Wagner is judged likely.
Cameroon.imp: Half of what Cameroon earns in foreign currency still sits with the French Treasury, which limits what the regional central bank can do with the country's own reserves and keeps Paris close to every money decision in the region. If the OSTI reporting is right, state oil money went to a private order chosen by the president, with no account to the public. Watch whether the Central African reserve rule is changed, and whether SNH's accounts are ever opened up.

Central African Republic.d:
In the Central African Republic the outside force sits inside the presidency itself. About 1,000 fighters of the Wagner Group, the Russian private military company tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, have been in the country since a Russia–CAR military agreement in August 2018. They guard President Faustin-Archange Touadéra and fight rebels alongside the army, and a Russian, Valery Zakharov, served as his national security adviser from 2018; the US Treasury sanctions him as linked to Wagner, and its listing shows he also held a Central African passport. Russia's defence ministry is folding these units into its Africa Corps, and the CAR remains its largest African deployment, estimated at 1,500 to 2,000. Reporting ties the deployment to gold, diamond and timber concessions, including logging in Lobaye.

Around it sits a criminal economy researchers say has merged with the state. Illicit gold exports are estimated at $180 million a year, flown out on military cargo aircraft registered in the country and laundered through UAE-linked exporters, and a government-backed fuel monopoly makes a further $17.5 to $30 million a year in unjustified profits. Tramadol, a painkiller, comes from Indian manufacturers through Kinshasa; miners take it to work long shifts and fighters take it in combat. Reporting from Bangui in July 2026 describes Wagner remnants supplying it to the presidential guard and a youth militia, with senior security officials said to control the market. The Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime concludes that political and military figures, criminals and foreign groups have aligned to control the country's criminal markets. Nothing has been charged.

From the older history, François Bozizé, president from 2003 to 2013, was reported to have become a Freemason under the sponsorship of Congo's president. The CAR also keeps half its reserves at the French Treasury through the regional central bank.
Central African Republic.imp: People in the CAR live in a country where the president's guards answer partly to a foreign force, and where gold leaves on military planes without passing through the treasury. Miners and fighters are kept going on smuggled tramadol, and university research links its rise to a near-20 percent increase in deaths in fighting over mines, around 500 in a year. With senior security officials said to run the drug market, there is no one at home to bring a case. Watch what Africa Corps takes over from Wagner, and where the gold goes.

Chad.d:
In Chad the drug trade has reached the army and intelligence services, while Turkey and the regional currency reach the state from outside.

Tramadol, a prescription painkiller trafficked across the Sahel, is the clearest case. A court in N'Djamena sentenced ten people in July 2020 over a transnational tramadol network, among them high-ranking security and intelligence officials. Analysts at the Institute for Security Studies who read the court papers described large sums moving among its members, some used to try to corrupt judges and the security services, so the institutions expected to enforce the law are among those the network worked on. Cocaine is rising on the same routes: UN figures show seizures across Chad, Burkina Faso, Mali, Mauritania and Niger climbing from an average of 13 kilograms a year in 2015–2020 to 1,466 kilograms in 2022, with no prosecution in any of the five.

Turkey's reach shows in the schools. Turkey treats the Gülen movement, a religious network that ran schools in many countries, as a terrorist group. In November 2017 the presidency announced that Idriss Déby had agreed to hand Gülen schools to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation by 18 December and to expel people linked to the movement, as Guinea, Niger, Senegal and Somalia also did that year.

Chad also deposits half its foreign reserves with the French Treasury through the Bank of Central African States. From the older record, Déby, president from 1990 to 2021, was named as a Freemason in 2009 and 2013 reporting, though no lodge is named.
Chad.imp: When senior army and intelligence officers are part of a trafficking network, Chadians cannot count on the services meant to stop it, and attempts to bribe judges mean even a conviction is hard won. The tramadol moving through the country feeds fighters and miners across the region. Families whose children attended Gülen schools saw them handed to a foreign government's foundation. Watch whether the 2020 verdict leads to further cases, and whether cocaine seizures reach court.

Comoros.d:
In the Comoros outside money reached the state through two things the government sells or regulates: passports and tobacco law.

Under a 2008 'economic citizenship' law, the islands sold passports in bulk to stateless people (bidoon) living in the Gulf, with Gulf money paying, in a scheme run with the Syrian-French businessman Bashar Kiwan. Prosecutors said it brought in about $200 million, much of which never reached the treasury. In November 2022 a court in Moroni, the capital, sentenced former president Ahmed Abdallah Sambi to life in prison for high treason and related charges; Kiwan was tried with him. The passport-sale industry is still recorded as present.

The tobacco case runs across the region. In 2015 BBC Panorama, using documents from a former employee of British American Tobacco (BAT), the world's second-largest listed tobacco company, reported that BAT arranged bribes totalling about $26,000 for officials in Rwanda, Burundi and the Comoros, partly to frustrate tobacco control laws based on the WHO's tobacco treaty. A 2021 University of Bath study counted 236 payments worth $601,502 across ten African countries. Britain's Serious Fraud Office closed its inquiry in 2021 without charges, and BAT denies wrongdoing.

The Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, is also present. The conditions scores show a high chance of powerful groups inside the state and weak checks.
Comoros.imp: Comorians lost much of an estimated $200 million that should have reached the treasury, while their citizenship was sold in bulk to people with no tie to the islands. If the tobacco payments worked, health rules were weakened to suit the industry. The Sambi verdict shows the courts can reach a former president. Watch whether citizenship sales return under other names, and whether tobacco law is tightened.

Congo, Dem. Rep..d:
In the Democratic Republic of Congo outside forces reach the state through its minerals and its war in the east, and in two provinces a neighbour has taken over the government.

M23, an armed group, took Goma in January 2025 and Bukavu after it. The UN Group of Experts reported in June 2025 that M23 operates under Rwandan command and that officials said President Kagame decided to take both cities. In North and South Kivu it found a 'systematic effort to dismantle existing State authority': new governors appointed, Rwandans placed over mining, tax, banking and border control, and 18 customary chiefs removed. Rwanda denies directing M23. On the government side, Erik Prince, founder of the US military contractor Blackwater, sent men and drones in February 2026 to help Congo's army hold the eastern city of Uvira, Reuters reported.

In the mining sector, foreign firms have paid their way in. Dan Gertler, an Israeli investor and friend of former president Joseph Kabila, was sanctioned by the US in 2017 over opaque and corrupt mining and oil deals made through that friendship; under a later settlement his Ventora group handed back licences and agreed to pay royalties to Gécamines, the state miner. He denies wrongdoing. Glencore, the Swiss commodity trader, paid $27.5 million to third parties from 2007 to 2018 intending part of it to bribe Congolese officials, US authorities said, and agreed in 2022 to pay Congo $180 million to settle.

Tramadol bound for the Central African Republic passes through Kinshasa.
Congo, Dem. Rep..imp: In Goma and Bukavu people now live under governors, tax collectors and mining officials put in place by an armed group that UN experts say a neighbouring army commands, and the customary chiefs they knew have been removed. Elsewhere, money from mining and oil deals that should have reached the state went partly to middlemen and officials. Watch who controls the eastern mines, and how the Glencore and Gertler settlement money is used.

Congo, Rep..d:
In the Republic of Congo the outside force recorded is the Masonic network that links the presidency to France and to neighbouring heads of state. Denis Sassou-Nguesso, the current president, is reported to be Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Congo-Brazzaville, which is linked to the Grande Loge Nationale Française (GLNF), one of France's main Masonic bodies. The reporting reaches past his own borders: a 2013 Jeune Afrique dossier said François Bozizé, then president of the Central African Republic, had been initiated as a Freemason under Sassou-Nguesso's sponsorship. His predecessor, Pascal Lissouba, president from 1992 to 1997, was reported to have been initiated at the Grand Orient de France lodge in Besançon.

Across Central Africa, in Gabon, Chad, the CAR and here, presidents have been reported at the head of lodges tied to Paris. Being a Freemason is lawful; what the reporting shows is a private channel between heads of state, and between them and French bodies, that citizens cannot see into. The record is press reporting, not official findings.

The money ties to France run through the regional central bank, the Bank of Central African States: Congo is one of six states that must deposit half their foreign reserves with the French Treasury. The commodity trader Gunvor is recorded as present, and the Italian oil company Eni is judged likely but undocumented. The conditions scores show a high chance of powerful groups inside the state and weak checks.
Congo, Rep..imp: If the reports are right, the president also heads a lodge tied to a French Masonic body, which gives that network a private line to the head of state and to his allies in neighbouring capitals. Congolese have no way to see what is discussed there or what is owed. Half the country's foreign reserves sit in Paris. Watch who in government and the oil sector is reported as a lodge member, and whether the Central African reserve rule changes.

Cote d'Ivoire.d:
In Côte d'Ivoire the record shows lodges close to the top of government and foreign commodity firms paying their way into its trade.

Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that Prime Minister Jeannot Ahoussou-Kouadio and Interior Minister Hamed Bakayoko were Freemasons, and that the state prosecutor, Simplice Koffi Kouadio, had been received by the Grande Loge de Côte d'Ivoire; it said President Alassane Ouattara was not officially known to be a member. The interior minister runs the police and the prosecutor decides who is charged, so lodge ties at that level bear on who is held to account, though membership is lawful. This fits a pattern across French-speaking West and Central Africa, where Burkina Faso, Mali, Guinea and Senegal have had presidents or ministers reported in lodges.

Commodity traders are the second route. Glencore, the Swiss trader, admitted in a British court in 2022 that bribes were paid in Côte d'Ivoire as well as Nigeria, Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea and South Sudan between 2012 and 2016, in its oil business. Gunvor, another trader, is recorded as present. Prigozhin's Russian influence network targeted the country with fake Facebook accounts removed in 2019. Opus Dei, the Catholic organisation, is present, and the French Grand Orient and Grande Loge Nationale Française are judged likely.
Cote d'Ivoire.imp: Ivorians cannot see whether the people who run the police and bring prosecutions owe loyalty to a private circle as well as to the law. Glencore's admission shows that bribes were paid to win oil business in the country, so officials sold access that belonged to the public. Watch who holds the interior ministry and prosecution service and what networks they belong to, and whether Ivorian officials in the Glencore case are ever charged at home.

Djibouti.d:
In Djibouti outside forces work through the state's port, its telecoms company and its debts.

China opened its first overseas military base there in 2017, and a China Merchants subsidiary has owned 23.5% of the Port of Djibouti since 2013. A US Congressional Research Service brief in June 2025 says Chinese institutions hold over half of Djibouti's $2.6 billion external debt, including a $1.2 billion loan from China's Exim Bank. Djibouti suspended repayments in 2022 and later agreed a moratorium. US officials warn the debt could give Beijing undue leverage; Djibouti says it will not hand port control to China. This is a reported concern, not a proven takeover, but it puts one foreign government in the position of base host, port shareholder and main creditor at once.

Western companies have paid officials directly. Ericsson, the Swedish telecoms equipment maker, admitted in its 2019 US settlement that it paid about €2.1 million to high-ranking officials to win a contract with the state-owned Djibouti Telecom. The settlement, over $1 billion in all, also covered China, Indonesia, Vietnam and Kuwait, and leaked Ericsson files published in 2022 described corruption in at least ten countries.

The conditions scores are moderate: a fair chance of powerful groups inside the state and weak checks, so the Ericsson case came to light through US prosecutors rather than at home.
Djibouti.imp: Djiboutians carry a national debt more than half owed to Chinese lenders, with repayments suspended, which gives the creditor weight in how the port and state finances are run. The Ericsson case means officials at the state telecoms company were paid by a supplier, so a contract the public relies on was won by bribery rather than price. Watch for any debt deal that trades port control or land, and whether Djiboutian officials in the Ericsson case face charges.

Egypt.d:
Egypt's state today is shaped by its fight with the Muslim Brotherhood, the Islamist movement founded there, and by a long history of foreign creditors and spy alliances.

The Brotherhood came closer than any movement on this map to taking a state by election. Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, won the presidency in June 2012. The army removed him on 3 July 2013, most of the leadership was jailed in the following months, and on 25 December 2013 the government declared the Brotherhood a terrorist organisation, two days after a car bomb at the Mansoura police headquarters killed 14 people; a different group, Ansar Bait al-Maqdis, claimed the bombing. Membership now carries up to five years in prison. In a case accusing Morsi of passing state secrets to Qatar, the top court in 2017 upheld his life sentence for leading an illegal group but threw out a 15-year term for stealing secret documents; Qatar denied the accusations. Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Gülen movement and the Unification Church are also recorded as present.

The older history explains why outside control is a live question. After the Khedive Ismail went bankrupt in 1876, Britain and France took joint control of Egypt's finances, and Evelyn Baring, of the Barings banking family whose bank held a large stake in Egyptian debt, became the British controller and then, from 1883 to 1907, the effective ruler, keeping Egypt's revenues committed to its European creditors. In 1976 Egypt's intelligence chief, Kamal Hassan Ali, signed the charter of the Safari Club, a secret alliance of the spy services of France, Saudi Arabia, Morocco, Iran and Egypt; in 1977 Egyptian and Moroccan troops were flown into Zaire to back Mobutu.
Egypt.imp: For Egyptians, the Brotherhood's ban means that belonging to the movement that won the 2012 election can now cost five years in prison, and where the line between membership and terrorism falls is decided by the government. The older history left a state used to having its money and security handled with foreign partners. Watch how the terrorism designation is used against political opponents, and whether any court reviews it.

Equatorial Guinea.d:
In Equatorial Guinea a foreign army now guards the man at the top. Teodoro Obiang has ruled since 1979. In autumn 2024 Russia deployed up to 200 troops of Africa Corps, the Russian defence ministry unit that took over most of the Wagner Group's work in Africa, to protect his presidency and to train elite units in Malabo, the capital, and Bata, according to the CTC Sentinel and other analyses. Obiang received the Africa Corps commander officially in Malabo in November 2025. Similar arrangements run in the Central African Republic, Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, where Russian forces guard leaders or fight alongside military governments.

Money is the other channel. Glencore, the Swiss commodity trader, admitted in a British court in 2022 that bribes were paid in Equatorial Guinea, along with Nigeria, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire and South Sudan, between 2012 and 2016. The country is one of six in the Central African CFA franc zone that still deposit half their foreign reserves with the French Treasury through the regional central bank, BEAC.

The Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, is also present. The conditions scores are among the worst on the map: a very high chance of powerful groups inside the state and very weak checks, so much of what goes on is likely unrecorded.
Equatorial Guinea.imp: With Russian soldiers protecting the president and training the elite units, the security forces answer in part to a foreign government whose terms are not public. Glencore's admission shows oil business in the country was won with bribes. With weak courts and press, Equatoguineans have little way to see either arrangement. Watch the size of the Russian presence and what Russia receives in return.

Eritrea.d: This is an estimate. Nothing is documented on the map for Eritrea, and the only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status. The conditions scores are among the worst on the map: a very high chance of powerful groups sitting inside the state and very weak checks, such as courts and a free press. That combination usually means outside influence goes unseen rather than absent. As a best guess, the routes most likely here are the ones recorded in the Horn of Africa: foreign governments seeking military footholds and lending that gives them leverage, as China has in neighbouring Djibouti.
Eritrea.imp: With very weak checks, Eritreans have little way to learn who has influence over their government or what has been promised to foreign partners. A blank record here says more about how closed the state is than about what is going on. Watch for foreign bases, port deals and loans, which elsewhere in the region have come with terms the public never saw.

Eswatini.d: This is an estimate. Nothing is documented on the map for Eswatini, and no organisation from the map's list is recorded as present or judged likely. The conditions scores sit in the middle: a moderate chance of powerful groups inside the state and fairly weak checks. As a best guess, the route most likely here is the drug trade that runs through neighbouring Mozambique, where researchers documented a heroin corridor protected by ruling party figures for three decades; relatives of its main figure were arrested in Eswatini, among other places. Foreign firms paying for contracts are the other common route in the region.
Eswatini.imp: A blank record may reflect a lack of looking as much as a lack of activity. For people in Eswatini, the thing to watch is whether trafficking networks from Mozambique use the country as a refuge or a route, as the arrests of a Mozambican trafficker's relatives there suggest, and whether officials who handle the border, police and big contracts are ever named in foreign cases.

Ethiopia.d:
In Ethiopia the clearest outside reach is into the building that houses the African Union, the continent's main political body, in the capital Addis Ababa. China built and paid for the roughly $200 million headquarters, opened in 2012, and the Chinese firm Huawei supplied most of its computer and network equipment. In January 2018 Le Monde, confirmed by the Financial Times, reported that AU staff had found in 2017 that the building's data had been copied every night to servers in Shanghai since 2012, and that microphones were hidden in walls and furniture. The AU replaced its servers and declined Chinese offers to set them up. China called the report 'ridiculous and preposterous', Huawei said its equipment was not the source, and no public evidence of a backdoor has been shown.

Inside Ethiopia's own government the record concerns faith rather than foreign money. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, in office since 2018, is a Pentecostal Christian who attends and sometimes preaches at the Ethiopian Full Gospel Believers' Church, and in 2019 formed the Prosperity Party, which governs today. Belonging to a church is not wrongdoing; the map records it because Pentecostal and evangelical networks are close to power in several countries, Kenya among them, where the president plans a church at State House.

The Tony Blair Institute, which places advisers inside governments, and Family Watch International are also recorded as present, and the Gülen movement is judged likely.
Ethiopia.imp: If the Le Monde reporting is right, for five years the private discussions of African governments at their own headquarters could be read in China. Ethiopia hosts that building, and the case shows that a headquarters paid for by one government can carry that government's equipment into everyone's meetings. Watch who supplies the AU's and Ethiopia's networks now, and how the prime minister's church ties shape policy on religion and the family.

Gabon.d:
In Gabon the lodges and the presidency have been one structure for half a century, and the record shows that structure outlasting a coup.

Omar Bongo, president from 1967 until his death in 2009, founded both of the country's main Masonic bodies, the Grand Rite Equatorial, affiliated with the Grand Orient de France, and the Grand Lodge of Gabon, linked to the Grande Loge Nationale Française (GLNF), and held the grand mastership until he died. In 2009 the GLNF's grand master installed his son Ali Bongo as grand master of both, the same year Ali became president. Ministers and the head of the National Security Council attended, and Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that the police chief, Antoine Embinga, was grand master of the Grande Loge symbolique du Gabon. Being a Mason is lawful; what the reporting shows is the head of state, ministers and police at the head of the same private circle, tied to bodies in Paris.

After the August 2023 coup the Grand Lodge replaced Ali Bongo with Jacques Denis Tsanga, governor of Haut-Ogooue province; the new leader, Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, reportedly declined the post. In November 2023 the Grand Orient de France's grand master, Guillaume Trichard, met Oligui in secret in Libreville and offered support to his transitional council, Gabonreview reported, describing Oligui as a non-practising Freemason. Oligui was elected president in April 2025. Gabon also deposits half its foreign reserves with the French Treasury through the regional central bank.
Gabon.imp: For Gabonese, the lodges have been a second ladder to power beside the parties and the army, one they cannot see into. The coup removed the Bongo family, but within three months a French Masonic leader was offering support to the new ruler, so the private channel to Paris carries on under a new president. Watch who in the new government is reported as a lodge member, and whether the French bodies' contact with the presidency continues.

Gambia.d:
In The Gambia outside forces held much of the economy under former president Yahya Jammeh, who left office in 2017, and the record is about what they did with it.

Lebanese businessmen whom the US designates as financiers of Hezbollah, the Lebanese Shia party and armed group, held state monopolies. OCCRP, an investigative journalism network, showed in 2019 that Mohamed Bazzi was one of Jammeh's closest associates and received monopolies including fuel supply, and that Ali Charara paid $35 million for half of the state telecoms firms Gamtel and Gamcel. OCCRP estimated that more than $100 million from Gambian telecoms reached Hezbollah.

Timber was the second business. Between 2014 and 2017 The Gambia exported nearly $163 million of rosewood to China, though its own rosewood was almost gone by 2011; most came from Senegal's Casamance region, where logging funds armed groups. The Swiss group TRIAL International says the holder of the exclusive export licence, Westwood Company, was co-founded by Jammeh and the Swiss national Nicolae Bogdan Buzaianu, and in 2019 filed a criminal complaint for pillage with Switzerland's Attorney General. The Environmental Investigation Agency documented the trade in 2020. The complaint is an allegation, not a verdict.

The Mouride Brotherhood, the Sufi order centred in Senegal, is also recorded as present. The conditions scores show a fair chance of powerful groups inside the state, with checks of middling strength.
Gambia.imp: Gambians paid fuel and phone bills to monopolies that, according to OCCRP, sent part of the money to a foreign armed group, and half their state telecoms firms were sold to a man the US says finances Hezbollah. Timber smuggled through the country paid for armed groups next door in Casamance. Jammeh is gone; watch whether these monopolies and stakes have been unwound, and whether the Swiss complaint reaches a court.

Ghana.d:
In Ghana two things show in the record: cocaine reaching the police, and Freemasonry openly present at the top of government.

The cocaine case is older but unresolved. In 2006 seventy-seven parcels of cocaine landed from a ship, the MV Benjamin, and disappeared, and a recording surfaced of a senior police officer meeting suspects at his home. A committee led by the Supreme Court judge Georgina Wood found the police account unsatisfactory, and the officer returned to duty. Ghana sits on the same West African route as Guinea-Bissau, Liberia and Sierra Leone, where cocaine has bought airport, port and police officials.

The lodges are a present-day matter, and in Ghana they are discussed openly. In May 2024 the Grand Lodge of Ghana honoured the Asantehene, the Asante king Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, for 25 years in Freemasonry, with the national security and transport ministers taking part as members. Alexander Afenyo-Markin, then majority leader in parliament, has said 'I am a Freemason and a Catholic'. At a vetting in January 2025 he asked the minister-designate George Opare Addo whether he was a Mason; Opare Addo said yes, named his lodge, 'Amity', and was confirmed in President Mahama's government. Former president John Kufuor has said he joined in 1967. Membership is lawful, and Ghana is unusual in having it said out loud in parliament.

Airbus, the European aircraft maker, and the Tony Blair Institute, which places advisers inside governments, are recorded as present.
Ghana.imp: Ghanaians can at least see which officials belong to lodges, because they say so in parliament. The open question is the one from the MV Benjamin case: cocaine vanished, a police officer was recorded with suspects, and he went back to work with nobody held to account. Watch whether new drug seizures reach court, and whether lodge ties shape appointments to security posts.

Guinea.d:
In Guinea outside forces came in through the iron ore, the presidential family and the schools.

Simandou holds one of the world's largest untapped iron ore deposits. In 2008 the government took two blocks from Rio Tinto and gave them to BSG Resources, controlled by the Israeli businessman Beny Steinmetz. A Geneva court found in January 2021 that he had bribed Mamadie Touré, a wife of President Lansana Conté, to get the rights, and sentenced him to five years; Swiss appeal courts upheld the conviction in 2022 and 2023, and Steinmetz denies wrongdoing. The same family appears in the drug trade. Ousmane Conté, the president's son, was arrested in 2009 by the junta that took over after his father's death and confessed on state television to involvement in the cocaine trade, though whether freely is unclear; the US designated him a kingpin in 2010, but no court verdict followed. That is the pattern along the West African coast, where admissions and foreign designations exist and local judgments do not.

Turkey reached in through education: by June 2017 Gülen-movement schools in Guinea had been taken over by Turkey's state Maarif Foundation, as in Niger, Senegal, Chad and Somalia. Turkey treats the Gülen movement, a religious network that ran schools in many countries, as a terrorist group.

Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that President Alpha Condé oversaw the Grande Loge de Guinée, the national Masonic lodge. The Tony Blair Institute, which places advisers inside governments, is recorded as present.
Guinea.imp: The rights to Guinea's biggest mineral deposit were won by bribing the president's wife, and the case was judged in Switzerland, not at home. The president's son admitted cocaine trafficking on television and was never judged, so Guineans never learned how far the trade reached into the state. Watch who now holds the Simandou rights and on what terms, and whether drug cases reach Guinean courts.

Guinea-Bissau.d:
Guinea-Bissau is where the cocaine trade went furthest into an African state, and its military command still shows it. Since the mid-2000s the country has served as a transit point for South American cocaine heading to Europe, and UNODC, the UN drugs and crime office, warned it was at risk of becoming Africa's first narco-state.

In 2013 the whole senior military command stood accused in New York at once. Former navy chief José Américo Bubo Na Tchuto was arrested by the US Drug Enforcement Administration in a sting at sea and pleaded guilty to cocaine conspiracy. Army chief Antonio Indjai, who led the 2012 coup, was charged with offering to store cocaine for the FARC, a South American armed group, and to sell it weapons including surface-to-air missiles. Air force chief Ibraima Papa Camara was charged too. Indjai and Camara stayed in Bissau and were never handed over. Na Tchuto came home, and in February 2022 President Umaro Sissoco Embaló blamed him for a failed attack on the government palace.

The courts at home do not try these cases: the country had not tried a drug case since 2005. Of 980 kilograms of cocaine seized in November 2021, the head of the judicial police said in 2022 that 975 had disappeared from official custody, with police and security staff suspected; one officer was arrested. The killings of President Joao Bernardo Vieira and the army chief of staff within hours of each other in March 2009 were never prosecuted; UN bodies link them to the cocaine trade, but no court has.
Guinea-Bissau.imp: For people in Guinea-Bissau, the men commanding the army, navy and air force have been the ones accused of moving cocaine, so the armed forces cannot be relied on to stop it, and power has changed hands through coups and killings tied to the trade. Seized drugs vanish instead of becoming evidence, and no Bissau court has tried a drug case since 2005. Watch what happens to the next large seizure, and who holds the military command.

Kenya.d:
Kenya has one of the heaviest records on the map, with outside forces reaching its courts, police, elections, central bank and security services.

Drug money has reached the courts. Two brothers running a heroin organisation in Mombasa admitted in New York in 2018 that they had paid Kenyan judges, prosecutors and police for two years to block their extradition; none of those officials has been named or charged at home. Harun Mwau, an MP and assistant transport minister responsible for the Ports Authority, was designated a drug kingpin by the US in 2011; he denies it and was cleared by a police inquiry researchers called controversial.

Elections have been worked on from abroad. Cambridge Analytica, a British political-data firm, ran Uhuru Kenyatta's 2013 and 2017 campaigns, rebranding his party twice and writing its manifesto, by the firm's own account. In 2022 the Israeli hacking outfit Team Jorge got into the Telegram account of William Ruto's digital strategist.

Foreign governments use its security services. In 2021 Turkish intelligence seized Fethullah Gülen's nephew there, and in October 2024 Kenya handed four Gülen-linked refugees to Turkey at Ankara's request; the UN said it was deeply concerned. In 2013 a Kenyan court convicted two Iranians alleged to be Quds Force members over explosives.

Foreign firms and faith sit close to power. Ruto cancelled the Adani Group's airport and power deals in November 2024, a day after its directors were charged with bribery in New York. Patrick Njoroge, a celibate member of the Catholic group Opus Dei, governed the central bank from 2015 to 2023, and Ruto, an evangelical, plans an 8,000-seat church at State House.

Older still: the ICC charged Kenyatta with organising attacks by Mungiki, a banned extortion sect, in the 2007–08 violence that killed about 1,300; the charges were withdrawn in 2014 amid witness interference.
Kenya.imp: Kenyans cannot be sure that a judge or prosecutor in a drug case has not been paid, because the officials the Akasha brothers bribed are still unnamed and may still be serving. Refugees in Nairobi have been seized and sent to the government they fled. Voters have had campaigns shaped by foreign data firms they never chose. Watch whether the bribed officials are ever identified, whether refugee handovers continue, and how the State House church is paid for.

Lesotho.d: This is an estimate. Nothing is documented on the map for Lesotho, and the only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status. The conditions scores lean towards risk: a fairly high chance of powerful groups inside the state and weak checks. As a best guess, the most likely route in is the one seen most often in southern Africa on this map: foreign businesses paying officials for state contracts or licences, as in Malawi, where 16 police and army contracts worth over $150 million went to firms linked to one businessman, and Namibia, where ministers are charged over fishing quotas.
Lesotho.imp: No case recorded is not the same as no influence, especially where checks are weak. For people in Lesotho, the thing to watch is how large public contracts, particularly for the police and army, are awarded, and whether foreign courts or anti-corruption bodies ever name Lesotho officials, which is how most such cases in the region have come to light.

Liberia.d:
In Liberia the cocaine trade is reaching the police and the main airport, and Freemasonry was for a long time the ladder to power.

The present first. After the country's largest recorded seizure, close to four tonnes of cocaine bound for Europe, the police inspector general said in 2026 that senior government officials were involved in trafficking. The national police charged the head of its own Major Crimes Unit and another official, and named a deputy commander responsible for security at Roberts International Airport as an active participant; twelve suspects were charged in the seizure, and a former vice-president was separately indicted on trafficking counts. These are charges, not convictions. Liberia has also shown the opposite response. In Operation Relentless, from 2010, senior officials who were offered bribes by South American and West African traffickers for safe passage reported them and worked with the US Drug Enforcement Administration, leading to convictions in New York, cooperation the DEA called unprecedented.

The older history: membership of the Masonic Order of Liberia was widely seen as a requirement for leadership in the ruling True Whig Party, and by the 1970s most high officials were Masons. William Tolbert, president from 1971, was its Grand Master. He was killed in Samuel Doe's 1980 coup, along with much of the Masonic leadership. Doe banned the order, later lifted the ban, and was himself initiated in 1989.

The National Endowment for Democracy and the Tony Blair Institute, which places advisers inside governments, are recorded as present.
Liberia.imp: For Liberians, the 2026 charges mean the unit meant to investigate serious crime and the officer guarding the main airport are accused of working for traffickers, so the agencies that should stop the trade are part of it. The 2010 case shows officials can say no and see traffickers convicted. Watch whether the 2026 charges reach verdicts, and whether the former vice-president's case goes to trial.

Libya.d:
Libya has rival authorities in Tripoli and in the east, and outside forces reach into both, while the smuggling economy holds them together.

In the east, Khalifa Haftar's Libyan National Army has been backed by Russia. A 2020 UN report counted 800 to 1,200 Wagner fighters with it, plus Syrians Wagner recruited and flew in, and a Pentagon report named the United Arab Emirates as Wagner's main funder there. Since spring 2024 Russia's Africa Corps has been replacing Wagner, and Russia uses eastern bases as logistics hubs for its African operations. Erik Prince, founder of the US firm Blackwater, was found by a UN panel in 2021 to have broken the arms embargo with a 2019 plan to supply aircraft and men to Haftar; he denies it. In Tripoli, the Muslim Brotherhood's party, Justice and Construction, had five ministers until 2014, and its member Khalid al-Mishri chaired the High Council of State, the upper advisory body, from 2018 to 2023.

Both sides share the smuggling. Libya buys fuel at world prices and sells it at home for about 0.15 dinars a litre, against two or three on the black market, and the difference is made by selling it abroad. International Crisis Group's assessment is that the racket helps keep the peace between the rival elites, who both take a cut. UN rules let ships be stopped if the Libyan government flags a cargo, but no such signal has come in years. On the coast, the Zawiya coast guard commander Abd al-Rahman Milad is under UN sanctions for fuel smuggling and migrant trafficking; he was detained and released without conviction. The US sanctioned a vessel and a Malta company moving fuel and drugs from Zuwarah.
Libya.imp: For Libyans, the fuel they are meant to get cheaply is sold abroad by people tied to both governments, and the state that should stop it profits from it. Migrants at sea face a coast guard whose commanders are themselves accused of trafficking. Foreign fighters keep the east armed. Watch whether Russia's bases in the east grow, and whether any Libyan authority ever flags a smuggling cargo.

Madagascar.d:
In Madagascar the record shows a Russian network working on the country's elections. The Russian outlet Proekt and the BBC reported in 2019 that 15 to 20 Russian political strategists tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, the businessman behind the Wagner Group, worked in the 2018 presidential race and dealt with as many as eight candidates, including the winner, Andry Rajoelina. One candidate, André Mailhol, said they gave him €5,000 in cash; the former prime minister Omer Beriziky said he was promised $2 million. Rajoelina denied being Russia's candidate and the BBC found no evidence he took Russian money; Prigozhin's representatives denied any link.

In October 2019 Facebook removed fake accounts it traced to Prigozhin's companies that targeted Madagascar and seven other African countries, the Central African Republic, Mozambique, DR Congo, Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon, Sudan and Libya, and said they meddled in the Mozambique and Madagascar elections. In several of those countries the same Russian network went on to supply fighters and advisers to governments; in Madagascar the documented reach stops at the campaign. The Wagner Group itself is recorded as present, and the French Masonic bodies the Grand Orient de France and the Grande Loge Nationale Française are judged likely.

The conditions scores show a high chance of powerful groups inside the state and weak checks.
Madagascar.imp: Malagasy voters in 2018 were choosing among candidates some of whom, by their own account, took cash or promises from foreign strategists, and much of what they read online may have been written abroad. They had no way to know who was paid. Watch for foreign money and fake accounts in future elections, and for any security deal with Russia, which is how this started elsewhere.

Malawi.d:
In Malawi the documented outside force is a foreign businessman's hold on police and army supply contracts. Zuneth Sattar is a UK-based businessman. In June 2022 Malawi's Anti-Corruption Bureau reported that the police and the Malawi Defence Force gave 16 contracts worth more than $150 million between 2017 and 2021 to five companies linked to him. President Lazarus Chakwera said 84 people were named in the report and withdrew all delegated powers from Vice-President Saulos Chilima; the former police inspector general, George Kainja, and the lands minister, Kezzie Msukwa, were arrested. Chilima denied wrongdoing and died in a plane crash in June 2024. No convictions are recorded.

The case reached from the people who buy supplies for the security forces up to the vice-presidency, and it came to light through Malawi's own anti-corruption bureau rather than a foreign court, unlike most cases in this region. British American Tobacco is judged likely present; its leaked payments elsewhere in East and Central Africa targeted officials handling tobacco laws. Malawi's conditions scores are among the better ones in Africa on this map: a lower chance of powerful groups inside the state, though checks are only middling.
Malawi.imp: Malawians paid, through public money, for police and army supplies bought from one man's companies on contracts the anti-corruption bureau questioned, worth more than $150 million over four years. The case also showed that a national bureau can reach a vice-president. Watch whether the arrests lead to trials and verdicts, whether any of the 84 people named face charges, and how police and army contracts are awarded now.

Mali.d:
Mali's military government now depends on Russian forces, and the record shows how the arrangement was built and what it brings.

In July 2023, a month after Mali's government asked UN peacekeepers to leave, the US Treasury sanctioned defence minister Sadio Camara, saying he organised the Wagner Group's deployment through trips to Russia in 2021, along with the air force chief and his deputy. In June 2025 Wagner announced it was leaving; Africa Corps, the Russian defence ministry unit that took over most of Wagner's African work, stayed on as the only Russian force, with about 2,000 troops, and several Wagner commanders moved across. Human Rights Watch and Le Monde have reported killings of civilians by Malian soldiers and Africa Corps members in 2025–26.

Under all of this runs the drug trade. Cocaine seizures across Mali, Burkina Faso, Chad, Mauritania and Niger rose from an average of 13 kilograms a year in 2015–2020 to 1,466 kilograms in 2022, and the UN found the proceeds moving into gold and property, naming armed groups in Mali among those who benefit. No prosecution has followed in any of the five states. The pattern is old: in 2009 a Boeing 727 that had flown from Venezuela was unloaded at a desert strip at Tarkint and burned, UN investigators pointed to protection by local officials and armed groups, and no senior conviction followed.

Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that President Amadou Toumani Touré, removed in that year's coup, oversaw the Grande Loge du Mali, the national Masonic lodge.
Mali.imp: Malians live with an army fighting alongside foreign troops accused of killing civilians, under a military government. Drug money flows into the gold and property markets and pays armed groups, and no case reaches court. Watch the reports of civilian deaths, what Russia is paid for its troops and in what form, and whether any trafficking case is ever prosecuted in Bamako.

Mauritania.d: This is an estimate. Nothing is documented on the map for Mauritania. Several organisations are recorded as present: the Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status; the Gülen movement, a religious network Turkey pursues abroad; the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist movement; and a group called Fight Impunity. The conditions scores lean high: a fairly strong chance of powerful groups inside the state and weak checks. As a best guess, the most likely route in is drug money. UN figures show Mauritania alone seized 2.3 tonnes of cocaine by mid-2023, and across the Sahel the proceeds are moving into gold and property, with no prosecution in any of the five states the UN studied.
Mauritania.imp: No case is recorded, but large cocaine seizures and weak checks make it likely that drug money is reaching officials or businesses somewhere. For people in Mauritania, watch whether seized drugs reach court and who is buying gold and property with unexplained money. Seizures that disappear from custody, as has happened in Guinea-Bissau, would be an early warning sign that officials have been reached.

Mauritius.d:
In Mauritius the documented outside force is a foreign contractor paying its way into a state power project. Burmeister & Wain Scandinavian Contractor, a Danish power-plant builder, was debarred by the African Development Bank in June 2020 for 21 months after the bank found, 'on the balance of probabilities', that it had paid members of the Mauritian administration through intermediaries during tenders for the Saint-Louis power station of the Central Electricity Board, the state utility. That is a lender's sanction rather than a court verdict, and no Mauritian official is named in the record.

It is the same route seen across Africa on this map, where foreign builders and traders pay officials for public contracts, as Ericsson did with Djibouti Telecom and Trafigura with Angola's state oil company.

The Grand Orient de France, France's largest Masonic body, is recorded as present; the Grande Loge Nationale Française, the Hindu nationalist RSS and Airbus are judged likely. Mauritius has among the better conditions scores in Africa on this map: a moderate chance of powerful groups inside the state and fairly strong checks on power.
Mauritius.imp: If officials were paid during the tender, Mauritians may be paying for electricity from a power station whose builder was chosen by bribery rather than price. The only penalty recorded came from a foreign lender, not a Mauritian court. Watch whether any official involved in the Saint-Louis tender is named or charged, and how the Central Electricity Board awards its next contracts.

Morocco.d:
Morocco appears on this map both as a country whose own politics has been reached by organised crime and as an outside force reaching into others.

The crime case is current. In June 2026 a Casablanca court sentenced 29 people after a two-year trial in the 'Escobar of the Sahara' case, among them a former regional council president, who got 12 years, and two former MPs from the governing party, who got 10 each. It began when a jailed Malian trafficker testified that his Moroccan political associates had seized his assets after his 2019 arrest, and it covered tonnes of cannabis resin moved across North Africa alongside Latin American cocaine. One defendant was acquitted and appeals are open.

Morocco also reaches outward. The 2021 Pegasus Project reported that it selected more than 6,000 Algerian phones, including politicians and senior officers, and President Macron and 14 French ministers, as targets for spyware made by the Israeli firm NSO Group; Morocco denies using it. In 1976 its foreign intelligence chief, Ahmed Dlimi, signed the charter of the Safari Club, a secret pact of five spy services, and in 1977 France airlifted Moroccan troops into Zaire to defend Mobutu.

At home, religion and government meet at the top. Ahmed Toufiq, minister over the country's mosques since 2002 under five prime ministers, follows the Boutchichiya, Morocco's largest Sufi order. The PJD, an Islamist party historically linked to the Muslim Brotherhood but never a branch of it, led the government from 2011 until its heavy defeat in 2021. Morocco closed Gülen-linked schools in 2017.
Morocco.imp: The Escobar trial shows Moroccans that lawmakers from the governing party and a regional council head were part of a trafficking network, and also that the courts convicted them. If the Pegasus reporting is right, Morocco's intelligence services spied on foreign leaders, which helped push Algeria to a diplomatic break and keeps the border region tense. Watch the appeals, and whether other councils and parliament seats tied to the trade are investigated.

Mozambique.d:
In Mozambique outside money reached the finance ministry, and a drug corridor has run alongside the ruling party for decades.

The 'tuna bonds' are the largest case. In 2013–14 three state companies borrowed $622 million from Credit Suisse and $535 million from Russia's VTB bank, under state guarantees never shown to parliament or the IMF, for tuna fishing and maritime security projects with Privinvest, an Emirati-Lebanese shipbuilder. The US said at least $200 million went in bribes and kickbacks to bankers and officials. When $2.2 billion of hidden loans came out in 2016 the IMF and World Bank froze support, and one study estimated two million people were pushed into poverty. A Brooklyn jury convicted former finance minister Manuel Chang in 2024; prosecutors said Privinvest paid him $7 million. Credit Suisse pleaded guilty in the US in 2021 and forgave $200 million of the debt, and London's High Court let Mozambique recover over $825 million from the estate of Privinvest's owner.

The drug route is older and still unpunished. Researchers documented a heroin trafficking system running for three decades with 'tight integration' between ruling party figures and traffickers, and near-zero heroin seizures as the evidence. Relatives of its main named figure were arrested in Portugal and Eswatini and one was shot dead in Maputo in 2012; none was charged in Mozambique. In 2010 the US designated a prominent Maputo businessman with reported ruling-party links as a drug kingpin, with his conglomerate and a shopping centre in the capital; banks closed their branches in his mall within a month, but he was never prosecuted.

Facebook in 2019 removed fake accounts run by Prigozhin's Russian network that meddled in Mozambique's election that October. Odebrecht, the Brazilian builder, is also present.
Mozambique.imp: Mozambicans carried the cost of loans they never approved: when the hidden debt surfaced, foreign support froze and an estimated two million people fell into poverty. The heroin corridor means figures in the ruling party are tied to the trade, so seizures stay near zero and nobody is charged at home. Watch how the money recovered from Privinvest and Credit Suisse is used, and whether any trafficking case ever reaches a Mozambican court.

Namibia.d:
In Namibia the documented outside force is a foreign fishing company buying access to the country's fish through people close to its ministers. In November 2019 WikiLeaks published the 'Fishrot Files', investigated by Icelandic, Al Jazeera and Namibian journalists, along with testimony from Jóhannes Stefánsson, former Namibia manager of Samherji, one of Iceland's largest fishing companies. They showed Samherji paying people close to Namibia's government to obtain quotas for horse mackerel.

Fisheries Minister Bernhardt Esau and Justice Minister Sacky Shanghala resigned the next day and were later arrested. With four associates, the 'Fishrot Six' are charged with racketeering, corruption and money laundering under the Prevention of Organised Crime Act. Iceland opened its own investigation into Samherji. Samherji denies paying bribes and blames Stefánsson, and the case is still before the Namibian courts, so nothing is proven yet. The case reaches both the minister who handed out the quota and the minister in charge of the justice system, which is part of why it has moved slowly.

The Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret society from South Africa's apartheid era, is judged likely present but nothing is documented, and the Mwalimu Julius Nyerere Leadership School is recorded as present. Namibia's conditions scores are moderate.
Namibia.imp: Fish in Namibian waters belong to the public, and the quotas are meant to earn money for the state and work for Namibians. If the charges are proven, quotas were handed out in return for payments to people around ministers, and the public got less for its fish. The trial has taken years. Watch for verdicts in the Fishrot case and for how fishing quotas are allocated now.

Niger.d:
Niger's military government has turned from the West to Russia, and the country sits on the cocaine route across the Sahel.

After the July 2023 coup the junta ended military cooperation with the US and France. Dozens of troops from Africa Corps, the Russian defence ministry unit that took over most of the Wagner Group's African work, arrived in Niamey in April 2024 and were stationed at Air Base 101 before US forces had left it. Estimates for 2025 put them at 200 to 300, mostly in intelligence, training and surveillance, and they are reported to have fought during a January 2026 attack on Niamey airport. Niger joins Mali, Burkina Faso and the Central African Republic in this arrangement.

The drug trade reaches local office. UNODC calls the Sahel a natural stopover between South America and Europe, and cocaine seizures across Niger and four neighbours rose to 1,466 kilograms in 2022 from an average of 13 a year in 2015–2020, with no prosecution in any of them. A local mayor was arrested with more than 200 kilograms of cocaine in his vehicle; no outcome is on record, and reporting on the trade carries physical risk to journalists.

Turkey reached in through the schools: by June 2017 Gülen-movement schools had been handed to its state Maarif Foundation. Mamadou Tandja, president from 1999 to 2010, was named as a Freemason in 2009 reporting; no lodge is named. The Archimedes Group, an Israeli political consulting firm Facebook removed for election meddling in Africa, is recorded as present.
Niger.imp: People in Niger now rely for security on a foreign force whose terms are not public, under a government that came to power by coup. Local officials on the trafficking route can be bought, as the mayor's arrest shows, and with no prosecutions across the region traffickers face little risk. Families lost the Gülen schools to a foreign government's foundation. Watch the Russian presence in Niamey, and whether drug seizures lead to trials.

Nigeria.d:
Nigeria has one of the fullest records on the map, and the outside forces in it are mostly oil companies, election-for-hire firms and secret fraternities.

Oil is where foreign money meets the state. A 2009 US diplomatic cable records a Shell executive telling the US ambassador that Shell had 'seconded people to all the relevant ministries' and knew what was done in them; Shell rejected the claim. Glencore, the Swiss commodity trader, admitted in Britain in 2022 to bribes in Nigeria's oil trade. In the OPL 245 case, Eni and Shell paid $1.1 billion in 2011 for an offshore block and the money went on to a company controlled by a former oil minister; a Milan court acquitted everyone in 2021. In 2023 a London court threw out an $11 billion award won by the firm P&ID, finding it had bribed a Nigerian government lawyer.

Elections have been worked on from outside and below. Cambridge Analytica and Israel's Team Jorge worked in 2015 to re-elect Goodluck Jonathan by discrediting Muhammadu Buhari, and Facebook in 2019 removed networks of the Israeli Archimedes Group aimed at Nigeria's election. A BBC investigation in 2021 found leaked papers suggesting 35 million naira went to a group it linked to Black Axe, a confraternity police abroad treat as organised crime, to 'protect votes' in Edo state, rewarded with 80 government roles; the group denies the link.

Drugs reach the police: Abba Kyari, who led the police Intelligence Response Team, is on trial accused of substituting seized cocaine. The constitution bars secret-society members from elected office. Lawful routes to the top run through the churches and the World Bank: a senior Redeemed Christian Church pastor was vice-president from 2015 to 2023, and a World Bank managing director became finance minister.
Nigeria.imp: For Nigerians, the oil deals that fund the state have repeatedly been struck with bribes or under suspicion of them, and courts abroad, not at home, have done most of the judging. Voters have faced foreign firms running smear campaigns and, according to the BBC, confraternity members paid to 'protect votes' and given state jobs. Watch the Kyari cocaine trial, and whether the constitutional bar on secret-society members is ever enforced.

Rwanda.d:
Rwanda appears on this map mostly as an outside force reaching into its neighbour, and more lightly as a place where outside advisers sit inside its own government.

In eastern Congo, the UN Group of Experts reported in June 2025 that the armed group M23 operates under Rwandan command and that Rwanda's army backed its capture of Goma; officials said President Kagame took the decision to take Goma and Bukavu. It found Rwandans placed over mining, tax, banking and border control in North and South Kivu. Rwanda denies directing M23.

At home, the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, a London non-profit that places advisers inside governments in more than 45 countries, has supported a Strategy and Policy Unit and a Government Action Coordination Unit and worked on Imihigo, the system of performance contracts for officials. Its largest donor is Larry Ellison's foundation, which gave over £52 million in 2023. The units sit inside the government's own offices, which puts a body funded largely by one private donor abroad close to how policy is made and checked.

British American Tobacco's leaked records name payments to Rwandan officials meant to frustrate tobacco laws, reported in 2015; BAT denies it and Britain's investigation closed in 2021 without charges. NSO Group, the Israeli spyware maker, and Opus Dei are recorded as present, and the World Economic Forum is judged likely.
Rwanda.imp: Inside Rwanda, the Blair Institute's units help shape how officials are measured and how the government's programme is delivered, with money that comes largely from one private donor abroad, and Rwandans have little say over that arrangement. If the BAT payments worked, tobacco rules were weakened. Watch how Rwanda's role in the Kivu provinces develops, and whether its tobacco law matches the WHO treaty.

Sao Tome and Principe.d: This is an estimate. Nothing is documented on the map for São Tomé and Príncipe, and the only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status. The conditions scores are among the better ones in Africa on this map: a low chance of powerful groups inside the state and middling checks. As a best guess, a small island state is most exposed by sea: through the cocaine route from South America that runs through West African ports, as in Guinea-Bissau, and through foreign firms seeking fishing or other rights, as in Namibia's quota case.
Sao Tome and Principe.imp: An empty record here fits the lower risk scores, but it can also mean no one has looked. For people on the islands, the thing to watch is how fishing and other licences are handed to foreign firms, and whether drug seizures in the region begin to name São Tomé ports, ships or officials, which is how the trade has first shown itself on the mainland coast.

Senegal.d:
In Senegal the strongest force near the state is a religious brotherhood with deep roots at home, and the record also shows Turkey and the drug trade reaching in.

The Mourides are a Sufi brotherhood with millions of followers and its own holy city, Touba, which has run with wide autonomy since 1928, and Senegal's presidents have long courted its leader, the caliph. Abdoulaye Wade went to Touba the day after his 2000 election and put Mourides in his government. President Bassirou Diomaye Faye, sworn in in April 2024, called on the caliph, Serigne Mountakha Mbacké, within two weeks, again in August 2024 and March 2025, and before the Grand Magal pilgrimage in August 2025, pledging state help with Touba's water and sanitation. That is lawful and public.

Turkey reached in through education: in 2017 the government closed more than a dozen Gülen-linked schools, attended by about 3,000 children, at Turkish request, and Turkey's state Maarif Foundation opened three schools that November. In 2020 President Macky Sall, while in office, accepted the Sunhak Peace Prize, a $1 million award funded by the Unification Church. The drug trade has touched parliament once: in 2019 a governing-coalition deputy was arrested in a cocaine operation, his immunity was lifted, and the case went no further. Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that Wade had been initiated into Freemasonry. Rosewood from Senegal's Casamance region, where logging funds armed groups, was exported through The Gambia.
Senegal.imp: Most of this happens in public, and Senegal's checks on power are among the stronger in Africa on this map. Presidents' visits bring state money for Touba, and the caliph's favour carries weight in politics that no election measures. About 3,000 children saw their schools closed at a foreign government's request. Watch drug cases on the coast and whether the 2019 legislator case is ever reopened.

Seychelles.d:
In the Seychelles the documented outside force works through the offshore registry, used by firms that serve customers elsewhere. KuCoin, a cryptocurrency exchange run by PEKEN Global Limited, was registered in the Seychelles while serving customers in countries where it had no licence. In 2025 it was penalised $297 million in the United States for failing to run effective anti-money-laundering checks and to report suspicious transactions, and its executives were separately indicted in the US over the Bank Secrecy Act and unlicensed money transmission. The penalty came from the United States, not the Seychelles.

The case fits a wider pattern on this map in which small states sell registrations or citizenship and the risk lands elsewhere, as when the Comoros sold passports in bulk to stateless people in the Gulf. The only organisation recorded as present is the Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status. The conditions scores are among the better ones in Africa on this map, with fairly strong checks at home; the weak point is what the country lets foreign firms do from its registry.
Seychelles.imp: Most of the harm here falls outside the islands, on people whose money passed through an exchange that did not check it. For Seychellois, a registry used this way can draw foreign penalties and pressure onto the whole financial sector. Watch whether the Seychelles tightens its rules for crypto and other firms registered there but doing business abroad, and whether its own regulators, rather than American ones, act first next time.

Sierra Leone.d:
In Sierra Leone the cocaine trade has reached close to the presidential family, according to Reuters. Jos Leijdekkers, a Dutchman on the Dutch and EU most-wanted lists, was sentenced in absentia in Rotterdam in June 2024 to 24 years for smuggling more than 7 tonnes of cocaine. Reuters reported in January 2025, using facial recognition and video, that he attended a New Year mass two rows behind President Julius Maada Bio in Bio's home town, that sources said he is married to the president's daughter Agnes, and that he has 'high-level protection'. Dutch prosecutors said he had lived in Sierra Leone for at least six months. The government said it was investigating and that the President did not know him, and dismissed the immigration chief after footage showed him with Leijdekkers. None of this is a court finding.

The older case shows the trade reaching the airport and the cabinet. In July 2008 a plane carrying around 700 kilograms of cocaine landed at Lungi airport marked with Red Cross insignia. Airport and security staff were convicted with the foreign crew in 2009, which US congressional testimony called historic for the region, and the transport and aviation minister was dismissed after the proceedings indicated he had given the plane landing clearance; that allegation was never tried.

The Tony Blair Institute, which places advisers inside governments, is recorded as present, and the United Grand Lodge of England is judged likely.
Sierra Leone.imp: If Reuters is right, a man Dutch courts sentenced for trafficking tonnes of cocaine is living under protection in Sierra Leone, and officials who should hand him over may be shielding him. The immigration chief's dismissal shows how close the case runs to the border service. Watch whether Leijdekkers is extradited to the Netherlands, what the government's investigation finds, and whether anyone who helped him settle is named.

Somalia.d:
Somalia's documented case is Turkey reaching into its schools, and the wider record shows several outside forces present in a state with little ability to see them. Turkey treats the Gülen movement, a religious network that ran schools in many countries, as a terrorist group and blames it for the 2016 coup attempt in Turkey. By June 2017 the movement's schools in Somalia had been taken over by Turkey's state Maarif Foundation after talks through Turkey's Foreign Ministry, the same handover made that year in Guinea, Niger, Chad and Senegal, and a pursuit that reached as far as Kenya, where Turkish intelligence seized Gülen's nephew in 2021. The handover is confirmed by Turkish government and Maarif statements.

Other organisations are recorded as present without a documented case: the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist movement; the Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status; and the security companies of Erik Prince, founder of the US firm Blackwater, whose men and plans have reached Libya and Congo.
