Somalia's conditions scores are among the worst on the map: a high chance of powerful groups sitting inside the state and very weak checks, so the single case here is likely a small part of what goes on.
Somalia.imp: A foreign government decided who would run schools Somali children attended, with the decision made in Ankara. With very weak checks, other outside forces, from foreign security firms to political movements, could be present without being recorded. Watch what role foreign security firms and governments take in Somalia's security forces, and whether any of their contracts or agreements are made public.

South Africa.d:
In South Africa the trouble now sits inside the police. In July 2025 KwaZulu-Natal's police commissioner, Lt Gen Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi, accused senior officials, Police Minister Senzo Mchunu among them, of colluding with a criminal syndicate. Mchunu was put on leave, the Madlanga Commission is hearing evidence, and by July 2026 thirteen police officers, including National Commissioner Fannie Masemola, faced criminal charges; a R228 million police health contract given to businessman Vusimuzi 'Cat' Matlala's company is at the centre. These are charges; Mchunu denies wrongdoing. Earlier, police chief Jackie Selebi, also president of Interpol, was convicted in 2010 over a drug trafficker's payments, and a colonel sold about two thousand police guns to Cape Flats gangs. On building sites from Durban to Gauteng and the Cape, 'business forums', the 'construction mafia', demand 30% of contracts and press ward councillors with bribes or threats; extortion costs near R49 billion a year, the Institute for Security Studies estimates.

The state companies and tax service carry the second story, proven mostly by inquiry and admission. Under President Jacob Zuma, the Zondo Commission found in 2022, ministers and the heads of Eskom (power) and Transnet (rail and ports) acted corruptly for the Gupta family, businessmen close to him; the Guptas deny it and the UAE refused to extradite them. Foreign firms worked the same offices: McKinsey, SAP and ABB admitted bribing officials at Eskom, Transnet, Johannesburg, Tshwane and the water department, and Zondo found the US consultancy Bain helped take over the tax service, SARS, which Bain denies doing wilfully. Thales, the French arms firm, and Zuma still await trial over the 1999 arms deal.

Behind this lies the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret men's society whose members held every premiership and presidency from 1948 to 1994 and, in 1979, all but two cabinet seats.
South Africa.imp: The offices reached are the ones people deal with every day: police stations, the tax service, the power company, the rail and port company and city councils. Bribes for consulting and engineering work at Eskom came out of the money of the company that keeps the lights on, and extortion on building sites makes housing and roads cost more and arrive later. Most of the proof came from inquiries and settlements in US courts, and few people have been convicted at home. Watch the Madlanga Commission, the police charges and the Thales–Zuma trial.

South Sudan.d:
In South Sudan, two outside hands reach into the president's own circle. The first is a neighbour's army. In March 2025, as President Salva Kiir's government detained ministers allied with First Vice President Riek Machar, Uganda sent special forces into Juba, the capital. Uganda's army chief, Muhoozi Kainerugaba, said his army 'recognises only Salva Kiir' and that any move against him was a declaration of war against Uganda. Uganda's parliament later approved the deployment, while South Sudan at first denied the troops were there. So the contest for power in Juba is now weighed partly by soldiers who answer to Kampala.

The second is money close to the presidency. Benjamin Bol Mel, a businessman near Kiir, has been under US anti-corruption sanctions since December 2017. In February 2025 Kiir made him one of the country's vice presidents and deputy secretary general of the ruling party, the SPLM; a decree removed him from both posts in November 2025. He went up and came down within nine months, by presidential decree each time.

The record is short, but South Sudan's conditions scores are among the harshest on the map: very high for outside actors embedded in the state, very low for the checks that would catch them, so these two cases are likely only part of what is happening. Glencore, the Atlas Network and the Order of Malta are recorded as present without a case. South Sudan sits in the patterns on governments reaching into other countries and on exposure, purge and reversal.
South Sudan.imp: For people in South Sudan, a foreign army now stands openly behind one side of a quarrel inside their government, which makes it harder to settle that quarrel by politics or in the courts. Senior posts can be handed to a man the US accuses of corruption and taken back by decree, with no public account of why. With few working checks in the state, decisions about security and senior jobs stay inside a small circle. Watch whether Ugandan troops stay and who is appointed to the vice presidencies next.

Sudan.d:
Sudan is at war, and outside powers are supplying both sides. The Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary that grew out of militias of the old ruler Omar al-Bashir, have fought the army since April 2023. For the RSF, UN monitors found 'credible' evidence, in a report leaked in January 2024, that the United Arab Emirates flew in weapons 'several times per week' through Amdjarass in northern Chad; the UAE says its 122 flights carried aid, and the International Court of Justice threw out Sudan's case against it in 2025 for lack of jurisdiction without ruling on the facts. Beside the army fights the al-Baraa bin Malik Brigade, an Islamist militia of up to 20,000 fighters; in September 2025 the US sanctioned it and Finance Minister Gebreil Ibrahim, saying the brigade gets training and weapons from Iran's Revolutionary Guards. Captagon pills are reported made in Khartoum, Blue Nile and Jabal Awliya and moved out through Kassala and the Red Sea ports, with the RSF and Darfur rebels implicated; no court has ruled.

Who holds the ministries goes back to 1989, when Bashir took power in a coup organised with Hassan al-Turabi's National Islamic Front, a movement that grew from the Muslim Brotherhood; Bashir admitted his role at trial in 2020. After 2019 a committee dismissed judges and prosecutors placed in their jobs under it, and a court ordered some back in 2021. The movement's leader, former foreign minister Ali Karti, is under US, Canadian and EU sanctions for blocking civilian rule. Russia came in through gold: Wagner arrived in 2017, and in 2020 the US sanctioned the Prigozhin-linked gold firm Meroe Gold for helping the effort to crush the 2018–19 protests. In 2017 Sudan also handed Gülen-movement schools to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation.
Sudan.imp: For people in Sudan, the war keeps going partly because foreign suppliers keep both sides armed, and a militia tied by US findings to Iran fights beside the army. The finance ministry, and so the public budget, is run by a man the US has sanctioned and ties to Turabi's Islamist movement. Gold and Captagon give armed groups income that no budget records. Watch new UN findings on arms routes, who holds the finance and security posts, and whether any court tests the Captagon reports.

Tanzania.d:
Tanzania is where the Chinese Communist Party now teaches the ruling parties of six southern African countries. The Mwalimu Julius Nyerere Leadership School in Kibaha took its first class in February 2022. It was built with a $40 million grant from the CCP's Central Party School, and CCP theoreticians teach there. The school belongs jointly to the CCP and six ruling parties: Tanzania's CCM, South Africa's ANC, Angola's MPLA, Mozambique's FRELIMO, Namibia's SWAPO and Zimbabwe's ZANU-PF. The ANC says more than 1,400 people have been through it, and its secretary-general led a delegation to the school's annual meeting in January 2024. A party school is lawful; what the record shows is a foreign ruling party teaching the cadres who go on to staff six governments, on Tanzanian soil.

The other strand is drugs, and the record on it is thin. In 2017 the president read out a public list of alleged drug traffickers, including a regional commissioner, and ordered arrests. Most of those detained were released and few prosecutions finished, so the list stands as a head of state's assertion, not a set of findings. In June 2025 the Financial Action Task Force, the global anti-money-laundering body, took Tanzania off its list of countries under increased monitoring.

Opus Dei and the Gülen movement are recorded as present without a case; BAE Systems and British American Tobacco are likely but undocumented. Tanzania sits in the pattern on organised crime inside the state, as a suspected case.
Tanzania.imp: For Tanzanians, the ruling party's coming officials are partly trained by a foreign party, at a school in their own country paid for by Beijing, with no public account of what is taught. On drugs, naming officials in public without trials left accusations nobody tested: those named could not clear themselves, and anyone guilty was not convicted. Watch who passes through the Kibaha school into government posts, and whether drug cases now reach court rather than a podium.

Togo.d:
In Togo a Russian force is settling into the country's port and army bases. Africa Corps is the force run by Russia's defence ministry that replaced the Wagner group in Africa. In November 2025 President Faure Gnassingbé and Vladimir Putin signed a defence agreement covering intelligence sharing, arms sales, joint exercises and Russian ships docking at Lomé, Togo's port. The Critical Threats project of the American Enterprise Institute reports that Africa Corps officers arrived in January 2026 and that by mid-2026 about 300–350 soldiers were in Lomé and at bases in the north. It also reports that on 9 July 2026 the sanctioned Russian ship Mikhail Britnev unloaded vehicles at Lomé bound for Africa Corps in Mali. These figures come from that project and have not been confirmed by Togo's government.

What Russia gets is a coastal port on the route to its forces inland in Mali, and a share of what Togo's own security services collect. What the government gets is not set out in the record. Three opposition parties have asked for a public debate on foreign troops, which has not happened.

The spyware firm NSO Group and the Archimedes Group are also recorded as present, and French Masonic lodges, the Grand Orient de France and the GLNF, are likely but undocumented. The conditions score is high for outside actors embedded in the state. Togo sits in the pattern on Russia's networks in Europe and Africa, as a target country.
Togo.imp: For people in Togo, a foreign army is settling into their port and bases under an agreement that neither parliament nor the public has debated. Intelligence sharing means a foreign government may see what Togo's own security services gather, including about Togolese citizens. Because Lomé now supplies Russian forces in Mali, Togo can be pulled into conflicts beyond its borders. Watch the opposition's call for a debate, the size of the deployment, and what else is unloaded at the port.

Tunisia.d:
In Tunisia the leaders of the party that won the first post-2011 election are now in prison, convicted of plotting against the state. Ennahda grew out of the Muslim Brotherhood tradition, the Islamist political movement, though it says it has no organisational link to the Egyptian Brotherhood. Its leader, Rached Ghannouchi, who was speaker of parliament from 2019 to 2021, has been jailed since April 2023. In February 2025 a court gave him a further 22 years for 'plotting against state security' in the Instalingo case, and in July 2025 another 14. In the same case the former foreign minister Rafik Abdessalem, his son-in-law, got 34 years, and the former prime minister Hichem Mechichi 35 years in absentia. Ennahda calls the case political. So the record here runs in two directions: a movement that reached government, and a state now using its courts against that movement's leadership.

The first half is the background. Ennahda won the October 2011 election for the assembly writing a new constitution and led the government until January 2014, with Hamadi Jebali and then Ali Laarayedh as prime minister and Abdessalem at the foreign ministry. Winning an election is lawful, and the map rates this case as 'possible', not proven infiltration.

The Trilateral Commission, Hizb ut-Tahrir and the Archimedes Group are recorded as present without a case. Tunisia sits in the pattern on movements that sought the state itself.
Tunisia.imp: For Tunisians, the leaders of the party they elected in 2011 are serving sentences of decades on plot charges, so whether the case is security or punishment of the opposition is the question in front of the courts. A former prime minister sentenced in absentia to 35 years cannot be judged by voters or in an open trial he attends. What evidence the Instalingo case rested on is not easy for ordinary people to see. Watch the appeals and whether other parties' leaders face similar charges.

Uganda.d:
In Uganda, outside groups reach the parliament that writes laws on sexuality and the police unit that watches the opposition. The first runs through two American Christian networks. The Fellowship, also called The Family, is a US network that runs prayer breakfasts for politicians. David Bahati chairs Uganda's National Prayer Breakfast, and journalist Jeff Sharlet reported that Bahati first floated his 2009 bill proposing the death penalty for homosexuality at the 2008 breakfast; Bahati has been a state minister since 2021 and was re-appointed in 2026. Family Watch International, an Arizona lobbying group with UN consultative status, was named by a Ugandan activist as lobbying for the 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act, which carries life imprisonment and in some cases death; the group once called its stance on the 2009 bill 'complicated'. Both links are reported, not proven, and holding Christian views is not wrongdoing. The World Bank stopped new lending to Uganda in August 2023 over the law.

The second is surveillance. In 2019 the Wall Street Journal reported that technicians from Huawei, China's largest telecoms equipment maker, working inside Uganda's police headquarters, helped the cyber unit get into the encrypted messages of opposition MP Bobi Wine. The Journal found no sign that Huawei in China or the Chinese state directed it, and Huawei denies it. The spyware firm NSO Group is also recorded as present.

In March 2025 Uganda itself reached outward, sending special forces into Juba to protect South Sudan's President Kiir. It sits in the patterns on churches placing members in the state and China's long arm abroad.
Uganda.imp: For gay Ugandans, the 2023 law means a possible life sentence, and in some cases death, under a law foreign lobbyists are reported to have pushed. The World Bank's halt on new loans means less outside money for public works that every Ugandan uses. If police can read opposition MPs' encrypted messages with foreign technical help, anyone who organises or campaigns against the government does so without knowing who is reading. Watch who leads the prayer breakfast and who supplies the police's surveillance tools.

Zambia.d:
Zambia's one documented case is about a church given a ministry of its own, and it was done in the open. The 1996 constitution declares Zambia a Christian nation. In September 2016 President Edgar Lungu turned a religious-affairs desk into a full Ministry of National Guidance and Religious Affairs and handed it to Rev. Godfridah Sumaili, a cleric he had appointed to parliament as a nominated MP rather than an elected one. She ran it until August 2021. After that year's election President Hakainde Hichilema folded the ministry into a department of the Vice-President's office, where it remains.

The rest of the record is presence without a documented case, and it points at two kinds of outside reach. One is technology and campaigning: Huawei is recorded here, and the 2019 Wall Street Journal report on Huawei technicians inside Uganda's police also said Huawei staff helped Zambia's government with domestic spying, which Huawei denied; SCL Group / Cambridge Analytica is recorded too. The other is churches: Pentecostal networks and the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God, a Brazilian church whose bishops hold office in Brazil. English Freemasonry, the collapsed bank BCCI and British American Tobacco are likely but undocumented. Zambia sits in the pattern on churches and movements placing members in the state.
Zambia.imp: For Zambians, religious leaders can be brought straight into cabinet by appointment, without facing voters, and a later government can take the post away again. The religious-affairs department still sits inside the Vice-President's office. The bigger unknown is the undocumented part: if foreign technicians help the government watch its own people, as was reported, critics and opposition organisers are exposed in ways they cannot check. Watch who advises the government on elections and who supplies its surveillance equipment.

Zimbabwe.d:
In Zimbabwe the line between state contracts and private fortune runs through the cabinet itself. Kudakwashe (Kuda) Tagwirei founded Sakunda Holdings, which grew through fuel trading with the commodity trader Trafigura and a $3 billion state farming contract, 'Command Agriculture', paid in Treasury bills from 2017 to 2019. The US sanctioned him in 2020, accusing him of misappropriating public funds and supporting senior officials; the UK followed in 2021 and the US extended the sanctions in 2024. In October 2025 he was co-opted onto the ruling ZANU-PF's Central Committee, and in October 2026 President Mnangagwa made him Minister of Economic Development and Investment Promotion. He denies the allegations.

Gold is the second channel. In 2023 Al Jazeera's undercover Gold Mafia investigation recorded intermediaries, one of them an ambassador-at-large, offering to wash cash through the state gold refinery and export it as bullion with an invoice. The government set up a commission, and the practice continued. This is reported, not proven in court.

Foreign parties reach in more lightly. In 2018 about 40 'election observers' from a body called AFRIC watched Zimbabwe's vote; investigative journalists later found AFRIC was organised by people linked to Yevgeny Prigozhin, the founder of Russia's Wagner group. ZANU-PF is also one of the six ruling parties behind the Chinese Communist Party's leadership school in Tanzania. English Freemasonry, BCCI and the Rhodes Trust are likely but undocumented. Zimbabwe sits in the patterns on criminal money in firms, spyware and elections for hire, and Russia's networks in Africa.
Zimbabwe.imp: For Zimbabweans, a man foreign governments accuse of taking public money now helps decide where investment and state deals go. If cash can be washed through the state refinery, the country's main export earns less for the public and more for whoever controls the trade. Election observers who are not what they claim make it harder for voters to know whether a count was fair. Watch which contracts Tagwirei's ministry awards and whether the gold commission's findings lead to charges.

Afghanistan.d:
Afghanistan is ruled by the Taliban, and the people running its police and security are, according to US and UN findings, tied to a neighbouring spy service and to armed groups abroad. The Haqqani network, a militant group within the Taliban that the US listed as terrorist in 2012, controls security in Kabul, and its leader Sirajuddin Haqqani is interior minister. In 2011 the top US military officer told the Senate the network acted as 'a veritable arm' of Pakistan's spy agency, the ISI; Pakistan denies it. UN sanctions monitors, who report each year, assessed in 2023 that at least three key Taliban government leaders are affiliated with al-Qaeda, and in December 2025 that al-Qaeda keeps close ties and a presence in several provinces, while the Pakistani Taliban (TTP), about 6,000 fighters, has strong support from elements inside the government. The Taliban reject the reports. The Taliban's shadow foreign minister in 2017 was a man the US had designated for drug trafficking in 2012, and who sits on a UN terrorism sanctions list too.

Under the US-backed republic before 2021 the inside hand was money. Kabul Bank, the largest private bank, paid the salaries of soldiers, police and civil servants; an anti-corruption committee found about $935 million taken, most loans going to 19 people and companies, among the shareholders the brothers of President Hamid Karzai and of the first vice-president, neither charged. The chairman and chief executive were jailed and the bailout cost over 5% of the economy. Across the provinces, US and UN assessments described officials and police commanders taxing and protecting opium, and very little of it reached a court. The opium money moved through hawala brokers in Kandahar, who settle by ledger and leave no bank record.
Afghanistan.imp: For Afghans, the ministry that runs the police is led by a man from a group a US commander called an arm of Pakistan's spy agency, and UN monitors place al-Qaeda close to the government. There is no independent court inside the country to test any of it. Before 2021 the bank that paid soldiers' and teachers' salaries was emptied by insiders, and the public paid for the rescue. Watch the UN monitors' yearly reports and money moving through hawala brokers, which leaves no record a bank could screen.

Armenia.d:
Armenia has one case on the map, it is happening now, and it is unresolved. It concerns who controls the country's electricity. Samvel Karapetyan, a Russian-Armenian billionaire, owns the Tashir Group, which ran Electric Networks of Armenia, the only company that delivers power to homes and businesses across the country. In June 2025 he backed the Armenian Church in its dispute with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and was detained over public calls to seize power, then charged with money laundering. Parliament then changed the law so the state can take over the grid company.

Two readings are open. One is that a private owner with Russian business ties used his hold on a national utility for political ends. The other, put by his lawyers and by critics of the government, is that the charges are a way to remove a rival before the 2026 election. No trial result has been reported, and the map rates the alleged plot only possible.

The Russkiy Mir Foundation, a Russian state-backed body that promotes Russian language and culture abroad, is listed as likely present but undocumented. The conditions scores are moderate, with middling resilience, and Armenia belongs to no pattern on the map yet.
Armenia.imp: For Armenians, the company that keeps the lights on has become the centre of a political fight. Either its private owner was using it for political ends, or the government is using criminal charges against an opponent before an election; no court has decided which. Whoever ends up running the grid controls something every household depends on. Watch the trial, who manages the grid company under the new law, and whether that law is used against other owners.

Azerbaijan.d:
In Azerbaijan the inside hand runs outward from the state rather than in. The economy rests on oil and gas, and the state oil company SOCAR sits at its centre, with the same people moving between the company, the ministries and the country's diplomacy. When Azerbaijan hosted the UN climate summit, COP29, in November 2024, its president was Mukhtar Babayev, formerly SOCAR's vice-president for ecology, and its chief executive was the deputy energy minister Elnur Soltanov. Global Witness, posing as investors, secretly filmed Soltanov discussing possible oil and gas deals in the run-up to the talks; critics said this broke the code of conduct for summit hosts. The map rates the case probable and rates its reach as worldwide, the top of its scale, because it reached into a global body meant to cut fossil-fuel use.

The oil company has also been used for foreign policy at home. In 2014, after Turkey's Prime Minister Erdoğan asked for help against the Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic movement his government pursues as a terrorist group, a company part-owned by SOCAR took over the movement's 11 high schools, 13 university-entrance centres and a private university in Azerbaijan.

The map also treats Azerbaijan as the home of what it calls 'caviar diplomacy', the network followed in its pattern on foreign money inside Europe's parliaments. Its conditions scores read poorly: 8.5 for powerful actors embedded in the state, and weak resilience at 4.0.
Azerbaijan.imp: For people in Azerbaijan, the state, the oil company and the diplomatic service are hard to tell apart, and there is little inside the country to check them. The same officials who run oil policy chaired a world summit on cutting fossil fuels, and an oil-company affiliate took over a school network at a foreign leader's request, so families' children changed schools for a diplomatic reason. Watch who represents the country abroad and what business they discuss there.

Bahrain.d: This is a best guess: the map has no documented case of an outside force inside Bahrain's government. Its one record runs the other way. In 2018 Bahrain obtained an Interpol Red Notice for Hakeem al-Araibi, a dissident footballer living as a refugee in Australia; Thailand arrested him, Interpol withdrew the notice because its rules bar requests from the country a refugee fled, and Thai prosecutors dropped the case in 2019. The Muslim Brotherhood and the Tony Blair Institute are recorded as present. The likeliest route in is Iran's Revolutionary Guards and their allied militias, listed as likely but undocumented; in Iraq the same network sits inside the armed forces. The conditions scores are middling.
Bahrain.imp: For people in Bahrain, the documented danger is the state's own reach: using an international police system to chase someone who fled abroad. Whether outside forces sit inside the government, the record does not yet show. Watch for Red Notices against exiles living abroad, for evidence, rather than claims, of Iranian-backed networks in the country, and for who funds political and religious groups there.

Bangladesh.d:
In Bangladesh the inside hand reaches through three doors: the drug route from Myanmar, the central bank's payment systems and, once, the army.

The drug door is at Cox's Bazar on the Myanmar border, where almost all yaba, a methamphetamine pill, enters the country. The district's member of parliament, Abdur Rahman Bodi, appeared on the government's own list of traffickers; he was convicted only of hiding wealth, the trafficking allegations never went to trial, and in 2019 some 102 dealers, several of them his relatives, surrendered in a staged ceremony. The crackdown that followed produced hundreds of killings in police custody or 'crossfire', and in 2022 the former police chief at Teknaf and colleagues were sentenced to death for murdering a retired army major who had filmed them. The convictions are for murder. The trade itself carries on.

The second door is the central bank. In February 2016 hackers inside the network of Bangladesh Bank sent orders to move $951 million from its account at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York; most were blocked, but $101 million got out, and about $66 million was still missing in 2025. US agencies tied the theft to a unit of North Korea's military spy agency and charged a North Korean programmer.

The third was the army. In January 2012 it said it had stopped a coup by serving and retired officers it linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, a movement that seeks to replace states with a caliphate and has been banned in Bangladesh since 2009.
Bangladesh.imp: For people in Bangladesh, the trafficking that runs through Cox's Bazar reached their member of parliament, and the crackdown on it killed hundreds of people while leaving the trade in place. A foreign state's hackers took part of the national reserves, which is public money, and most of it has not come back. Watch whether trafficking cases against officials ever reach trial, and how the central bank guards its payment systems.

Bhutan.d: This is a best guess: the map has no documented case for Bhutan and records no outside organisation as present, or even likely. The scores are moderate, with a fairly low reading of 3.0 for powerful actors embedded in the state and middling resilience, meaning the courts, press and parliament that would catch such actors are of middling strength. Bhutan's two large neighbours, India and China, both carry long records on this map, but nothing in either reaches into Bhutan. Any outside hand would most likely come through a larger government's influence or large foreign-funded projects, and the record shows neither yet.
Bhutan.imp: For people in Bhutan, the lack of cases may mean little is happening, or that little has been looked for. The first signs of an outside hand elsewhere are usually foreign money in politics and unexplained winners of large public contracts, so those are what to watch, along with who funds political parties and whether the press is free to report on them.

Brunei.d: This is a best guess: the map has no documented case for Brunei. One organisation is recorded as present: China's police 'overseas service stations', offices abroad linked to Chinese police that elsewhere have been used to keep watch on Chinese nationals. The conditions scores are moderate, with a low reading of 3.0 for powerful actors embedded in the state and middling resilience. If anything reaches inside, the likeliest route is China's reach toward Chinese nationals living in Brunei, but no case shows it touching Brunei's own government or its officials.
Brunei.imp: For people in Brunei, there is nothing on the record yet to point to, which may mean little is happening or little has been looked for. The thread worth watching is whether Chinese police offices operate in the country, what they do, especially toward Chinese residents, and whether Brunei's own authorities know about them or allow them to work alongside the local police.

Cambodia.d:
In Cambodia the inside hand belongs to the scam-compound economy, and it reaches the people around the ruling family. Across the country, compounds hold trafficked workers under debt bondage and make them run online investment fraud, and US and UK sanctions findings repeatedly name political protection as the reason they operate in the open.

The largest of these businesses was the Prince Group, built by Chen Zhi, a Fujian-born Cambodian citizen who advised Hun Sen, the long-time prime minister, as well as the interior minister and the head of the National Assembly. In October 2025 the US indicted him, seized about 127,271 bitcoin, worth some US$14 billion, and with the UK sanctioned 146 people and firms; more were added in June 2026. A sitting senator, Kok An, and his network were sanctioned in April 2026. In January 2026 Cambodia stripped Chen Zhi of citizenship and sent him to China. No Cambodian court has prosecuted any of those named.

The money moves through Phnom Penh. Huione Group's payment arm has Hun To, a cousin of Prime Minister Hun Manet, as a major shareholder and director; the US Treasury found Huione laundered over US$4 billion, including North Korean hackers' takings, and Cambodia's central bank pulled the payment arm's licence. Its online marketplace handled tens of billions before closing. The UN drugs agency describes the region's 340-plus casinos, online gambling and dollar stablecoins as a parallel banking system for drug, gambling and fraud money, and as Macau cracked down the business moved into Cambodia.

Hun Sen also accepted two awards from the Unification Church and hosted its political arm's 2019 summit. The older background is a 2003 heroin case against a military intelligence general, released within weeks after the seized drugs were burned in public.
Cambodia.imp: For Cambodians, the compounds work openly because, according to US and UK findings, people connected to power protect them, and no Cambodian court has tried anyone named. The workers held inside are trafficking victims, and the money moves through a firm tied to the prime minister's cousin. Banks and casinos that move value without a record also carry drug money. Watch whether Cambodian prosecutors act on their own, who takes over Prince and Huione assets, and whether the compounds simply move.

China.d:
China appears on the map mostly as the outside hand rather than the place reached into. It works in three directions: the Communist Party inside companies, Chinese officials inside international bodies, and Chinese chemical firms inside the drug trade abroad.

Inside companies the party's presence is written into law. Any firm with three or more party members must set up a party organisation, and by 2018 nearly three-quarters of private companies had one; some foreign joint ventures have been asked to write it into their charters. ByteDance, owner of TikTok, has a party committee and a state fund on its board, and admitted in 2022 that staff used TikTok data to track journalists. A leaked list of about 1.95 million party members showed hundreds at foreign banks, drug makers and aircraft firms in Shanghai; it showed membership, not spying.

In international bodies, China's vice-minister of public security, Meng Hongwei, served as Interpol's president until he vanished on a trip home in 2018 and was jailed for bribery; his wife says the case is political.

In the drug trade, US indictments since 2018 charge chemical firms in Wuhan, Hebei, Shandong and Shanghai with selling fentanyl and its precursors to Mexican cartels and US buyers, mostly for cryptocurrency. These are charges against people beyond US reach; China has since controlled some of the chemicals. Macau's two largest junket operators, which brought high-stakes gamblers to its casinos, had their heads jailed in 2023.

Foreign firms reached in too: JPMorgan paid $264 million for hiring about 100 officials' relatives to win business, and a Coca-Cola-founded group, ILSI, had its office inside the national disease agency and steered obesity policy toward exercise rather than diet.

The older background includes a 1993 remark by the police minister that 'patriotic' triads deserve respect.
China.imp: For people in China, the party sits inside the companies they work for and some apps they use, openly and by law, though membership lists are not public. Abroad, the same state placed its own vice-minister at the head of the world's police network, and Uyghurs who fled have been detained in other countries. Chemical sellers charged in the US face no trial at home. Watch party clauses in company charters, Red Notices against exiles, and whether China prosecutes its own precursor sellers.

Cyprus.d:
Cyprus's record is about selling access to Europe: to its passports and its banks. Both cases are closed, and both are still felt.

From 2007 to 2020 Cyprus sold citizenship, and with it the right to live and work across the European Union, to investors. In October 2020 Al Jazeera aired an undercover film in which the Speaker of the House, Demetris Syllouris, and MP Christakis Giovanis appeared willing to help a fictional Chinese investor with a money-laundering conviction get a passport. Both resigned and the scheme was closed. A state inquiry under former judge Myron Nicolatos found more than half the passports had been granted unlawfully. Four men were sent to trial, and one was cleared in 2023.

The bank side ran through non-resident accounts. FBME Bank, registered in Tanzania but run from Cyprus, was named by the US Treasury in 2014 as a primary money-laundering concern over accounts used by organised crime and sanctioned parties. Cyprus wound it up, and its owners fought the finding in arbitration for years.

The Trilateral Commission is recorded as present. The United Grand Lodge of England, Turkey's Grey Wolves and PrivatBank under its former Ukrainian owners are listed as likely present but undocumented. The conditions scores are moderate.
Cyprus.imp: For Cypriots, the passport scheme meant the head of parliament was filmed offering to help a convicted launderer become a European citizen, and an official inquiry found most passports had been granted unlawfully. Banks serving non-residents carried organised-crime money through the island's financial system. Watch the remaining trials, whether unlawfully granted passports are withdrawn, and how banks check accounts held by people who do not live there.

Georgia.d:
Georgia has one documented case, and it concerns the man at the top of its ruling party; the map rates it among its most serious. Bidzina Ivanishvili made his fortune in Russia in the 1990s, founded the ruling Georgian Dream party and, as its honorary chairman, nominates the prime minister. In December 2024 the US Treasury sanctioned him 'for undermining Georgian democracy and advancing the interests of the Russian Federation'. Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia sanctioned him too, and the European Parliament describes him as having 'personal and business links to the Kremlin'. He denies acting for Russia.

These are decisions by foreign governments, not a court finding, and the map rates the Russian link probable. If it holds, the outside hand sits at the point where the head of government is chosen, which is why the case scores so high on severity even though it is a single record.

Georgia appears in the map's patterns on Russia's networks and on foreign money in European politics, as a target country. The Grand Orient de France, a French Masonic body, and the Gülen movement are recorded as present, and the Atlas Network, a US-based network of free-market think tanks, as likely. The conditions scores are moderate.
Georgia.imp: For Georgians, the person who picks the prime minister is under Western sanctions for allegedly serving another country's interests, and no court has tested that claim, so voters cannot see what ties, if any, shape his decisions. Watch the government's course toward Russia and the EU, how protest and dissent are treated, and whether any court, at home or abroad, examines the allegations.

India.d:
In India the largest presence inside government is a domestic movement, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation founded in 1925 from whose political wing the governing BJP grew. Prime Minister Narendra Modi was a full-time RSS organiser before it seconded him to the BJP in 1985; in his second government 38 of 53 BJP ministers had RSS roots, and Vice-President C. P. Radhakrishnan, who chairs the upper house, has been with it since he was 16. The RSS publishes no membership rolls. Membership of a lawful organisation is not wrongdoing; the record shows how many top offices one movement fills.

Criminal networks reach the legislatures. After the 2024 election 251 of 543 MPs declared pending criminal cases, 170 of them serious; these are cases, not convictions. In Uttar Pradesh, Mukhtar Ansari won the Mau seat five times, much of it from prison, before dying in custody in 2024.

Companies reaching officials are being pursued mostly by foreign courts. US prosecutors charged Gautam Adani in 2024 over more than $250 million in alleged bribes for solar contracts, which he denies, and a French judge is investigating the Rafale fighter deal that India's Supreme Court cleared.

Indian chemical and drug firms sit in supply chains abroad. Since 2025 the US has charged or sanctioned Indian suppliers shipping fentanyl precursors toward the Sinaloa Cartel, and investigators traced about $130 million of the opioid tapentadol from more than 60 Indian exporters to West African countries that never approved it.

The Indian state also reaches abroad: in 2026 Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty in New York over a plot to kill Sikh activist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun that prosecutors say an officer in the Cabinet Secretariat, home of the foreign spy agency RAW, directed.
India.imp: For people in India, many top offices are held by people formed in one movement that does not say who its members are, and nearly half the lower house faces pending criminal cases. The largest bribery allegations are being pursued in New York and Paris, not at home. Pills from Indian exporters reach West African street markets. Watch who is appointed to ministries and regulators, whether Indian investigators act on the Adani charges, and how exporters of opioids and precursor chemicals are policed.

Indonesia.d:
In Indonesia the inside hand today belongs mostly to large mass organisations, religious and paramilitary, and to foreign companies buying their way into state firms and regulators.

Mass organisations are a route into the top offices. Nahdlatul Ulama, the country's largest Muslim organisation, saw its supreme leader Ma'ruf Amin become vice-president from 2019 to 2024 after President Joko Widodo chose him as running mate. Pemuda Pancasila, a paramilitary group founded in 1959 that took part in the 1965–66 killings, was part of the ruling Golkar party from 1982 to 2001 and is known for extortion and protection work. In the other direction, the state banned Hizb ut-Tahrir Indonesia in 2017 for aiming to replace the state with a caliphate and warned civil servants who were members they would be dismissed. In 2023 a police general about to take command in Jakarta was convicted of having seized methamphetamine swapped for alum and sold.

Foreign firms have paid officials in state companies and ministries. The former head of the state airline Garuda was jailed for eight years in 2020 for bribes prosecutors traced to Rolls-Royce and Airbus. Monsanto settled US charges in 2005 over a $50,000 bribe to an environment ministry official assessing its genetically modified cotton, and US regulators found its local affiliates had paid at least 140 officials.

The roots go back to the 1960s. The Ford Foundation paid for University of Indonesia economists to earn doctorates at Berkeley, and after Suharto took power they ran his economy: Widjojo Nitisastro headed the planning agency for 16 years and Ali Wardhana was finance minister for 15. Their programme opened the country to foreign investors. John Perkins later claimed his engineering firm inflated forecasts so Indonesia would borrow heavily; reporters confirmed his career but not his larger claims.
Indonesia.imp: For Indonesians, mass organisations with millions of members are a route to the vice-presidency and the ruling parties, and one of them earns money from extortion on city streets. Foreign firms have paid officials at the state airline and at the ministry that judged whether a GM crop was safe. Watch who mass organisations place on party tickets, how regulators judge foreign companies' products, and whether drug cases against senior police officers keep reaching court.

Iran.d:
In Iran the inside hand is the state's own armed force, sitting inside the economy. The Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), Iran's ideological military, run an engineering arm, Khatam al-Anbiya, that controls more than 812 registered companies building dams, tunnels, oil and gas fields and defence works, with about 1,700 government contracts by 2012; The same year a consortium including Guards-linked foundations paid about US$7.8 billion for control of the Telecommunication Company of Iran, which runs the network the state uses to watch and filter communications; a Guards unit said in 2018 it had sold out.

Inside the courts, defence lawyers describe the revolutionary courts that hear drug cases as fast-tracking low-level defendants while trafficking networks go untouched, and one lawyer has alleged that one of two named Tehran judges was corrupt. With no independent forum the claim cannot be tested, while the country hangs hundreds of people a year for drug offences.

Outward, Iran is the sponsoring state behind armed allies placed inside other governments, most visibly in Iraq's state-funded militias.

The older background is the Shah's era and the early revolution. Nematollah Nassiri, head of the secret police SAVAK, signed the 1976 Safari Club pact with the intelligence chiefs of France, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Morocco. Jafar Sharif-Emami, Grand Master of Iran's Masonic Grand Lodge, was twice the Shah's prime minister. After 1979 the Hojjatieh Society, a religious group, suspended itself when Khomeini attacked it Iran's reading of 9.5 for powerful actors embedded in the state is the joint highest on the map.
Iran.imp: For Iranians, the Revolutionary Guards are not only soldiers: they build the dams, work the oil and gas fields and for years held the telephone network, so the military shares in the contracts the state hands out and, for a time, in the wires that carry people's calls. Drug courts pass death sentences with little outside check on the judges. Watch which firms win state contracts, who owns the communications networks, and whether any independent review of drug cases appears.

Iraq.d:
In Iraq armed groups backed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards are part of the state's own armed forces and are paid from its budget. The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) formed in 2014 to fight Islamic State from about 67 mostly Shia factions, almost all Guards-backed, and a 2016 law made them a branch of the armed forces under the prime minister. In 2024 the PMF chief of staff said publicly that it took orders from Iran's supreme leader. Kata'ib Hezbollah, which the US lists as a terrorist group staffs three PMF brigades. The PMF's chairman, Falih al-Fayyadh was sanctioned by the US in 2021 over the killing of protesters in 2019 and still holds the post. A 2025 bill to tighten state control was tabled under US pressure.

Inside the civil service, the hand is money. In 2021–22 about $2.5 billion was taken from the tax authority through 247 cheques to five front companies posing as oil firms owed refunds. A Baghdad court convicted 10 people in 2024, including a former head of parliament's finance committee and the former director of Prime Minister Mustafa al-Kadhimi's office; several senior tax and Rafidain Bank officials have not been charged.

Drugs are the newest thread. Captagon seizures rose about 3,380% from 2019 to 2023, most of it across the 600-kilometre Syrian border, and Iraq has moved from transit route to production site; the state now drug-tests teachers and officials. A former governor's son on the intelligence service payroll got life for drug offences in 2018, then was pardoned.
Iraq.imp: For Iraqis, part of the army they pay for answers, by its own chief of staff's account, to the leader of another country, and its chairman is under sanctions over protesters' deaths. Public money was taken from the tax authority with help from officials close to a prime minister, and only some have been tried. Watch the PMF reform bill, who controls the PMF budget, and whether the remaining tax and bank officials are charged.

Israel.d:
In Israel the inside hand runs in two directions: domestic companies and a foreign government reaching the prime minister's office, and Israeli firms reaching into other governments.

At home, the leading case is in court now. Prosecutors say Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while also communications minister, gave regulatory decisions worth large sums to Shaul Elovitch, controlling owner of Bezeq, Israel's largest telecoms company, in return for favourable coverage on Elovitch's news site Walla!. He is charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust, denies it, finished his testimony in June 2026 and has asked President Herzog for a pardon. A second investigation concerns Qatar, which mediates in the Gaza war and hosts Hamas's political office: police arrested two Netanyahu aides, Jonatan Urich and Eli Feldstein, on suspicion of being paid through a US lobbyist's firm to promote Qatar's image in Israel. Netanyahu was questioned as a witness, not a suspect, and calls it a political witch hunt. Lower down, Israeli courts have convicted police officers for passing investigation files to crime organisations.

Abroad, NSO Group sells its Pegasus phone-hacking spyware only to governments, under Israeli defence ministry export licences. State clients' use of it has been tied to surveillance of journalists and dissidents and the US blacklisted the firm in 2021. Teva and Allergan settled US opioid claims in 2022 for about $4.25 billion and $2.37 billion without admitting wrongdoing.
Israel.imp: For Israelis, the open questions are whether a prime minister traded regulatory favours over the country's main phone company for news coverage, and whether his aides took money to promote a foreign state during a war; neither has been decided. Spyware licensed by their own defence ministry has been used against journalists elsewhere. Watch the trial's outcome or any pardon, the Qatar investigation, and which governments receive spyware export licences.

Japan.d:
In Japan the outside hands on government today are mostly religious and nationalist lobbies working through the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP),. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, elected by the Diet in October 2025, has served in the Diet members' league of Nippon Kaigi, the country's largest nationalist lobby (about 38,000–40,000 members), which campaigns to revise the constitution. Japan Press Weekly, the English service of the Communist Party paper Akahata, counted 10 of her first 19 ministers in that league, 12 in the league of Shinto Seiji Renmei, the political arm of the Association of Shinto Shrines, and five with ties to the Unification Church. These are press membership lists, not findings that the groups set policy, and the cabinet reshuffled in September 2026 has not been counted.

The Unification Church, a Korean-founded church, is being wound up. The LDP's own 2022 survey found 179 of its 379 Diet members tied to it, and church documents seized in South Korea are reported to say it backed 290 LDP candidates in 2021. In March 2026 the Tokyo High Court upheld the dissolution order, which found 1,559 victims of unlawful donation solicitation and about ¥20.4 billion taken. Komeito, the party of the Buddhist lay movement Soka Gakkai, governed with the LDP for most of 1999–2025 and is now in opposition.

Lower down, every prefecture now bars business with the yakuza, Japan's crime groups (9,400 members in 2025), after regulators found Mizuho Bank letting about ¥200 million in loans reach gang members and police arrested yakuza brokers skimming workers' pay on the Fukushima clean-up. A Diet commission found the old nuclear regulator had been 'captured' by TEPCO, the plant's operator.

The church's ties to the LDP go back to 1968, when former prime minister Nobusuke Kishi, Abe's grandfather, co-founded its anti-communist political arm.
Japan.imp: Many of the people running Japan's government belong to lobbies that want to change the constitution and how history is taught, and the public learns who belongs mostly from press lists rather than official disclosure. The church case shows a religious group's volunteers and votes reaching a large part of the ruling party while its followers were pressed for money. Watch the membership counts for the reshuffled cabinet, the church's liquidation, and whether regulators keep acting on gang money and on industries that help write their own safety rules.

Jordan.d:
Jordan's state is pressed from two directions today: an Islamist movement that holds the largest bloc in parliament, and drug smugglers from Syria who have reached into the army guarding the border.

The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928, sits in parliament through its political arm, the Islamic Action Front, which won 31 of 138 seats in September 2024. In April 2025 the interior minister banned all Brotherhood activities and said its assets would be seized, after 16 people, Brotherhood members among them, were arrested over an alleged weapons plot the group said it knew nothing about. In January 2026 the US Treasury listed the Jordanian branch as terrorist. These are government decisions, not court findings against any official.

Along the Syrian border the trade is captagon, a pill drug carried south toward the Gulf. Jordan's State Security Court has convicted serving and former soldiers of moving captagon and weapons across the border in cases since 2022, so the smugglers have paid people inside the force meant to stop them. Since Assad fell in December 2024, the loads come on GPS-guided helium balloons launched from the empty Hamad desert. Jordan intercepted 128 attempts between July 2025 and April 2026, has seized at least 46 million pills since mid-2025, and has struck inside Syria five times. Whether firms or money networks inside Jordan handle the balloon trade is only suspected.

The Order of Malta and Hizb ut-Tahrir, a movement that seeks a caliphate, are recorded as present without documented cases.
Jordan.imp: For people in Jordan, the party that won the most seats in 2024 belongs to a movement their government has banned and the US now lists as terrorist, so how the ban is applied to those 31 seats decides part of who represents them. The captagon convictions show that soldiers guarding the border can be paid to let loads through. Watch the State Security Court cases, the treatment of the Islamic Action Front, and whether balloon seizures ever lead to anyone on the Jordanian side.

Kazakhstan.d:
Kazakhstan has little on this map, and its one case shows the government declining a foreign request rather than carrying it out. The Gülen movement, a Turkish religious network that Turkey's government calls 'FETÖ' and pursues abroad, co-founded 33 Turkish-Kazakh high schools here. After Turkey's July 2016 coup attempt, Ankara asked Central Asian governments to close Gülen-linked schools, and Kazakhstan declined. In October 2016 the sponsoring foundation, KATEV, renamed the schools 'Bilim' Innovative Lyceums; RFE/RL found no Kazakh government order behind the change. The map marks the case only as possible. In neighbouring Kyrgyzstan, by contrast, a Gülen school head was taken out of the country to Turkey in 2021.

Several outside bodies are recorded as present without a documented case: Opus Dei and the Order of Malta, two Catholic organisations; Hizb ut-Tahrir, a movement that seeks a caliphate; and Turkey's nationalist Grey Wolves. The World Economic Forum, Russia's Russkiy Mir Foundation, Interpol and Airbus are marked as likely. The conditions scores are middling: a fair number of state-embedded actors (6 of 10) and below-average resilience (4.7), meaning the institutions that would expose outside influence are not strong.
Kazakhstan.imp: For families whose children attended those schools, the schools stayed open under a new name, and on this record the government handed no one to Turkey, unlike some neighbours. Because Russian and Chinese state bodies are not documented here yet, the map says little about the outside forces most likely to matter to Kazakhs. Watch whether the refusal to close the schools holds, and whether new cases appear involving Russia or China.

Korea, DPR.d:
North Korea is closed to outsiders, so this map records it mainly as a state that reaches into other countries rather than one that is reached into. Three of its own bodies work abroad: the remote IT-worker programme, the Lazarus Group (state hackers, also called TraderTraitor) and the Reconnaissance General Bureau, its main intelligence agency. With Iran and Myanmar it is one of only three countries on the FATF blacklist, the list on which the global anti-money-laundering standard-setter calls on others to take action, a list unchanged since Myanmar was added in 2022.

The one documented case from inside is old and disputed. In 2003 the North Korean freighter Pong Su delivered 125 kilograms of heroin to a beach in Victoria, Australia, and was boarded by Australian special forces. In 2006 a jury acquitted the captain and senior crew of importation, not persuaded they knew the cargo, and the ship was later sunk as a bombing target. No court found the state behind the shipment.

The Unification Church, a Korean-founded church, is recorded as present. The conditions scores are near the top of the scale: power held by people embedded in the state (10 of 10) and almost no resilience (1.6), so very little about who inside the state profits from trade abroad can come to light.
Korea, DPR.imp: People in North Korea have no free press or independent courts that could show who inside the state profits from smuggling, hacking or work abroad, so almost nothing reaches a record like this. What can be seen is the effect outside the country: ships, IT workers and hackers working for the state. Watch foreign court cases and sanctions actions, which are where evidence about North Korea's state businesses usually comes out.

Korea, Rep..d:
In South Korea the courts are now working through how two churches reached into both main political parties, and the largest business group's dealings with the state keep returning to court.

The Unification Church, a Korean-founded church led by Han Hak-ja, used its money to expand political influence around the 2022 presidential election, a Seoul court found in August 2026, sentencing Han to two years; the church will appeal. The money reached the household of then-president Yoon Suk Yeol, whose wife Kim Keon-hee was jailed in January 2026 for taking a Chanel bag and a diamond necklace from the church, and his People Power Party, whose former floor leader Kweon Seong-dong lost his seat over 100 million won. It reached the other side too: Chun Jae-soo, oceans minister in the Democratic Party government, resigned in December 2025 after a church official said he had been given cash and two luxury watches. Police booked him as a bribery suspect; he denies it.

The second church, Shincheonji, worked through party membership rather than gifts. Investigators found at least 56,472 of its members signed up to the People Power Party between 2021 and 2023, and its 94-year-old founder, Lee Man-hee, was indicted in July 2026 under the law that bars forcing anyone to join a party.

Samsung, the largest business group, appears twice. Its heir, Lee Jae-yong, was convicted in 2017 of bribing entities controlled by a friend of President Park Geun-hye, then pardoned in 2022 and made chairman. Prosecutors now charge that a former Samsung executive copied a Samsung chip plant in China with about US$340 million from the Chengdu government; he denies it.

The church's place near the state goes back to the 1970s: a 1978 US House inquiry found a Moon organisation business made M-16 rifles for Seoul.
Korea, Rep..imp: For South Koreans, these cases show a church's money and members reaching a president's household and party leaders on both sides, and the courts now acting on it. Party sign-ups are a quiet route: mass memberships can tilt who gets nominated without voters noticing. Watch the appeals by Han Hak-ja and the church, the Shincheonji trial, the police case against Chun Jae-soo, and whether pardons undo the sentences, as one did for Samsung's heir.

Kuwait.d:
Kuwait's one case on the map, marked only as possible, is an Islamist party that competes in the open. The Muslim Brotherhood is a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928 with branches across the region. After Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990, the Kuwaiti branch broke with the international movement and founded its own party, the Islamic Constitutional Movement, known as Hadas. Hadas regularly won several seats in parliament through the 1990s and 2000s and sometimes had ministers in the cabinet, until a coalition including it boycotted the 2013 elections and was left out of parliament. It is on the map because of its roots in a movement that crosses borders, not because it works in hiding.

Two other outside forces are recorded here without a documented case: the Trilateral Commission, a private forum of business and political leaders, and Gulf-state and private networks that fund Salafi preaching. The telecoms firm Ericsson is marked as likely. The conditions scores sit in the middle (state-embedded actors 6 of 10, resilience 5.4). Around Kuwait the Brotherhood is treated harder: Saudi Arabia has listed it as terrorist since 2014, Jordan banned it in 2025, and in January 2026 the US designated its Jordanian, Egyptian and Lebanese branches.
Kuwait.imp: For Kuwaitis, the Brotherhood's influence here has come through elections, where voters can see it and vote against it, which is different from the hidden placement this map records in other countries. Pressure from neighbours and from Washington to treat the movement as terrorist is growing. Watch whether Hadas returns to parliament and the cabinet, and whether Kuwait comes under pressure to ban it as Jordan did.

Kyrgyzstan.d:
In Kyrgyzstan the record points to the state's borders and courts: crime networks working through customs, and a foreign intelligence service taking a man out past the border guards.

The largest case concerns Raiymbek Matraimov, a former deputy chief of customs. In December 2020 the US Treasury sanctioned him under the Magnitsky Act, a US law used to punish corrupt officials abroad, for a customs scheme that moved hundreds of millions of dollars out of the country. Journalists from OCCRP and Kloop who documented it were prosecuted or forced out, while he settled a domestic case by repaying money and served no prison term at the time. The courts treated Kamchybek Kolbayev, a crime boss the US named a drug kingpin in 2011, the same way, releasing or lightly sentencing him again and again until he was killed in a security operation in 2023.

Turkey reaches in over the Gülen movement, a Turkish religious network that Ankara calls 'FETÖ' and pursues abroad. In mid-2021 Orhan Inandi, a Kyrgyz citizen who headed the Sapat network of Turkish-founded schools, disappeared in Bishkek; Turkey's president then said on television that he had been 'captured and taken to Turkey'. Kyrgyz military prosecutors opened proceedings against border officers of the national security committee who let him be taken out. Hizb ut-Tahrir, a movement that seeks a caliphate, and Turkey's nationalist Grey Wolves are marked as likely.

Conditions are poor: many state-embedded actors (8.5 of 10) and low resilience (3.8).
Kyrgyzstan.imp: For people in Kyrgyzstan, the customs case is about money that should have reached the public purse leaving through the border, with the reporters who exposed it punished rather than the official. The Inandi case shows a foreign government could take a citizen past the state's own border guards. Watch whether the proceedings against those guards reach a result, and whether journalists covering customs and organised crime can keep working.

Laos.d:
In Laos, a stretch of the Mekong in Bokeo province, in the far north-west, is governed largely by a casino company that the US calls a criminal organisation, and the Lao state has not acted against it. In 2007 the government gave Kings Romans Group, headed by the Chinese casino operator Zhao Wei, a 99-year lease to set up and run the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone. In January 2018 the US Treasury designated Zhao Wei's network, saying the Kings Romans casino stored and distributed drugs from Myanmar's United Wa State Army and laundered the proceeds. The owner denied it, and the casino kept operating and expanding.

The US State Department reports that the zone is run in part by criminal organisations, that confusion over who is in charge between Lao officials and zone security blocks investigations, and that no complicit official has been investigated, prosecuted or convicted. UNODC, the UN's drugs and crime office, links the zone to cyber-fraud compounds and flagged a 2020 river port built by a company tied to the organisation. What the concession gives the network is land, a port and a state's lease to work under.

Outside scrutiny is reaching the banks instead: in February 2025 the FATF, the international body that sets anti-money-laundering standards, put Laos on its list of countries under increased monitoring. Meanwhile Laos arrested more than 20,000 people for drug offences between 2015 and 2019. Hong Kong and Macau triads are marked as likely present but not documented.
Laos.imp: For people in Laos, part of their country is governed under a lease by a group the US calls a criminal organisation, and no official has been prosecuted over it. Tens of thousands of ordinary people have been arrested on drug charges while the zone's owners have not been touched at home. Watch whether Lao authorities ever act inside the zone, what happens to the fraud compounds there, and whether the FATF listing is lifted or tightened.

Lebanon.d:
Lebanon's state is shared with an armed party, and its banks with the politicians who borrowed from them.

Hezbollah, a Shia party with its own armed wing, aligned with Iran and listed as terrorist by at least 28 countries including the US and UK, holds about 14 of 128 seats. In Prime Minister Nawaf Salam's government, formed in February 2025, its picks run the health and labour ministries, and with its ally Amal it controls six portfolios. In August 2025 the cabinet approved the aim that only the state hold weapons and the Hezbollah- and Amal-aligned ministers walked out; the army's disarmament plan has no timeline, and Hezbollah's leader rejects disarmament. In January 2026 the US also listed Lebanon's Muslim Brotherhood branch, the party al-Jamaa al-Islamiya, as terrorist.

An economist's study found that 18 of the 20 main commercial banks had major shareholders linked to political elites, about 43% of the sector's assets. They lent heavily to the state and to the central bank under Governor Riad Salameh until the system collapsed in 2019 and froze people's savings; Salameh was detained in 2024 and charged with embezzling $42 million. Drug money has moved through the same system. The Lebanese Canadian Bank carried cocaine proceeds through used-car sales and its successor forfeited $102 million with no banker prosecuted, and the related Joumaa network, which Treasury says benefits Hezbollah, used exchange houses and its own ships. In February 2026 a military court gave the captagon trafficker Nouh Zeaiter four months, after twice sentencing him heavily in his absence.

Foreign governments reach in as well. In 2017 Prime Minister Saad Hariri announced his resignation from Saudi Arabia, and Lebanon's president said the Saudis were holding him; Saudi Arabia denied it and Hariri withdrew the resignation.
Lebanon.imp: For people in Lebanon, the banks that held their savings were largely owned by the same political class that borrowed from them, and when the system collapsed in 2019 depositors lost access to their money. An armed party also sits in the cabinet while the state tries to take its weapons away. Watch the Salameh case, whether the army's disarmament plan gets a timeline, and whether any banker or official is ever tried over the drug money that passed through Lebanese banks.

Malaysia.d:
In Malaysia outside hands reach in mainly through money: a global bank's deals that fed a prime minister's accounts, and a drug trade that buys police on the export route.

1MDB was a state investment fund. Goldman Sachs bankers Tim Leissner and Roger Ng arranged its bond deals with the financier Jho Low, and US authorities say money was diverted and used to bribe officials in Malaysia and the UAE. Goldman settled with Malaysia in 2020 for about $3.9 billion; Leissner pleaded guilty and Ng was convicted in New York in 2022. Malaysia's own courts reached the top last: in December 2025 the High Court found former prime minister Najib Razak guilty on all 25 counts tied to over $1 billion in his personal accounts and sentenced him to 15 years. He is appealing.

At street level, Malaysia sits on the export route from the Golden Triangle drug-producing region and hosts the busiest transhipment port in the region. Its anti-corruption commission keeps prosecuting narcotics officers, mostly in Johor and the Klang valley, for releasing suspects and reselling seized drugs.

Turkey's reach shows up too. In May 2017 Malaysian police held three Turkish men under a security law allowing 28 days' detention without trial and deported them, after Ankara cancelled their travel documents and accused them of links to the Gülen movement, a religious network it calls 'FETÖ'. Human Rights Watch condemned the deportations. Opus Dei, Airbus, Russia's GRU military intelligence and the World Hongmen association of Wan Kuok-koi, a former triad leader, are recorded as present without cases here.
Malaysia.imp: For Malaysians, 1MDB is about money from a public fund ending up in a prime minister's accounts, with a global bank arranging the deals, and the verdict at home came years after the US cases. The police cases show that drugs seized by officers can be sold again by the same officers, so convictions of officers matter as much as the size of seizures. Watch Najib's appeal, what happens to the money recovered from Goldman, and the next narcotics-officer cases in Johor.

Maldives.d: Nothing is documented for the Maldives on this map yet, so what follows is a best guess, not a finding. No secret society, religious movement, crime group, foreign government or company is recorded here, not even as likely. The conditions scores sit near the middle: a moderate share of power held by people embedded in the state (5.5 of 10) and below-average resilience (4.0), meaning the institutions that could expose capture are not strong. The most likely route in would be money from foreign governments or companies seeking favours from officials over contracts and leases, as the map records in other small states. That is an estimate.
Maldives.imp: For people in the Maldives, an empty record means no case has been documented here yet, not that none exists. With weak checks on officials, large contracts and leases are the place to look. Watch who wins them, who stands behind the companies involved, and whether courts, auditors and reporters are able to follow the money from those deals back to the officials who signed them.

Mongolia.d:
Mongolia's one documented case shows its own officials stopping a foreign removal rather than helping it. On 27 July 2018 Veysel Akcay, general manager of the Empathy Worldwide Educational Institution, which ran Turkish-Mongolian schools linked to the Gülen movement, was seized in Ulaanbaatar. The Gülen movement is a Turkish religious network that Turkey's government calls 'FETÖ' and pursues abroad; the same campaign took a school head out of Kyrgyzstan in 2021 and saw three Turkish men deported from Malaysia in 2017. Here, Mongolian authorities temporarily grounded a plane at the airport, and Akcay was released the same day. Turkish Minute and the Stockholm Center for Freedom reported that Turkey's MIT intelligence service carried out the abduction; Mongolian authorities said they had no specific knowledge of one and were investigating. The map marks the case only as possible.

China's reach is recorded but not yet shown by a case: Chinese police 'overseas service stations', offices that Chinese police run abroad, are listed as present, and the Unification Church, a Korean-founded church, as likely. The conditions scores are middling (state-embedded actors 5.5 of 10, resilience 5.3).
Mongolia.imp: For people in Mongolia, the case shows a foreign intelligence service may have tried to take someone off their streets, and that their own aviation and security officials stopped the flight. Gülen-linked teachers and staff living here are the people most exposed. Watch whether the investigation the authorities announced ever reports, and whether the Chinese police offices recorded here come under any official review.

Myanmar.d:
Myanmar has been run by a military government since 2021, and in its border regions that government shares the state with armed groups and crime networks.

The army placed a Karen militia, the Karen Border Guard Force, under its command. Its leader, Colonel Saw Chit Thu, partnered from 2017 with She Zhijiang's Yatai group to build Shwe Kokko and dealt with the Dongmei group of Wan Kuok-koi, a former 14K triad leader,. The junta gave him one of its highest honours in 2022; the UK and the US have since sanctioned him over forced labour in scam centres. In Shan State, armed groups made into official border guard forces operate where the largest volumes of methamphetamine are produced (marked only possible). In the Kokang zone the first leader, Bai Suocheng, was also a Shan State MP for the army-backed USDP while his family ran scam and gambling centres. Myanmar handed him to China in 2024, a Shenzhen court sentenced him to death, he died in custody, and four Bai group members were executed in February 2026.

Religion is the second hold on the state. Ma Ba Tha, a Buddhist nationalist monks' group formed in 2014, saw texts proposed by its members become four race and religion laws in 2015, covering conversion and marriage between Buddhist women and non-Buddhist men. After the coup the junta dropped sedition charges against Wirathu, a leading Ma Ba Tha monk known for anti-Muslim sermons, and honoured him in 2022.

Myanmar is one of three countries, with Iran and North Korea, on the FATF blacklist. The pattern is older: the Hong Pang Group, the business arm of the United Wa State Army, was founded in 1998 with drug revenues under a ceasefire deal and sanctioned by the US in 2005 and 2008.
Myanmar.imp: For people in Myanmar, armed groups the army has made part of the state run scam compounds and drug production in border areas, and those forced to work there have no court of their own to turn to. Laws drafted from monks' texts govern whom Buddhist women may marry. Action against the bosses has come from China and from foreign sanctions, not from Myanmar's courts. Watch who replaces the Kokang and Karen bosses, and whether the scam compounds simply move.

Nepal.d:
Nepal's one case on the map, marked only as possible, concerns China's ruling party and the leadership of Nepal's own. In 2020 the governing Nepal Communist Party was split by a revolt against Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli. In May and July, Chinese ambassador Hou Yanqi met Oli, President Bidya Bhandari and senior leaders Madhav Kumar Nepal and Jhala Nath Khanal, reportedly urging them to stay united, and in December China sent a delegation led by Guo Yezhou of the Chinese Communist Party's International Department, which handles its ties with foreign parties. Former ministers and diplomats criticised the meetings as interference; the embassy said it only wished to see the party united.

Organisations from both large neighbours are here. The RSS, an Indian Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation, is recorded as present, as is the Unification Church, a Korean-founded church; the Atlas Network, which links free-market think tanks, is marked as likely. In February 2025 the FATF, the international body that sets anti-money-laundering standards, put Nepal on its list of countries under increased monitoring, in the same session as Laos. Conditions are weak: many state-embedded actors (8 of 10) and low resilience (3.9), so the institutions that would expose outside influence are thin.
Nepal.imp: For Nepalis, the question is whether decisions about who leads their government are shaped by a neighbouring power's diplomats in private meetings, which leave little record beyond press reports. The FATF listing brings outside checks on how money moves through Nepal's banks. Watch for foreign envoys taking sides in party disputes, for Indian as well as Chinese organisations building ties with Nepal's parties, and for whether the FATF listing is lifted.

Oman.d: Nothing is documented for Oman on this map yet, so what follows is a best guess, not a finding. Two outside bodies are marked as likely but unproven: BCCI, the Bank of Credit and Commerce International, which US prosecutors said secretly and illegally took over a Washington bank with help from a former Saudi intelligence chief, and Le Cercle, a private, invitation-only political discussion club. The conditions scores sit near the middle: a moderate share of state-embedded actors (4.5 of 10) and average resilience (5.3). The most likely route in would be private banking ties and personal contacts between ruling circles and foreign figures, the kind of channel those two bodies represent. That is an estimate.
Oman.imp: For people in Oman, no case means none has been documented, not that none exists. Private banking ties and personal contacts with foreign figures are hard for the public to see in any country. Watch whether information about state finances, foreign advisers and the real owners of companies that win state contracts becomes open to the public and the press.

Pakistan.d:
Pakistan's record runs through the army, courts, central bank and parties, and much of it is disputed. The clearest case still in force concerns Turkey: in December 2018 the Supreme Court ordered the government to ban the Gülen movement, a Turkish religious network Ankara calls 'FETÖ', and to hand the Pak-Turk schools it ran to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation.

In May 2019, while Pakistan was negotiating an IMF bailout, an IMF staff member, Reza Baqir, was made governor of the State Bank a day after his predecessor was removed; the map marks any influence as only possible. The Karachi-based Khanani group of exchange houses laundered money for drug organisations and designated terrorist groups; its head pleaded guilty in the US in 2016.

In politics, families who hold hereditary custody of Sufi shrines draw income and votes from devotees, and one of them, Shah Mahmood Qureshi, custodian of the Bahauddin Zakariya shrine in Multan, was foreign minister twice. In Karachi, Uzair Baloch led the Lyari gang the Peoples' Aman Committee, aligned with the Pakistan Peoples Party that governs Sindh; a military court gave him 12 years for espionage in 2020, and claims that party leaders protected him are disputed. Drug law has also been turned on politicians: a provincial minister charged in 2019 with carrying heroin was acquitted in 2022.

The army has been reached before: in 2012 a military court convicted a brigadier and four majors of links to Hizb ut-Tahrir, a banned group seeking a caliphate, which had tried to recruit officers for a coup.
Pakistan.imp: For Pakistanis, these cases touch the central bank, the army, the courts and the parties, but many are unresolved or disputed. Shrine families turn religious devotion into votes, and a gang's ties to a governing party are claimed but contested. Drug charges have been used against a politician as well as against traffickers. Watch who is appointed to run the State Bank during IMF talks, and whether courts test the claims that gang leaders were protected.

Philippines.d:
In the Philippines today a church votes as a bloc, an outlawed online gambling industry has reached into town halls, and the drug war that began in 2016 is before the International Criminal Court.
