The Iglesia ni Cristo (INC), a Philippine church of about 2.6 million members by the 2015 census, tells its members how to vote and calls it the 'Unity Vote'. It backed Benigno Aquino III in 2010, Rodrigo Duterte in 2016, and in 2022 Ferdinand Marcos Jr., Sara Duterte and 12 Senate candidates. Duterte made its head a presidential special envoy, and in June 2026 the church put about 12,000 people on EDSA, Manila's main avenue, for Senator Rodante Marcoleta, a member elected with its support who was set to be charged over 75 million pesos in undeclared campaign money. Apollo Quiboloy, another preacher, whom Duterte called his spiritual adviser, is held on child-abuse and trafficking charges and indicted in the US.

POGOs were Chinese-run online gambling firms licensed from 2016 to serve players in China; Senate hearings in 2024 tied many to fraud, trafficking and torture. Alice Guo, mayor of Bamban, was found to be a Chinese citizen and sentenced to life for trafficking in 2025, and a court issued an arrest warrant for Harry Roque, Duterte's former spokesman, over another hub; he denies it. The industry was banned by executive order in 2024 and by law in 2025, though the shutdown displaced operations rather than ending them.

Between 6,000 and more than 30,000 people were killed in anti-drug operations from 2016, and the former president was surrendered to the ICC in 2025. Companies reached in as well: Pharmally, a firm with ₱625,000 in capital, won ₱8.68 billion in pandemic contracts, and State Grid Corporation of China owns 40% of the national grid operator.
Philippines.imp: For Filipinos, a church's bloc vote can help decide Senate seats, and it brings crowds to the streets when one of its members faces charges. The POGO cases show foreign-run businesses got local officials, even a mayor, on their side before the state acted. The drug war killed thousands while the trade went on, and a senator who questioned it was jailed for years on charges that failed. Watch the Marcoleta case, the ICC proceedings, the Roque warrant, and whether the banned gambling operations come back under another name.

Qatar.d:
Qatar appears on this map as a target, and both of its cases point to a neighbour, the United Arab Emirates, reaching into the emir's own words and phone.

In late May 2017 Qatar's state news agency and government social media were hacked and carried false quotes from Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani praising Hamas and calling Iran an 'Islamic power'. On 5 June Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Egypt and Bahrain cut ties with Qatar and began a blockade. In July the Washington Post, citing US intelligence officials, reported that senior UAE officials discussed the hacks the day before they happened; the officials could not say whether the UAE did the hacking or paid for it, and the UAE called the report false.

Separately, Reuters reported in 2019 that Project Raven, a UAE surveillance unit run through the Emirati firm DarkMatter and staffed partly by former US intelligence operatives, targeted the emir himself, among other governments and activists, using an iPhone exploit called Karma. In 2021 three of those former operatives signed deferred-prosecution agreements with the US Justice Department and paid $1.68 million. No court has made a finding against the UAE government.

Gulf-state and private networks that fund Salafi preaching, and the group Fight Impunity, are recorded as present; the Muslim Brotherhood and Interpol are marked as likely. The conditions scores are middling (state-embedded actors 6.5 of 10, resilience 5.5).
Qatar.imp: For people in Qatar, these cases show how a neighbouring government's agents could put false words in their ruler's mouth and spy on his phone, and how the hack set off a blockade of the country. Most of what is known comes from journalists and US officials, not courts. Watch for further court cases involving surveillance firms and for new disclosures about who is hacking Gulf governments.

Saudi Arabia.d:
Saudi Arabia appears on this map mostly as a state that reaches into its own companies and into other countries,.

At home the crown prince's government has shown it can take businesses from their owners without a court. From November 2017 an anti-corruption committee under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman held princes and business leaders at the Ritz-Carlton in Riyadh. The government said settlements with 87 people recovered about US$107 billion in property, companies, cash and other assets; some detainees later said they had been beaten and intimidated.

The kingdom is also the destination market for captagon pills smuggled from Syria and Lebanon through Jordan and Iraq. It executed 330 people in 2024, a large share for drug offences and many of them foreign couriers; no Saudi official appears in any adjudicated drug case on the map. Abroad, it has listed the Muslim Brotherhood as terrorist since 2014, it is recorded as a state that exports religion through the Muslim World League, and in 2017 Lebanon's prime minister announced his resignation from Riyadh.

The older ties ran through Washington. In 1974, after the Arab oil embargo, the two countries set up a Joint Commission that US auditors found in 1979 was funded almost entirely from a Saudi account at the US Treasury. Kamal Adham, head of Saudi intelligence until 1979, signed the 1976 charter of the Safari Club, a pact of five countries' intelligence chiefs, and as a major shareholder in the bank BCCI later paid a $105 million fine over its secret takeover of a Washington bank.
Saudi Arabia.imp: For people in Saudi Arabia, the 2017 purge showed that the state can take businesses and assets from their owners through a committee rather than a court. In the drug cases the heaviest punishment falls on foreign couriers rather than on anyone with power. Watch how the companies and assets taken in 2017 are used, how many people are executed for drug offences, and whether any official is ever charged in the captagon trade.

Singapore.d:
Singapore has strong institutions by this map's measure (resilience 7.8 of 10), and most of its record shows the state catching outside influence rather than being captured by it.

Its Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act of 2021 lets the Home Affairs Ministry designate people at risk of being used by foreign actors, who must then disclose donations and foreign links. In February 2024 it named the first: Philip Chan Man Ping, a Hong Kong-born businessman and patron of two government-linked grassroots bodies, who had attended China's Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, a united front body, as an overseas delegate. In 2017 the ministry expelled Huang Jing, a US-citizen professor at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, calling him an agent of influence of a foreign country it did not name; he denied it.

On money, Trident Trust and Asiaciti Trust, two of the largest offshore service providers in the 2021 Pandora Papers, administered structures for sanctioned and criminally implicated clients. Singapore's regulator fined Asiaciti for anti-money-laundering failures; neither firm has been charged over drug money. At street level, 32 men were convicted in 2025 for possessing or moving drug proceeds, facing prison and caning.

The largest case reached the US Navy from here. Leonard Francis ('Fat Leonard'), whose Singapore-based Glenn Defense Marine Asia supplied Navy ships in Asian ports, overbilled the Navy and bribed officers for years, and a civilian Navy contracting officer in Singapore quashed an early inquiry. Twenty-two people pleaded guilty, and Francis was sentenced to 15 years in 2024.
Singapore.imp: For people in Singapore, the government now has a law to name people it believes foreign states are cultivating, and it has used it. That exposes influence, but it rests on ministry judgements rather than court findings. Offshore trust firms are where the ownership of money stops being traceable, and their regulatory fines contrast with prison and caning for small-time launderers. Watch who is designated next and whether trust firms ever face charges.

Sri Lanka.d:
In Sri Lanka the outside hand that runs deepest is a Buddhist nationalist movement that found friends in the presidency, and the courts are now undoing the protection it received.

Bodu Bala Sena (BBS, 'Buddhist Power Force') is a Sinhala Buddhist nationalist monks' group founded in 2012; its leader, the monk Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara, told a 2013 rally that followers 'must become an unofficial civilian police force against Muslim extremism'. Its ties ran through the Rajapaksa family. In 2013 Defence Secretary Gotabaya Rajapaksa, the president's brother, opened its training centre in Galle District, and as president himself he appointed Gnanasara in 2021 to chair a task force drafting a single legal code under the slogan 'One Country, One Law'. The Bar Association said the task force would take over the work of Parliament.

Gnanasara was jailed for six years in 2018 for contempt of court during the case over the disappeared journalist Prageeth Eknaligoda, then pardoned by the president in 2019. In September 2026, on a petition by Sandhya Eknaligoda among others, the Supreme Court ruled the pardon arbitrary and invalid, and in October the Court of Appeal ordered him to serve the rest of his sentence.

Ranil Wickremesinghe, president from 2022 to 2024, is listed as a member of the Mont Pelerin Society, a society of free-market thinkers; no forum has found it directed his decisions. In 2019 the arrest in Dubai of a trafficking figure, Madush, produced photographs of him with police officers and politicians; he was killed in police custody in 2020 before the inquiry ended.
Sri Lanka.imp: For Sri Lankans, especially Muslims, the record shows a monk accused of stirring hatred being honoured and protected by those in power, and then the courts reversing that protection. The task force episode shows a movement leader given a role in writing law without Parliament. Watch whether the Supreme Court ruling limits future pardons, whether Gnanasara serves the sentence, and whether the death in custody in the Madush case is ever explained.

Syria.d:
Bashar al-Assad's government fell in December 2024, and Syria's record is now about the drug state it left behind and what has replaced it.

Under Assad, captagon, a pill trafficked to Jordan and the Gulf, was made and moved through the state itself. In 2023 the US, UK and EU sanctioned three of Assad's cousins, his brother Maher, who commanded the army's Fourth Armoured Division; the EU called the trade a regime-led business model. One Latakia factory run by a presidential cousin produced 84 million pills in 2020, according to the US Treasury, and a sitting MP was sanctioned over companies that made and moved the pills. These are government findings; no court has tried the trade. In August 2026 a Damascus court sentenced Bashar and Maher al-Assad to death in absentia for murder, torture and crimes against humanity, not for drugs; both live in Russia, which refuses to extradite them, and Human Rights Watch questioned whether the trial was fair.

Today the interior ministry says domestic production has been virtually eradicated, and UNODC counted 15 industrial-scale labs dismantled. But Sweida province has become the main trafficking centre, with labs held by local armed factions, and 177 million pills were intercepted across the Arab region in the year to December 2025.

Foreign forces and companies reached in too. Iran's Revolutionary Guards Quds Force commanded alongside Assad's forces from 2012, with Hezbollah fighters, and was reported to hold 55 bases in 2023, until Iran evacuated its commanders in December 2024. The French cement maker Lafarge paid about $5.92 million to the Islamic State and al-Nusra Front in 2013–14 to keep its Jalabiya plant open; it pleaded guilty in the US in 2022, and a Paris court convicted it and former executives in April 2026.
Syria.imp: For Syrians, the old state ran a drug trade through its own army division and members of the ruling family, and those named have fled or face sentences passed in their absence. The trade has not ended; it has broken up among smaller armed groups in places like Sweida that are harder to police. Foreign powers held bases on Syrian soil for more than a decade. Watch whether the new authorities keep production down without new protectors taking over, and whether any trial ever tests the captagon accusations.

Taiwan.d:
Taiwan is where China's Communist Party works hardest to reach inside another government, and Taiwan's courts are now testing that reach case by case. The money and instructions found so far land low and wide: small parties, local council candidates, village and ward chiefs, and staff working near the president and the foreign minister. China's united front system, the party's machinery for winning over or recruiting people abroad, pays for campaigns and trips, and Taiwan's Anti-Infiltration Act makes taking its money and direction a crime. The chairman of the small Gong He Party was jailed for campaigns paid for from Fujian; in Chiayi a former KMT council candidate was jailed for taking village chiefs on trips paid by a Chinese city office; four former DPP aides, one an assistant to the foreign minister and one a Presidential Office consultant, were jailed for passing President Lai's travel schedules to Chinese military intelligence; and in September 2026 a retired cabinet official got five years for trying to recruit people with access to military and legislative work. A former lawmaker and two people in a 2022 New Taipei council campaign are charged but not tried. The cases touch several parties, and the convictions can be appealed.

Organised crime is part of the same picture. The Chinese Unification Promotion Party was founded by Chang An-lo, a former leader of the Bamboo Union triad (a criminal gang). In July 2026 the Interior Ministry said it would ask the Constitutional Court to dissolve it, citing espionage, election interference and 98 crime cases linked to members since 2010. The court has not ruled.

The chip industry is reached too: in 2026 former TSMC engineers were jailed for passing 2-nanometre chip secrets to help Japan's Tokyo Electron. In the Cold War the World Anti-Communist League was based here.
Taiwan.imp: Voters in Taiwan cannot see who paid for a local campaign or a free trip to the mainland unless prosecutors dig it out, and most of what has been found sits in village and council politics, where small sums go a long way. Courts are deciding these cases one by one, and most rulings can still be appealed. The chip secrets much of the island's income depends on have already leaked once from inside TSMC. Watch the Constitutional Court's decision on the Chinese Unification Promotion Party.

Tajikistan.d:
In Tajikistan the main outside force inside the state is the drug trade. The country sits on the route that carries Afghan heroin north into Central Asia, roughly 90 tonnes a year across the region, and estimates from 2014 put drug money at up to 30 percent of Tajikistan's economy. Along the Afghan border in Khatlon province, officers paid to stop the trade have been caught working for it: in 2012 a military court jailed five Border Guard officers, the longest sentence going to the former chief of the Vakhsh checkpoint, who had 20 kilograms of hashish in his office, and a senior Khatlon police official was arrested the same day with 12 kilograms of heroin. Higher up, the record is allegation rather than proof. In 2000 the ambassador to Kazakhstan was arrested in Almaty with 86 kilograms of heroin in his car, and at the trial over the 2001 murder of the deputy interior minister, prosecutors argued he was killed for refusing to pay for a heroin consignment. Most arrests are of small dealers, so the documented record stops at checkpoint chiefs.

The government also moves against outside religious movements. The Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic network that ran schools abroad and that Turkey now treats as a terrorist group, had seven schools here; in 2015 President Emomali Rahmon closed them by decree and turned them into state schools for gifted children. The conditions scores are poor: state-embedded criminal actors score 9 of 10 and the ability to resist 2.5.
Tajikistan.imp: Along the Afghan border, the people meant to stop heroin moving north have been caught moving it, so a family in Khatlon cannot count on the checkpoint or the local police being on the law's side. With a large share of the economy possibly tied to the trade, it is hard to know which officials answer to it, and prosecutions rarely reach above checkpoint level. Outside movements can be shut by a single decree. Watch whether any border case ever reaches higher ranks.

Thailand.d:
In Thailand, drug and gambling money is reaching into the upper house of parliament and the top of the police, and both cases are still open. A sitting senator, Upakit Pachariyangkun, was indicted in 2023 on trafficking and laundering charges tied to a Myanmar businessman arrested in Bangkok and sanctioned by the US for supporting Myanmar's military government. His son-in-law was among those arrested, and over 400 million baht in property was seized from his homes. The case runs from drug production in Myanmar's Shan State into the Thai Senate. The same year the deputy national police chief was removed and investigated over an alleged protection arrangement with an online gambling network, a case that split the police leadership in public. Gambling money and drug money use the same protection and the same laundering routes. Both men are charged, not convicted.

Thailand also figures in the online drug trade. The administrator of AlphaBay, a dark-web drug market ten times the size of Silk Road at its peak, was arrested in Bangkok in 2017 and died in custody a week later, so the evidence was never tested in court.

An elite network appears too. The World Economic Forum, the Davos forum, picks people under about 40 for its Young Global Leaders programme, and its 2025 class included Paetongtarn Shinawatra while she was prime minister. Being chosen is not wrongdoing, and the record shows no influence on her decisions. The Constitutional Court removed her from office in August 2025. State-embedded criminal actors score 7 of 10.
Thailand.imp: For people in Thailand, the cases reach the senators who vote on laws and the police chiefs who enforce them, and neither has reached a verdict. If trafficking money from across the Myanmar border can reach a senator's household, the drug laws people live under are being shaped close to the trade they target. Watch the senator's trial, the police case, and whether the property seizures hold. When a key suspect dies in custody, as in AlphaBay, the public never hears the evidence.

Timor-Leste.d:
Timor-Leste's case is about a richer neighbour spying on it over the wealth under its sea, and the country still lives with the result. Its main future income lies in the oil and gas fields of the Timor Sea. In 2004, while the two countries negotiated over those fields, the Australian Secret Intelligence Service (ASIS), Australia's foreign spy agency, planted listening devices in the government building in Dili, near the cabinet room, to learn Timor-Leste's position. The talks produced the 2006 CMATS treaty, which limited Timor-Leste's claims at sea.

It came out because a former ASIS officer, known as 'Witness K', raised it. In 2013 Australia raided him and Timor-Leste's lawyer, Bernard Collaery. Timor-Leste went to the International Court of Justice, which in 2014 ordered Australia not to interfere with its legal communications, and to the Permanent Court of Arbitration. A new treaty in 2018 replaced CMATS and split revenue 80–20 in Timor-Leste's favour. In Australia, the people prosecuted were those who revealed the operation: Witness K pleaded guilty in 2021 to a secrecy offence, and the case against Collaery was dropped in 2022.

This is the only documented case for Timor-Leste, recorded twice on the map and rated established, which is why its overall score is low. State-embedded criminal actors score 4.5 of 10 and the ability to resist 3.9.
Timor-Leste.imp: For people in Timor-Leste, the oil and gas money that pays for the country's schools, clinics and roads was governed for years by a treaty negotiated while a foreign spy service listened in on their cabinet. Taking the dispute to international courts won a fairer split in 2018. The people punished were those who exposed the bugging, not those who ordered it. Whenever the government negotiates over the sea or its resources, how its own meetings are protected matters.

Turkiye.d:
In Türkiye the state itself is the largest force on this map, reaching into courts, police, army and business in the name of rooting out an infiltrator. The government blames the July 2016 coup attempt, and a 2013 corruption probe into Prime Minister Erdoğan's circle, on the Gülen movement, an Islamic network it now calls the terrorist group 'FETÖ'. After the 2013 probe it sacked the prosecutors and dropped the case. After the coup attempt it removed 2,745 judges in one day, about 15,000 military personnel, roughly 23,000 police and some 150,000 public employees in all, by decree rather than by trial. Its trustee fund, the TMSF, seized 784 companies said to be Gülen-linked, worth TL 42.3 billion; more than 600 were returned, and by October 2025 the fund held 1,056 businesses in all. The chase reaches abroad: the state religious directorate, the Diyanet, had its imams report on Gülen followers from 38 countries, and Interpol refused 773 Turkish arrest requests as political.

The same courts have convicted and then cleared. About 300 officers convicted in the 2012 'Sledgehammer' coup-plot case were acquitted in 2015 after the evidence was found forged, and the 2013 'Ergenekon' convictions, which included three opposition MPs, were overturned in 2016 for lack of proof the network existed. The government now blames those prosecutions on Gülen-linked officials.

Organised crime runs alongside nationalist politics. The 1996 Susurluk crash put a police chief, an MP and a wanted Grey Wolves gunman (the Grey Wolves are the youth wing of the nationalist MHP party) in one car, and parliament found state bodies had used the group. Crime boss Alaattin Çakıcı was freed in 2020 under a law passed with the MHP. This goes back to the Cold War, when a NATO 'Counter-Guerrilla' sat inside the army.
Turkiye.imp: For people in Türkiye, a judge, officer, teacher or police officer can lose a job by decree on an accusation of Gülen links, and the courts that rule on such accusations have convicted people before and later found the evidence forged. A state fund that controls over a thousand businesses gives the government direct power over jobs and media. Public accusations that ministers protected crime bosses have never been tested in a courtroom. Watch what happens to the seized companies and how the remaining Gülen trials proceed.

Turkmenistan.d:
In Turkmenistan the documented outside force is a foreign religious movement, and what the record shows is the state removing it with long prison terms. The Gülen movement, a Turkish Islamic network that opened schools across Central Asia in the 1990s and that Turkey's government now treats as a terrorist group, ran schools here until 2011, when Turkmenistan closed or took over most of them. In late 2016, the year of the failed coup attempt in Turkey, more than 100 people were detained, most with some Gülen link. Eighteen men were convicted in closed trials and given 12 to 25 years for inciting hatred and taking part in a criminal organisation. The map files the case under 'Churches and movements placing members in the state' and 'Turkey's long arm: chasing the Gülen movement'.

These facts come from a joint 2017 statement by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and the Norwegian Helsinki Committee, and are rated established. Because the trials were closed, no one outside can see what evidence was used, and the government publishes little, so rights groups are the main source of what is known. With sentences that long, the case is still felt.

It is the one documented case for Turkmenistan, so its overall score is low. Its conditions are among the weakest anywhere: state-embedded criminal actors score 9 of 10 and the ability to resist only 2.2.
Turkmenistan.imp: For people in Turkmenistan, a past tie to a school or religious group that was once allowed to operate can bring up to 25 years in prison, decided in a courtroom the public cannot enter. Families learn what happened mainly through foreign rights groups, because the state publishes little. Watch for further arrests tied to foreign religious or educational groups, and whether any of the eighteen men are released.

United Arab Emirates.d:
The United Arab Emirates appears on this map in two roles: as the place where money from crime networks elsewhere is settled, and as a government buying its way into international bodies. Dubai is the settlement point. US Treasury actions have named exchange houses and trading companies here moving money for Afghan heroin networks and other sanctioned groups. Dubai free-zone companies, whose real owners are visible only to the zone authority, turned up behind a Bosnian cocaine organisation that prosecutors say also paid politicians at home. A US drug agency task force found that Kaloti, one of the world's largest gold refiners, bought metal from suspected launderers, and an auditor had found more than $5.2 billion in cash-for-gold deals in 2012; Treasury dropped the case and the company denies it. Hidden company ownership kept the UAE on the FATF 'grey list' of weak anti-laundering countries from 2022 to 2024. In 2025 North Korean hackers stole about $1.5 billion from Dubai crypto exchange Bybit through a software supplier.

Abu Dhabi reaches outward. From 2021 to 2025 a senior UAE interior ministry officer, Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi, was president of Interpol, the global police cooperation body, after the UAE gave its foundation donations reported at about $54 million, roughly the other 194 members' dues combined; Interpol rejects that this bought the vote. French anti-terror prosecutors opened an inquiry into torture complaints against him, which he denies. At the 2023 COP28 climate summit, the president, also head of the state oil firm ADNOC, had talking points on company deals for meetings with governments; he called the claims false.

At home the state lists the Muslim Brotherhood and the local group Islah as terrorist, and jailed 56 Islah members in 2013. In 1991 Abu Dhabi owned 77% of BCCI, a bank that collapsed in fraud.
United Arab Emirates.imp: For people in the UAE, the banks, gold traders and free zones around them carry money from drug networks on other continents, and company ownership is hidden from the public, so residents cannot see who owns many of the firms they deal with. The government that placed its officer at the head of Interpol has jailed members of a domestic Islamist group for plotting to seize power. Watch whether the French torture inquiry goes further, whether company ownership becomes visible after the grey listing, and how the gold and crypto trades are supervised.

Uzbekistan.d:
In Uzbekistan, foreign telecom companies bought their way into the mobile phone market through the president's family, and courts and regulators in several countries have since confirmed it. When mobile phones spread, a company needed state licences and radio frequencies to operate. Three foreign firms got them by paying companies controlled by Gulnara Karimova, elder daughter of the late president Islam Karimov. VimpelCom settled US bribery charges in 2016 for $795 million; Telia, the Swedish-Finnish telecom group, agreed in 2017 to pay about $965 million to US, Dutch and Swedish authorities; and Russia's MTS settled in 2019 for $850 million. Uzbek prosecutors put her kickbacks at $869.3 million, and the reporting group OCCRP said she took over $1 billion from Scandinavian and Russian telecom firms. Access to a whole national market passed through one family at the top, and the money was traced because prosecutors in the US and Europe acted. Karimova was convicted in Uzbekistan in 2017 and 2020 and is in prison; Switzerland dropped its own trial in 2026.

Beyond this, China's police 'overseas service stations' are recorded as present. Turkey's Gülen movement, the Turkish nationalist Grey Wolves and Hizb ut-Tahrir, an Islamist group that seeks a single Islamic state, are likely present, but no case is documented for them. The conditions scores are weak: state-embedded criminal actors score 7 of 10 and the ability to resist only 3.8.
Uzbekistan.imp: For people in Uzbekistan, the mobile service they bought came from companies that had entered the market by paying the president's daughter, and hundreds of millions of dollars left the country through her firms. The money was found only because foreign prosecutors went after the companies. Watch whether licences in other sectors, such as energy or mining, go through family-linked firms in the same way, and whether money recovered in these cases is returned to Uzbekistan.

Vietnam.d:
In Vietnam, drug networks running between Laos and Vietnam have reached into the police squads meant to catch them, under some of the harshest drug laws anywhere. In Hanoi, two former officers of a district drug investigation team were indicted in 2024 for shielding a Laos–Vietnam network that moved 137 kilograms. In Viet Tri, in Phu Tho province, a senior officer was sentenced to life in 2025 for paying for 12,000 drug tablets he meant to use in a staged arrest. Vietnam executes traffickers caught with such amounts, which shows the scale of what these officers were covering. The cases so far reach district and city level.

The other case runs the opposite way: the state naming an outside group as an infiltrator. Viet Tan is a pro-democracy party founded by Vietnamese exiles in 1982 and based in the United States. In October 2016 Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security designated it a terrorist organisation, saying it trained people to enter Vietnam and plotted sabotage. Human rights groups and foreign governments dispute this, and the US government has said there is no evidence it is a terrorist group. Vietnamese courts have jailed people accused of membership, and the label stays in force.

Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation, is recorded as present, with no case against it. State-embedded criminal actors score 7 of 10 and the ability to resist 4.8.
Vietnam.imp: For people in Vietnam, the drug squads meant to keep trafficking out of their towns have in some cases protected it, or staged arrests. At the same time, links to an exile party the state calls terrorist can bring prison, though outside governments see no evidence for the label. Watch whether drug-corruption cases reach above district level, and how the terrorism label is used in court against people accused of membership.

Yemen.d:
In Yemen, foreign governments sit inside the war and inside the government fighting it. The documented case is the United Arab Emirates. The Southern Transitional Council (STC) was formed in May 2017 with UAE help to seek a separate state in the south. In April 2022 it joined the eight-member Presidential Leadership Council that heads the internationally recognised government, and its leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi became a vice-president, so a movement built with a foreign power's help sat at the top of the state.

That arrangement has now broken down. After an STC offensive in December 2025 and a Saudi-backed counter-offensive, al-Zubaidi fled to the UAE in January 2026 and was removed from the council. A delegation in Riyadh announced the STC dissolved; its UAE-based spokesman rejected that. The case is rated probable and still unfolding, with Abu Dhabi and Riyadh backing opposite sides inside the same government.

Other outside forces are recorded as present: the Muslim Brotherhood, Hezbollah, the network of Iran's Revolutionary Guards Quds Force and allied militias, and the UAE's DarkMatter / Project Raven, but this map documents no specific case for them yet. Conditions are severe: state-embedded criminal actors score 8 of 10 and the ability to resist only 1.9.
Yemen.imp: For people in Yemen, decisions about the south, and about who governs it, have been shaped in Abu Dhabi and Riyadh as much as inside Yemen, while the war goes on around them. A vice-president whose movement a foreign state helped build has now fled to that state. Watch who replaces al-Zubaidi on the leadership council, whether the STC really dissolves, and which foreign capitals the remaining council members answer to.

Australia.d:
In Australia the outside hands sit in three places: borders and building sites, where organised crime has people inside; politics, where China and India have cultivated donors, MPs and police; and banks and casinos that let criminal cash through. Courts have convicted Border Force and state police officers for helping drug imports through Sydney and Melbourne, where wholesale drug prices are the highest of any market on the map. In Victoria, the construction arm of the CFMEU union, which works on state-funded projects, has been under federal administration since 2024 after reports that bikie gang members held roles in it.

On foreign states, donor Huang Xiangmo, who chaired a council described as a peak body for groups tied to the Chinese Communist Party's United Front influence arm, gave, with associates, about A$2 million to Labor and over A$1 million to the Liberals; Senator Sam Dastyari resigned over him, his residency was cancelled on ASIO advice, and an inquiry traced A$100,000 in disguised cash from him to NSW Labor. Di Sanh Duong became the first person convicted under the 2018 interference law. Two Indian intelligence officers were expelled in 2020 after a 'nest of spies' cultivated politicians and a state police force. The Port of Darwin, near a base used by US Marines, is leased for 99 years to Landbridge, whose owner has Party ties; both parties pledged in 2025 to take it back and the company is fighting in arbitration.

Money: Commonwealth Bank and Westpac paid record penalties for laundering-reporting failures, and Crown and The Star were both found unfit for casino licences. AUSTRAC sought A$400 million from The Star, which was rescued by a A$300 million investment. A PwC partner shared confidential Treasury tax plans with 53 colleagues.
Australia.imp: For Australians, this shows up at the docks, on public building sites and in the casinos. Corrupt border officers let drugs in, a union on taxpayer-funded projects carried gang members, and casinos and banks let laundered money move for years before regulators caught it. Foreign governments have reached ministers through donors and community groups. The country's tools do work: ASIO advice, anti-corruption commissions, the interference law and large penalties. Watch the Darwin arbitration, the CFMEU inquiries and whether Treasury keeps hiring firms that advise the companies it taxes.

Fiji.d:
In Fiji the outside hand on record is China's police ministry working inside the national police force, the same arrangement found across the western Pacific in Kiribati, the Solomon Islands and Vanuatu. It rests on a 2011 cooperation agreement signed while Fiji was under military rule. From 2013 China's Ministry of Public Security posted two officers at a time inside the Fiji Police Force, and in 2021 it added a police liaison officer at its embassy. What that access allowed was shown in 2017, when Chinese police working with Fijian officials arrested 77 Chinese nationals in Fiji and flew them to China.

In March 2024 Home Affairs Minister Pio Tikoduadua said Fiji had asked China to withdraw its embedded officers. The agreement itself was kept, with reviews every six months, and Fijian officers still go to China for training. So the officers are gone but the channel is still open. Fiji's drug intelligence chief has also raised concern that traffickers moving cocaine through the Pacific are reaching into law enforcement, as police in Papua New Guinea have admitted. Shincheonji, a South Korean church, has a recorded presence but no case links it to government.
Fiji.imp: For people in Fiji, the question is who their police answer to. A foreign police service inside the force could see local records and help arrest people on Fijian soil, as it did in 2017. Training abroad keeps shaping how officers think about policing and protest. Watch the six-monthly reviews of the 2011 agreement, whether their findings are published, and whether drug money is reaching officers here as it has in Papua New Guinea.

Kiribati.d:
In Kiribati, China's police are working inside the national force today, part of a wider pattern in the western Pacific where Fiji, the Solomon Islands and Vanuatu have taken in Chinese police advisers or training. It follows a diplomatic switch. Kiribati recognised Beijing instead of Taiwan in 2019 and asked China for policing help in 2022. The acting police commissioner, Eeri Aritiera, confirmed in 2024 that up to a dozen uniformed Chinese officers work alongside local police on six-month rotations. They do community policing, teach martial arts and give IT support for a crime database.

The database is the part to notice: it holds information on residents, and foreign officers helping to run it gain sight of it. No case shows this access being misused, and the arrangement is public and acknowledged. Fiji shows where such arrangements can lead, since Chinese officers there took part in arresting and removing 77 Chinese nationals in 2017. Kiribati's scores for criminal actors inside the state are among the lowest on the map, and its capacity to resist is modest, which leaves the police deal as the main route in on record. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, also has a recorded presence.
Kiribati.imp: For people in Kiribati, foreign officers on patrol and helping run the crime records change who can see their information and act on it. Policing that answered only to Kiribati now has a second partner with interests of its own. Officers who rotate every six months also take what they learn home. Watch whether the rotations continue after review, whether the terms are published, and who controls the crime database.

Marshall Islands.d:
In the Marshall Islands the one proven case is outsiders paying lawmakers to carve out a piece of the country, and it was proven in a New York court rather than at home. From about 2016 to 2020, Cary Yan and Gina Zhou, China-born businesspeople who had bought Marshallese passports, paid tens of thousands of dollars to officials, legislators among them, to pass a law creating a semi-autonomous 'Rongelap Atoll Special Administrative Region'. Rongelap is an atoll, and the plan would have given it its own rules. Both pleaded guilty in the United States and were sentenced in 2023, Yan to 42 months.

The United States then barred former president Kessai Note and MP Mike Halferty from entry for taking the bribes, a sanction, not a conviction; Note denies it. The case follows a pattern seen across small Pacific states in the record: in Nauru, Australian firms are charged with or reported as paying ministers; in the Solomon Islands, MPs say both Beijing and Taipei offered them money over diplomatic recognition. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta has a recorded presence.
Marshall Islands.imp: For Marshallese people, the scheme would have turned part of their country into a zone with rules written for its investors, and the votes for it were bought. Bought passports gave the buyers a way in. The case was exposed by US prosecutors, not by Marshallese institutions. Watch for new special-zone or passport schemes before parliament, and whether officials named by the US face any process at home.

Micronesia.d:
In the Federated States of Micronesia the record holds one serious accusation, made from the top. In March 2023 the outgoing president, David Panuelo, sent a 13-page letter accusing China of 'political warfare' against his country: bribery of officials and threats, aimed at keeping Micronesia on Beijing's side, or at least neutral, in any war over Taiwan. He wrote that he had considered switching diplomatic recognition to Taiwan. China rejected the claims, and no court or inquiry has tested them, so this stays an allegation.

It fits what the record shows around the western Pacific, where the contest between Beijing and Taipei is played out in small parliaments and police forces. In the Solomon Islands, MPs said both governments offered them money over the 2019 recognition switch, and a fund paid for by China later reached 39 of 50 MPs. In Kiribati, Fiji and Vanuatu, Chinese police work alongside or train local forces. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta also has a recorded presence.
Micronesia.imp: For Micronesians, a president's warning that officials are being paid or pressured by a foreign power means public decisions on security and alliances may not be made on their merits. Because nothing was investigated, people cannot tell how far it went. Watch whether later governments look into Panuelo's claims and whether new aid or security deals are published in full.

Nauru.d:
In Nauru the money that reaches politicians comes from Australia, through the two things that keep the island's economy going: phosphate, its main mineral, and Australia's offshore asylum centre. On phosphate, Australian prosecutors have charged Getax Australia, a Gold Coast trader, with conspiring to bribe Nauruan politicians from 2007 to 2012 to win deals; the case keeps being delayed. In a related case a Sydney businessman, Mozammil Bhojani, admitted paying over $120,000 to a Nauruan MP and a minister and was jailed in 2018.

On detention, Australia pays contractors such as Broadspectrum, Canstruct and Paladin to run the centre. A 2023 investigation by the Sydney Morning Herald and The Age found subcontracts worth millions went to firms tied to Nauru's leaders, including over $120,000 in suspect payments to justice minister David Adeang and about $2.6 million to a company of Lionel Aingimea, who later became president. The reporters said they were not claiming the payments were bribes, Adeang denies it, and they reported that Australia's Home Affairs department had been warned of bribery allegations since 2010.

The same Australian contractor model reached Manus Island in Papua New Guinea, where a former Paladin director alleged payments to officials there. On Nauru, the phosphate case is charged and the detention payments only reported.
Nauru.imp: For people on Nauru, the decisions that bring in most of the country's money, phosphate sales and the asylum centre contracts, may have been shaped by payments to the people making them. Residents cannot see who gets paid under these deals, and the cases have been pursued in Australia rather than at home. Watch the Getax trial, if it is held, and whether Australia publishes which local firms its contractors pay.

New Zealand.d:
New Zealand's record is light and mostly about networks and money rather than proven capture. The sharpest case concerns China. Jian Yang, a National Party MP from 2011 to 2020, had been a Communist Party member and taught at Chinese military schools that trained intelligence linguists before he moved to New Zealand. Reports in 2021 said he retired after intelligence agencies raised concerns, and that the prime minister and opposition leader agreed Labour MP Raymond Huo would also leave. Both parties were involved and no charge followed. Organisations tied to the Chinese state are present, as in Australia, though the record has less on them here.

On money, SkyCity, the casino operator, agreed a NZ$4.16 million penalty in 2024 for failing to monitor high-value play, and faced similar proceedings in Australia over its Adelaide casino, in a country paying the world's highest methamphetamine prices.

The rest is lawful membership of private networks, not wrongdoing. Ruth Richardson, Finance Minister from 1990, belonged to the Mont Pelerin Society, a free-market thinkers' society. Jacinda Ardern, prime minister from 2017, was in the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme. David Seymour, ACT leader and Deputy Prime Minister since 2025, worked for a Canadian think tank in the Atlas Network, which links free-market groups; Atlas's chair is the daughter of an ACT co-founder. A Round Table group existed from 1910.
New Zealand.imp: For New Zealanders, the main concern on record is quiet: foreign-linked people inside parliament, handled by private deals between party leaders rather than in public. Casinos remain a place where drug cash can be washed. Networks linking ministers to outside think tanks are legal, but people may want to know who funds them. Watch how foreign interference is handled in the open and how SkyCity's controls hold up.

Palau.d:
In Palau the record shows an organised crime leader trying to buy a foothold through former officials, and Palau's president stopping it. Wan Kuok-koi, known as 'Broken Tooth', is the former head of Macau's 14K triad, a criminal gang; the US sanctioned him in 2020 and its Treasury says he sits on a Chinese Communist Party United Front body, the Party's influence arm. OCCRP, a network of investigative reporters, found in 2022 that he visited Palau in 2018 as a 'guest of the government'. A former postmaster general and a former governor of Airai state became directors of his Palau 'Hongmen' cultural association, registered in 2019 to plan a casino zone on the island of Angaur.

President Tommy Remengesau opposed the casino in April 2019, and the association applied to dissolve. OCCRP did not find that the Chinese state directed the effort. The approach resembles others on the map in the Pacific: special zones sought through local officials, as with the bribed Rongelap law in the Marshall Islands. Hong Kong and Macau triads are likely present but not documented.
Palau.imp: For Palauans, a casino zone run by a triad leader would have brought gambling money, and the crime that follows it, onto a small island, with former officials as local partners. It was stopped by a president's refusal, not by any law. The episode also showed that former officials can lend their names to such ventures. Watch for new casino, special-zone or 'cultural association' proposals, and who sits on their boards.

Papua New Guinea.d:
In Papua New Guinea, outside interests have reached the police, the prime minister's office and Australia's detention business, and the country's own conditions scores are among the weakest in this region. Drug traffickers are using the country as a stopover. After a plane carrying 548 kilograms of cocaine crashed near Port Moresby in 2020, the police commissioner said publicly that there are criminals in uniform in the constabulary. The Australian organisers were convicted in Victoria and the pilot jailed, but the officers said to have enabled night flights were never charged.

At the top, the government of Peter O'Neill borrowed about US$1.2 billion through the Swiss bank UBS in 2014 to buy shares in Oil Search, an oil and gas firm, against cabinet advice and before parliament agreed; the treasurer who objected was removed. A Commission of Inquiry found the loan unlawful, said the state lost about $432 million while UBS earned about $83 million, and proposed a 10-year ban on the bank. O'Neill was later charged with lying to the inquiry.

Third, Australia paid Paladin A$530 million to run its asylum centre on Manus Island from 2017 to 2019. A former Paladin director alleged in 2023 that over $3 million went to a businessman close to senior PNG officials, including a $1.5 million invoice marked 'Visas'. The company's ex-chief denies it, and this remains an allegation, as in Nauru.
Papua New Guinea.imp: For Papua New Guineans, police who help traffickers make communities less safe, and an unlawful loan cost the state hundreds of millions that could have gone to services. Offshore detention contracts may have paid officials rather than the public. Watch whether officers named in the cocaine case are charged, whether the UBS ban is enforced, and the outcome of O'Neill's case.

Samoa.d: This write-up is a best guess: the map has no documented case for Samoa. The one organisation with a recorded presence is Shincheonji, a South Korean church, and nothing links it to government. Samoa's conditions scores are low to middling; criminal actors inside the state score low and its capacity to resist sits near the middle. Judging from its neighbours, the likeliest routes in would be those seen elsewhere in the Pacific: Chinese police placed in local forces, as in Fiji, Kiribati and the Solomon Islands, or money reaching members of parliament, as in the Marshall Islands and Nauru. That is an estimate, not a finding.
Samoa.imp: No case of outside capture is recorded for Samoa. That could mean little is happening or that little has been looked at. The warning signs nearby are foreign police inside local forces and payments to lawmakers. Residents can watch for new policing agreements with foreign governments, for outside money reaching MPs, and for whether such deals are published in full.

Solomon Islands.d:
The Solomon Islands is where the contest between Beijing and Taipei has reached furthest into a Pacific government, through money to MPs and Chinese police on the ground. In 2019 Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare ended 36 years of ties with Taiwan and recognised China. MPs told reporters both governments had offered them hundreds of thousands of dollars over the vote, and anger over the switch fed the riots in Honiara in November 2021.

After the switch, China funded the prime minister's discretionary fund, as Taiwan had done before. The prime minister's secretary told a parliamentary committee in 2022 that about US$2.49 million from China was paid out in 2021, and that 39 of the 50 MPs got payments in two tranches, in the same month Sogavare survived a no-confidence vote. The opposition said he used it to stay in power; his office denied it.

China sent police advisers after the riots and signed a 2022 security agreement that lets the government call in Chinese police and military. In 2025 Chinese police began a local trial of a community surveillance model called 'Fengqiao'; it was stopped after local objections. In May 2026 Matthew Wale, the opposition leader who had made that accusation, became prime minister and promised to review the security deal. The conditions scores here show high levels of criminal actors inside the state.
Solomon Islands.imp: For Solomon Islanders, when most MPs take money from a fund paid by a foreign government, it is hard to know whose interest a vote serves. Foreign police trying out surveillance methods in local communities change how people are watched. Riots in the capital showed how far that distrust can go. Watch Wale's review of the security agreement and whether the prime minister's fund is opened to audit.

Tonga.d:
Tonga's one documented case is older but explains a lasting weakness: its state money was once run by a royal favourite and lost. Before 1997 Tonga sold passports to Hong Kong residents and put the money into the Tonga Trust Fund. American adviser Jesse Bogdonoff, whom King Taufa'ahau Tupou IV named his official court jester in 1999, moved the fund into a viatical firm, one that buys the life-insurance policies of people who are ill. The firm went bankrupt in 2002, and about $33 million was lost, around 40 per cent of a year's state revenue. Tonga sued him, and he settled in 2004 without admitting fraud.

The passport-sale business behind it is a trade still found in small states, in which citizenship is sold to raise money; buyers gain a new nationality and the state gains a fund that few people oversee. In the Marshall Islands, bought passports later gave a pair of businesspeople the standing to bribe lawmakers. Tonga's conditions scores show a fair amount of criminal activity inside the state and middling capacity to resist. The record has nothing current in Tonga, so the present picture is thin.
Tonga.imp: For Tongans, the lost fund meant less for schools, roads and services, and it showed how a single adviser close to the throne could move the state's savings. Passport sales also let outsiders acquire citizenship with little scrutiny. Watch for any return of passport or citizenship sales, who controls the money they raise, and whether the fund's accounts are published.

Tuvalu.d: This write-up is a best guess: the map has no documented case for Tuvalu and no organisation with a recorded presence there. Its conditions scores are low, with criminal actors inside the state among the lowest on the map and a middling capacity to resist. Judging from neighbours in the record, the likeliest routes in would be a foreign government offering police cooperation, as China has done in Kiribati and the Solomon Islands, money reaching MPs, as in the Marshall Islands, or an outside business seeking a special zone, as in Palau. That is an estimate, not a finding.
Tuvalu.imp: No case of outside capture is recorded for Tuvalu. In a very small state a handful of people can decide a great deal, so one deal can matter. Any change is most likely to arrive through foreign aid, police or business offers. Residents can watch who funds such deals, whether their terms go before parliament, and whether they are published.

Vanuatu.d:
In Vanuatu, China's police ministry is building a role inside local policing, following the same path it took in Fiji, Kiribati and the Solomon Islands. Chinese police advisers have worked in Vanuatu since 2023. In September 2025 the internal affairs minister, Andrew Solomon Napuat, met China's Minister of Public Security, Wang Xiaohong, in Beijing. China gave police equipment worth about NZ$720,000, including motorcycles and drones, and the two governments said they were discussing a wider policing partnership. Nothing in the record shows wrongdoing; this is an open, agreed arrangement.

What matters is where such deals have led nearby. In Fiji, Chinese officers embedded under a 2011 pact took part in arresting 77 Chinese nationals and flying them to China, and were later asked to leave. In the Solomon Islands, a security pact allows Chinese police and military to be called in, and a surveillance-policing trial there was stopped after local objections. Drones and a broader partnership could give a foreign ministry a similar place in how Vanuatu watches and polices its people. Vanuatu's conditions scores are middling for criminal actors inside the state and capacity to resist.
Vanuatu.imp: For people in Vanuatu, equipment and advisers from a foreign police ministry can shape who is watched and how arrests are made. Drones extend that reach over towns and islands. Watch the terms of any wider policing partnership, whether they come before parliament, whether foreign officers gain access to local records, and whether people in Vanuatu are ever handed to China, as happened in Fiji.

Albania.d:
Albania is in the middle of clearing organised crime out of its own state, and drug money keeps finding new ways back in. Since 2017 an EU-monitored vetting has checked every judge and prosecutor in the country, and about half of those assessed have been removed or forced out, mostly because they could not explain their wealth; these are administrative removals, not criminal convictions. A 2015 'decriminalisation' law, agreed across parties, bars people with serious convictions at home or abroad from office. By 2020 it had pushed out seven MPs, three mayors, among them the mayor of Kavaja over an Italian drug-trafficking record, and about 600 state employees.

The reach has gone to the top of the police. Saimir Tahiri was interior minister, in charge of the police, until 2017. Italian police arrested his cousin in a probe into a group moving over 3.5 tonnes of cannabis, and wiretaps mentioned him; he was convicted in 2019 of abuse of office, but not of trafficking. Now the money is cocaine. In 2026 the special anti-corruption prosecutor, SPAK, issued 20 arrest warrants and seized over 100 million euros, tracing cocaine proceeds into coastal land and high-rises going up in Tirana. Its file refers to meetings with senior state officials it does not name. These are charges, not verdicts.

Iran reached in too. Albania hosts about 3,000 members of an Iranian opposition group, the MEK. In 2022 a cyberattack shut down government online services; Albania found Iran behind it and cut ties, and Iran called this baseless.
Albania.imp: For people in Albania, the vetting and the decriminalisation law have removed hundreds of judges, prosecutors, lawmakers and officials who should not have been deciding their cases or writing their laws. But cocaine money is now going into the coast and the towers of Tirana, and that decides who owns them. Senior officials named only as meeting the traffickers have not been identified. Watch whether SPAK names them, whether the vetted courts convict at senior levels, and who ends up holding the coastal land.

Andorra.d:
In Andorra, a foreign head of state sits inside the government by law, and the banking system is where foreign crime money was said to have entered. Under the 1993 constitution, whoever is president of France is automatically one of Andorra's two co-princes, alongside the Catholic Bishop of Urgell; Emmanuel Macron has held the role since 2017. Acting alone, the French co-prince appoints a member of the Constitutional Tribunal and of the judicial council and must agree to treaties. Together with Andorra's head of government he appoints the head of government, calls elections and signs laws into force. This is open and written into law.

The banking story is unsettled. In March 2015 the US Treasury's anti-laundering office, FinCEN, named Banca Privada d'Andorra (BPA) a 'primary money laundering concern', saying its senior managers served criminal groups from Russia and China and Venezuelan launderers, moving hundreds of millions through US banks. Andorra took the bank over the next day and wound it up within a week, and clients had to prove their own money legitimate to get it back. Then the record split. FinCEN withdrew its finding in 2016 and Spanish courts dismissed laundering cases against the bank, but in July 2025 an Andorran court sentenced eighteen executives, the former chief executive to seven years and a 30 million euro fine. They are appealing, and some named clients have never been convicted.

Andorra's conditions scores are strong: few state-embedded criminal actors (1 of 10) and good resilience (8).
Andorra.imp: For people in Andorra, part of the country's top authority belongs to whoever French voters elect, and he takes part in choosing their head of government and signing their laws; that is legal and public. The BPA case showed that one foreign regulator's notice can close a national bank overnight and leave its customers proving their savings legitimate, while courts in different countries reach different answers years later. Watch the appeal of the 2025 sentences and whether former clients recover their funds.

Austria.d:
Austria is one of the places where Russia's reach into a European government has gone furthest, through open party ties and a spy inside the security service. In 2016 the leaders of the Freedom Party (FPÖ) signed a five-year cooperation pact with United Russia, Putin's party, and FPÖ ministers then sat in government from 2017 to 2019. Karin Kneissl, the FPÖ's foreign minister, at whose wedding Putin was a guest, joined the board of Rosneft, Russia's state oil company, in 2021 and moved to Russia in 2023. These ties were legal. The criminal case reached the interior ministry: in May 2026 a Vienna court convicted Egisto Ott, a former officer of Austria's old domestic intelligence agency, of spying for Russia through Jan Marsalek, the fugitive former Wirecard executive. Ott searched police databases for people Moscow wanted found, passed on a journalist's address, sold a secure laptop and handed over three work phones from the interior minister's office. He plans to appeal.

Turkey reaches in through religion and nationalism. Austria bans foreign funding of religious bodies, and in 2018 it reviewed the permits of about 40 imams of ATIB, the Austrian branch of Turkey's state religious directorate, saying ATIB got round the ban. Since 2019 the salute of the Grey Wolves, a Turkish nationalist movement, is banned. Raids in 2020 against suspected Muslim Brotherhood networks were later ruled unlawful.

Vienna is also the banking hub for the Balkan corridor: Raiffeisen Bank International is under supervisory pressure over its eastern exposure, with no penalty imposed. Former chancellor Sebastian Kurz was a WEF Young Global Leader, which is not a finding of influence. In the Cold War a secret anti-communist force was raised by a later interior minister, and the US hid more than 80 weapons caches here.
Austria.imp: For people in Austria, the clearest lesson is that one insider could open police databases and ministry phones to a foreign power, and that a governing party had a formal pact with Putin's party while its ministers held office. Muslim and Turkish-Austrian communities are caught between foreign state influence over their mosques and police raids a court later found unlawful. Watch Ott's appeal, further cases tied to Marsalek, and how the Raiffeisen inquiries end.

Belarus.d:
In Belarus, Russia's hold reaches the presidency and the army, and both governments say so openly. After the disputed 2020 election, when Alexander Lukashenko faced mass protests, Vladimir Putin promised him a 1.5 billion dollar loan. In February 2022 Russian forces launched part of their invasion of Ukraine from Belarusian soil, and the same month a referendum rewrote the constitution to drop the ban on nuclear weapons and allow permanent Russian bases. In 2023 Russia supplied Iskander-M missiles, which can carry nuclear warheads, and Putin said warheads had been delivered; he has said Russia keeps control of them. The decision to use weapons stationed in Belarus rests in Moscow, and Belarusian territory has served as a launch ground for Russia's war.

This is the one documented case for Belarus, rated established, severe and happening now. It places Belarus as a target country in 'Russia's networks in Europe and Africa' and 'Governments buying officials in other countries'. The Russkiy Mir Foundation, a Russian state body promoting Russian language and culture abroad, and Interpol are likely present, but no case is recorded for them. The conditions are poor: state-embedded criminal actors score 9 of 10 and the ability to resist only 3.1.
Belarus.imp: For people in Belarus, decisions about war and nuclear weapons on their own soil are now made with Moscow, and Russia says it controls the warheads. The 2022 referendum removed the constitutional limits that once stood in the way. Because both governments state this openly, the question is less what is hidden than what citizens can still decide. Watch for more Russian bases, troop movements and any further changes to the constitution.

Belgium.d:
Belgium hosts the European Union's institutions and Europe's largest cocaine port, and outside forces are reaching into both. In Brussels, foreign governments and companies are accused of paying members of the European Parliament, which votes on laws for 27 countries. In the Qatargate case police seized about €1.5 million in cash in 2022; prosecutors say Qatar and Morocco paid to sway Parliament through Fight Impunity, an NGO run by former MEP Pier Antonio Panzeri, who took a plea deal. Vice-president Eva Kaili and others are charged and deny it, and in February 2026 an appeals court let the case go on. In a second case, prosecutors allege people around a former lobbyist for Huawei, the Chinese telecoms firm, paid MEPs to sign a 2021 letter against curbs on foreign 5G equipment; eight are charged, and Parliament lifted one Italian MEP's immunity in June 2026. Spies work the same buildings: Hungary's EU mission ran a recruitment ring against Commission staff from 2012 to 2018, and the US NSA bugged EU offices. NATO's Mark Rutte and five Commissioners attend the private Bilderberg meetings, which is legal.

In Antwerp, cocaine networks buy people with access. Port workers, police and customs staff have been convicted of extracting containers and passing information, and in 2022 the justice minister was put under protection after a kidnap plot. Seizures reached 116 tonnes in 2023.

Foreign governments reached the Belgian state too. A former senator took money from China's Ministry of State Security, but a gap in the law blocked prosecution. Belgium ended Saudi control of the Great Mosque of Brussels in 2018, then found Moroccan intelligence officers and a Turkish Diyanet employee in the body that followed. Britain's GCHQ hacked the state telecom Belgacom. A 1991 Senate inquiry exposed the Cold War NATO stay-behind network.
Belgium.imp: For people in Belgium, cash from foreign governments and companies has reached lawmakers who write rules for all of Europe, and most of those cases are charges still to be tested. At home, the cocaine trade through Antwerp buys port staff and police, and threats have reached the justice minister. A Belgian politician paid by Chinese intelligence could not be prosecuted. Watch the Qatargate and Huawei trials, whether Belgium closes that legal gap, and how port staff are screened.

Bosnia and Herzegovina.d:
In Bosnia and Herzegovina, foreign governments hold real power inside the state from two opposite directions, and cocaine money has reached officials. The Office of the High Representative, set up under the 1995 Dayton peace deal, answers to the Peace Implementation Council, a group of foreign governments. Since 1997 its 'Bonn powers' have let it impose binding laws and remove officials; by 2004 it had dismissed 139 officials, 58 of them in one day. Germany's Christian Schmidt has held the post since 2021, and Russia, China and some Bosnian politicians call his appointment illegitimate and want the office closed.

Russia backs those resisting him in Republika Srpska, the country's Serb-run entity. Its police signed a cooperation deal on intelligence and counter-terrorism with Russia's interior ministry in 2016, and its leader Milorad Dodik, who pushed for secession, met Putin at least five times from 2022. In 2025 a Bosnian court banned Dodik from politics for six years for defying the envoy. The US had sanctioned him for obstructing the peace deal, then lifted the sanctions in October 2025, a day after he met Russia's foreign minister.

Cocaine networks are the third force. In April 2024, in Operation Black Tie, 23 people were arrested in Sarajevo for trafficking and laundering for the circle of a kingpin already sentenced in the Netherlands, and Europol said corrupt officials were among them. Bosnian prosecutors also allege that a separate organisation, run by trafficker Gacanin through Dubai companies, paid politicians and worked with the head of the state security service. These are charges, not verdicts.
Bosnia and Herzegovina.imp: For people in Bosnia, laws can be imposed and elected officials removed by an envoy who answers to foreign governments, while Russia backs the leaders resisting him, and voters have limited say over either. Cocaine networks are accused of reaching officials and even the head of the state security service. Watch whether the High Representative's office stays open, what Dodik does under his ban, and whether the officials arrested in Operation Black Tie come to trial.

Bulgaria.d:
In Bulgaria the question is who has a hold over the institutions meant to check crime: the courts, the prosecutors and the customs service. In 2021 the US used its Magnitsky law, which sanctions corrupt officials abroad, in its largest action ever against a single country, naming Bulgarian officials and business figures, several in customs and border posts, over networks that included protection for smuggling. Those posts sit on the Balkan smuggling route, and Bulgarian prosecutions largely did not follow. In the courts, Martin Bozhanov, known as 'the Notary', is alleged to have gathered compromising material on judges and prosecutors to pressure them; Bulgarian National Radio reported he threatened prosecutors too, and former Prosecutor General Ivan Geshev was questioned. The claims are under investigation and untested in court.

Russia's reach is recorded but not proven. Prosecutors charged Nikolay Malinov, a former MP who leads Bulgaria's largest pro-Russia group, in 2019 with collecting state secrets for the Russian Institute for Strategic Studies, a Russian state think tank. While on bail he went to Moscow, where Putin gave him a state award. A Sofia court acquitted him of all charges in May 2026. The Russkiy Mir Foundation, a Russian state body promoting Russian language and culture abroad, is likely present, with no case recorded.

Bulgaria belongs to 'Organised crime inside the state', where it is proven, and 'Russia's networks in Europe and Africa'. State-embedded criminal actors score 7.5 of 10 and the ability to resist 5.3.
Bulgaria.imp: For people in Bulgaria, the worry is that the judges hearing their cases may be under private pressure, and that the customs officers at the border may be protecting the smuggling they are meant to stop. Foreign sanctions named officials, but cases at home mostly did not follow. Watch how the 'Notary' investigation develops, whether judges named in it are cleared or charged, and whether any customs or border official named in 2021 is prosecuted.

Croatia.d:
Croatia's documented case is about a foreign state-influenced company buying control of the national oil company through the prime minister, and it still shapes who runs Croatian oil. INA is Croatia's national oil company; MOL is Hungary's state-influenced oil company. Croatian courts found that Prime Minister Ivo Sanader took a 10 million euro bribe from MOL's chief executive, Zsolt Hernádi, in exchange for handing MOL management control of INA. A first conviction in 2012 was quashed in 2015; Sanader was convicted again in 2020, and the Supreme Court confirmed it in 2021. It is rated established.

The paying side has never faced a Croatian court. Hungary has not handed Hernádi over, and MOL denies the bribe. MOL's role at INA came out of that deal, so a neighbouring country's company holds a place in Croatia's oil business that Croatian courts found was bought, while the neighbouring government keeps the man accused of paying out of their reach.

Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members are encouraged to excel in public life, and the Order of Malta are recorded as present, with no case against them. Croatia's overall score is low because this is the one documented case; state-embedded criminal actors score 6 of 10 and the ability to resist 5.9.
Croatia.imp: For people in Croatia, a national company that belonged to the public had its management handed to a foreign firm in exchange for a bribe to the prime minister, and fuel and oil decisions at INA were shaped by that bargain. Only the Croatian side has been punished. Watch who controls INA now, whether Hernádi ever faces a court, and how future deals over state companies are made and disclosed.

Czech Republic.d:
In the Czech Republic the open question is the prime minister's own company, and foreign states have used Prague to reach into European politics. Agrofert, a large farming, food and chemicals group founded and owned by Andrej Babiš, receives EU farm subsidies. A European Commission audit published in 2021 found he still controlled it while in government, a conflict of interest. Babiš took back sole ownership in October 2025, became prime minister again in December, and in February 2026 moved the shares into a new trust, saying the conflict was resolved.

Russia's reach came through a website run from Czech territory. In March 2024 the government sanctioned Voice of Europe, along with Ukrainian politician Viktor Medvedchuk and an associate; the Czech security service said it was funded from Russia, and a newspaper, citing a foreign ministry source, reported payments to politicians in six EU countries. China's came through a businessman: Ye Jianming, head of the oil group CEFC and a former deputy secretary-general of a Beijing 'friendship' body, the CAIFC, was made economic adviser to President Miloš Zeman while CEFC bought Czech assets. Ye was detained in China in 2018.

Older records: Václav Klaus, prime minister and later president, is a member of the Mont Pelerin Society, a free-market thinkers' society, which is not a finding of influence. In 1939, after Germany occupied Prague, the Bank for International Settlements, the central banks' bank, passed 23 tons of Czechoslovak gold to Germany's central bank.
Czech Republic.imp: For people in the Czech Republic, the main issue is whether the head of government can keep state decisions, including on farm subsidies, apart from his own business; that is a question about trust arrangements rather than a crime. Foreign states have used Prague as a base to buy voices in European politics. Watch how the new Agrofert trust works in practice, how EU subsidy money flows to it, and whether more politicians are named in the Voice of Europe case.

Denmark.d:
Denmark's record is mostly about its closest ally reaching in, and Danish institutions being used to reach others. In Greenland, a self-governing part of Denmark that President Trump has said the US should take over, Danish media reported in 2025 that at least three Americans, said by unnamed sources to have ties to the Trump administration, were stirring anti-Danish feeling. Denmark's police intelligence service confirmed an influence campaign was under way and the foreign minister summoned the top US diplomat; who is behind it is not proven. The alliance has also run through Danish soil. An internal review called Operation Dunhammer, finished in 2015, found that Danish military intelligence let the US National Security Agency tap internet cables at Danish stations, and that the NSA used this in 2012–2014 to wiretap German Chancellor Angela Merkel and other German politicians, and reportedly senior figures in Sweden, Norway and France. The defence minister was told in 2020, the intelligence chief was suspended, and the public learned in 2021.

Danish institutions have also carried other people's money. Danske Bank pleaded guilty in the US in 2022 to bank fraud conspiracy and forfeited $2 billion over about €200 billion moved through its Estonian branch. The world's largest container lines appear in cocaine seizures as vessel owners; the record does not accuse them.

King Frederik X is a former WEF Young Global Leader, which is not a finding of influence. In the Cold War, a NATO stay-behind network, 'Absalon', was hidden inside military intelligence and disbanded after 1990.
Denmark.imp: For people in Denmark, their own intelligence service helped a foreign power spy on neighbouring governments, and the same ally is now suspected of working on public opinion in Greenland. The state's checks found both, but late. Danske Bank shows how a single foreign branch of a Danish bank can move enormous sums unseen. Watch what Danish intelligence finds about the Greenland campaign, and how cable-tapping arrangements with allies are overseen.

Estonia.d:
Estonia today is closing doors that a foreign church and foreign money once had open. The Estonian Orthodox Church of the Moscow Patriarchate, with about 150,000 faithful, answers to the Russian church, and Estonia has been loosening that tie by law: it refused to renew the residence permit of the church's head, Metropolitan Eugene, as a security risk over his support for Russia's war, and he left in February 2024; that May the Riigikogu, the parliament, named the Moscow Patriarchate an institution that supports Russian military aggression; and in 2025 it tightened the churches law to cut foreign control.

The banks were the other door, now shut. In 2012–2014 leaked records published in 2017 show about $2.9 billion moving through UK shell companies with accounts at Danske Bank's Estonian branch, almost half from an account linked to Azerbaijan's ruling Aliyev family, some of it reaching sitting MPs in Germany and Slovenia. In 2018 the Estonian regulator had Versobank, a small bank serving mostly foreign clients, closed for money-laundering failures; with a second Baltic bank, ABLV, closed within months, that shut the Baltic route for such money.

At the top, ministers sit in private forums where politicians meet business. Kaja Kallas attended the Bilderberg conference in 2024 as prime minister and is now the EU's foreign policy chief; economy minister Erkki Keldo is in the World Economic Forum's 2025 Young Global Leaders class. The lists are public; what is said there is not. The Russkiy Mir Foundation and the Russian Laundromat are likely present but not documented here.
Estonia.imp: For people in Estonia, the clearest outside pull runs through a church whose leadership answers to Moscow, and the state has dealt with it in the open, through permits and laws anyone can read. The bank cases show how billions passed through Estonian accounts on their way to foreign politicians without most residents knowing; regulators closed that route in 2018. Worth watching: how the new churches law is applied, and which ministers attend private forums like Bilderberg and the Davos network, since those meetings keep no public record.

Finland.d:
In Finland, what the record shows today is the head of state and a recent prime minister moving in two private networks where politicians meet business. President Alexander Stubb, in office since March 2024 and earlier prime minister and finance minister, lists on his official presidential CV his membership of the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leader network (2009) and its Global Future Council on Europe (2018). The Forum, best known for its Davos meeting, picks people under about 40 each year for this network. Stubb also appears on the Bilderberg lists for 2024 and 2025, both times as sitting president. Bilderberg is a private yearly conference of about 130 European and North American politicians, executives and academics, with no public record of what is said. Sanna Marin, prime minister in 2019–23, was on the 2025 Bilderberg list, and the German parliament's research service lists her among the Young Global Leaders. No forum has found that either network directed a Finnish decision.

The older story is a hidden army. After the 1944 armistice with Moscow, two officers at Military Headquarters, Colonel Valo Nihtilä and Lieutenant Colonel Usko Haahti, began hiding weapons around the country, enough to arm an estimated 35,000 men, with 5,000 to 10,000 people taking part. When it came out in 1945 the security police questioned more than 5,000 people, and 1,488 were convicted under a 1947 law, most serving a few months. The Club of Rome is likely present but not documented.
Finland.imp: For people in Finland, nothing on the record shows an outside group steering the state now.
