What is documented is that the president and a former prime minister take part in private forums where officials and business leaders talk with no minutes kept. That is lawful and openly listed, but voters cannot see what is said there. Worth watching: whether positions the president takes at home line up with the agendas of those rooms.

France.d:
In France the outside forces with a hand in the state today are mostly companies, consultants and foreign governments, with drug money reaching parts of the police.

Companies and advisers sit close to the ministries. A Senate inquiry found in 2022 that the state's use of consultants since 2017 was "sprawling and opaque" and shaped policy. It sent McKinsey, the US consulting firm, to prosecutors over its taxes; in September 2026 they seized €65 million, and the case continues. Leaked Uber files suggest that Emmanuel Macron, as economy minister, brokered a secret deal for Uber inside the cabinet; he says he was proud to help. The drug firm Servier was convicted in 2021 over Mediator, and the medicines regulator was fined for failing to act. Bankers pass into top office: Pompidou and Macron both came from Rothschild. No inquiry has found the bank directs policy, and the claim that Macron is "the Rothschilds' president" is a form of an antisemitic conspiracy theory.

Foreign governments work through parties and territories. Marine Le Pen's party, now the largest group in the National Assembly, took a €9 million loan from a Moscow bank; the interior minister accused Azerbaijan of stirring New Caledonia's 2024 riots, which Baku denies; Macron's number appeared on a spyware list linked to Morocco, which denies it. France has banned Turkey's Grey Wolves movement.

In Marseille, anti-crime officers were convicted of stealing seized cannabis and money, and a former national anti-drug chief is under investigation, which he denies. A 2025 state report warned of Muslim Brotherhood influence in town halls, while finding no sign Muslims in France seek an Islamic state.

The roots: Grand Orient lodges filed army officers for promotion in 1901–04; Paris hosted the CIA's Congress for Cultural Freedom; and French lodges chartered lodges in former African colonies.
France.imp: For people in France, the strongest documented pull on the state comes from firms and consultants whose advice ministries follow, and from bankers who move into top office, which is lawful but puts the same people on both sides. Courts have acted on a deadly drug, police theft and bribery abroad, and the McKinsey probe is still open. Worth watching: who the state hires for advice, how foreign governments work through parties and overseas territories, and whether drug money keeps reaching Marseille's police.

Germany.d:
Germany is where foreign spy services are most often caught working inside the political system, and where top offices pass back and forth with finance houses.

China: an aide to an AfD member of the European Parliament was convicted in 2025 of spying for China's Ministry of State Security, and three Germans are on trial in Düsseldorf, charged with passing naval technology to the same service. Russia: Jan Marsalek, operating chief of the payments firm Wirecard until its 2020 collapse, is wanted and, investigators say, worked for Russian intelligence since at least 2010; AfD politician Petr Bystroň is under investigation over cash from a Russian-funded network, which he denies; and former chancellor Gerhard Schröder chaired the board of Rosneft, Russia's state oil company, until 2022. Iran: the Islamic Centre Hamburg was banned in 2024 as Tehran's outpost. Azerbaijan: two CDU MPs lost their immunity in 2021 over its money.

Inside Germany's own forces, a sitting Berlin judge and former MP is on trial as the would-be justice minister of the Reichsbürger group around Prinz Reuss, which prosecutors say planned to storm parliament. At Hamburg and Bremerhaven, customs officers have been convicted of clearing cocaine containers.

Business sits close to the top. Chancellor Friedrich Merz chaired BlackRock's German arm until 2020; Jörg Kukies went from Goldman Sachs to finance minister. A banker's diaries record meetings with Olaf Scholz, then Hamburg mayor, before a €47 million tax claim on Warburg bank was dropped; Scholz denies any influence. The financial regulator BaFin turned on Wirecard's critics, and a study found the risk agency copied industry text into its glyphosate review, which it rejects.

The roots: the US NSA monitored Chancellor Merkel's phone, the CIA funded Radio Free Europe from Munich until 1971 and the BND's NATO stay-behind network was wound up in 1991.
Germany.imp: For people in Germany, the clearest risk today is foreign intelligence working through parliamentary staff, companies and politicians, and courts are convicting people for it. Alongside that, chancellors and finance ministers come from banks and asset managers, which is lawful but puts the same people on both sides of financial decisions. Worth watching: the spy trials and the Reichsbürger verdicts, whether the Warburg tax questions are ever settled, and whether regulators like BaFin side with firms against their critics again.

Greece.d:
Greece lives with two things outside forces left inside its state: a debt shaped by private banks, and a far-right party courts found was a criminal organisation, with suspected friends in the police.

The debt runs through the banks' advisers. As Greece entered the euro in 2001, Goldman Sachs arranged swaps that worked as a hidden loan of about €2.8 billion, not shown in the debt figures; Bloomberg reported Greece paid about €600 million in fees and the obligation grew to €5.1 billion. Goldman says they met EU rules. When the crisis came, Lucas Papademos, central bank governor at the time of the swaps, was installed as unelected prime minister in 2011–12 to secure the second bailout; he never worked for Goldman. Lazard, an investment bank, advised the government on the 2012 bond swap and was rehired in 2015. Bribery cases against former prime ministers and health ministers over the drug firm Novartis were dropped, though Novartis paid about $347 million in the US partly over bribing Greek hospital staff and doctors.

Golden Dawn held as many as 21 seats in parliament in 2012–15. In 2020 an Athens court found its leaders guilty of running a criminal organisation "dressed in the mantle of a political party", and in March 2026 an appeal court upheld 42 convictions. Police polling stations in Attica gave it just over 20% in 2012, against about 6% nearby, and the Council of Europe's rights commissioner said he had strong evidence of ties.

The roots are military: IDEA, a secret officers' society, prepared the 1967 coup, the colonels ruled until 1974 and were convicted of treason in 1975, and a NATO stay-behind branch ran until 1988. Prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis sat at Bilderberg in 2025.
Greece.imp: For people in Greece, the hidden debt deal cost the country far more than shown, and the decisions were made by a small circle of officials and bank advisers. A party that sat in parliament has been convicted as a criminal gang, with suspected support inside the police. Worth watching: who advises the finance ministry on debt, how police deal with far-right violence.

Hungary.d:
In Hungary the documented outside reach comes from two directions, China and Russia, and both reached officials at a high level. Under an agreement signed in February 2024 by Interior Minister Sándor Pintér and China's Minister of Public Security, Chinese officers may patrol alongside Hungarian police in tourist areas and at large events. The ministry denies that Chinese police stations exist in Hungary, but the rights group Safeguard Defenders listed two in Budapest, in the Józsefváros and Kőbánya districts; elsewhere such stations have been used to pressure people China wants back.

Russia reached the European Parliament through a Hungarian seat. Béla Kovács sat there for Jobbik, a nationalist party; prosecutors accused him of spying on EU institutions for Russia, and in 2022 Hungary's top court, the Curia, sentenced him in absentia to five years. He lives in Russia.

Only these two cases are documented, so Hungary's overall score is low, but its conditions score is high: actors embedded in the state are strong and the checks that resist them are weak, which makes outside reach easier. Scientology, the Polish legal institute Ordo Iuris and the network of Viktor Medvedchuk, a Ukrainian politician close to Moscow, are likely present but undocumented.
Hungary.imp: For people in Hungary, the patrol deal means foreign police can work beside your own under an arrangement made between ministers, while the government denies the stations rights groups found in Budapest. The Kovács case shows a Russian spy reached a Hungarian seat in the European Parliament. With weak checks on power at home, worth watching: how far the Chinese policing deal extends, and who it is used against.

Iceland.d: Nothing is documented on this map for Iceland yet, so what follows is a best guess. The Mont Pelerin Society, a network of free-market economists and politicians, has documented presence, and the large fishing company Samherji is based here. A NATO stay-behind network from the Cold War is likely but undocumented. Iceland's conditions are strong: actors embedded in the state score very low and the checks that resist them score very high, so outside groups have few easy openings. The most likely route in, as an estimate, is through big home companies and their dealings abroad, or through policy networks that shape economic ideas, rather than through people placed inside the state.
Iceland.imp: For people in Iceland, there is no documented case of an outside group steering the state, and the strong conditions scores mean it would be hard to do quietly. If anything does appear, it is most likely to come through large companies based here, such as those in fishing, and their dealings in other countries, so that is the place to keep an eye on.

Ireland.d:
In Ireland today, the country's leaders sit in a private network where politicians meet business, and a foreign police force tried to work on Irish soil until the state shut it down.

The network is the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme. The Forum, best known for its Davos meeting, picks people under about 40 each year for a five-year circle of meetings and courses. Its 2025 class includes Simon Harris, the former Taoiseach (prime minister) who is now Tánaiste (deputy prime minister). In 2018 the Forum named Leo Varadkar while he was sitting Taoiseach, and he was on the list for the private Bilderberg conference in 2024, weeks after stepping down. These are open selections, not findings of influence.

China's police reached into Dublin. In 2022 the rights group Safeguard Defenders reported that police in Chinese cities ran unofficial "overseas service stations" abroad to pressure people China wanted back; one, run for Fuzhou police, was on Capel Street. That October Ireland's foreign ministry ordered it to close.

The older story is a Catholic brotherhood. The Knights of Saint Columbanus, a lay Catholic order based in Ireland, had members at the top of the 1948 government, including Taoiseach John A. Costello and Justice Minister Seán MacEoin, who reportedly assured the Order that conflict between Church and State would be avoided. One Knight in the Labour party is reported to have worked against the Mother and Child health scheme that Archbishop McQuaid opposed. These accounts rest mainly on two biographies.
Ireland.imp: For people in Ireland, the documented ties of today's leaders run to open, listed networks rather than hidden groups, though what is said there is not public. The Dublin station showed that a foreign police force can try to reach people living here, and the state closed it. The Knights story is a reminder that health and social policy were once shaped by a Catholic order with members in cabinet. Worth watching: who shapes those policies now.

Italy.d:
Italy's record is the deepest on this map, and most of it is about home-grown mafias inside local government and the building trade. In Calabria, Campania and Sicily, clans of the 'Ndrangheta (the Calabrian mafia), the Camorra around Naples and Cosa Nostra in Sicily steer town councils so that contracts for building, waste and transport go to their firms. Those three regions account for 360 of the 402 decrees by which the government has dissolved a council for mafia control since 1991; Puglia, where Bari's clans placed members in the city transport company, adds 26. The 'Ndrangheta has also moved north: top-court rulings describe its construction firms rooted among Emilia-Romagna businessmen, and in 2024 Reggio Emilia's prefect barred 80 firms from public works as EU recovery money arrived. Investigators document its hold on hiring at Gioia Tauro, the largest transhipment port. It reaches past town halls: a president of Sicily, Berlusconi's aide in the Senate and an economy undersecretary have been convicted of aiding the clans, and the 2023 Rinascita-Scott trial convicted 207 people, a former senator among them, with appeals running.

Foreign states reach in nearer the top. The Lega, whose leader Matteo Salvini is deputy prime minister, has a party pact with Putin's United Russia reported to run to 2027, and a Milan judge found 2018 talks on Russian oil money aimed at illegal party funding, though never completed. Former Chinese vice-minister Qu Dongyu heads the Rome-based UN food agency (FAO), and the government has curbed Chinese state firm Sinochem's control of tyre maker Pirelli.

The background is the lodge P2, whose 1981 list of 962 names held ministers, 44 MPs and the heads of all three intelligence services. It produced the 1982 ban on secret societies that prosecutors still use.
Italy.imp: For people in Calabria, Campania, Sicily and Puglia, a dissolved council means appointed commissioners run the town for 18 to 24 months, and 83 councils or health authorities have been dissolved more than once. A building or waste contract there may have gone to a clan firm. In the north the same risk sits in public works paid for with EU recovery money. What to watch: prefects' bans on firms, the Rinascita-Scott appeals, the Lega's agreement with United Russia, and foreign state ownership of strategic companies.

Latvia.d:
Latvia's record is about two channels Russia has used to reach in, and Latvia's moves to close them. The first runs through church and politics. Until 2022 the Latvian Orthodox Church was a self-governing part of the Russian Orthodox Church under the Moscow Patriarchate. That September parliament, on a bill from President Egils Levits, made it fully independent of any church authority abroad and required the president's office to be told of its bishops' appointments; no Orthodox church had recognised the new status by mid-2026. In politics, leaked emails published in January 2024 showed Tatjana Ždanoka, co-chair of the Latvian Russian Union and a member of the European Parliament for twenty years, reporting to officers of Russia's security service, the FSB, from at least 2004. Latvia's State Security Service opened a criminal case, still an investigation, and the European Parliament penalised her under its code of conduct.

The second channel is banking. Money from the Global Laundromat, a scheme that moved an estimated $20–80 billion out of Russia between 2010 and 2014 through fake debts approved by Moldovan judges, passed on through Latvian banks. In 2018 the US Treasury named ABLV Bank, which served shell-company clients, a primary money-laundering concern; depositors ran and the bank wound itself up within weeks, with no trial. In 2021 the US designated Chatex, a crypto exchange that had reappeared as the successor to one already blacklisted, along with supporting companies in Latvia and Estonia. Each of the four documented cases ended in a ban, a designation or an open investigation.
Latvia.imp: For people in Latvia, the Orthodox Church now stands outside Moscow's control but without recognition from any other Orthodox church. When a bank is cut off overnight, as ABLV was, ordinary depositors face the run alongside the shell companies. What to watch: the outcome of the Ždanoka investigation, how the church's status is settled, and whether crypto services designated abroad reappear under new names with Latvian companies behind them.

Liechtenstein.d: This is a best guess: nothing is documented on the map for Liechtenstein. The only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic religious order, and its presence is not a case. The scores are very low, with almost no sign of outside actors embedded in the state and resilience of 8.4 out of 10. Other small financial centres on the map show where pressure usually arrives: in Malta through betting and bank licences and the sale of citizenship, in Monaco through a Russian billionaire courting officials, a case since closed. If an outside force reached into Liechtenstein, finance, through trusts and company registration, is the likeliest route.
Liechtenstein.imp: There is no recorded case touching people in Liechtenstein today. If anything is worth watching, it is the financial sector: who owns the trusts and companies registered there, and whether checks on foreign clients' money keep pace with what Malta, Latvia and other financial centres on this map were caught missing. In those places the trouble began with licensed banks and firms that served foreign clients without asking enough questions.

Lithuania.d:
Lithuania's current record is about criminal networks from elsewhere in Europe using the country to park money and run services, not about anyone inside its government. In February 2026 police in Iceland, Lithuania, Spain, Belgium and Denmark arrested 24 people from a group that sold cocaine, MDMA, ketamine and methamphetamine in Iceland and put the proceeds into real estate and other property in Lithuania. Matrix, an invitation-only encrypted phone network on more than 40 servers that appears in Lithuania's record, was taken down in December 2024 after French and Dutch investigators read 2.3 million of its messages over three months; it had first turned up on the phone of a man convicted of murdering a Dutch crime journalist. Both are charges, not verdicts, and neither involves a Lithuanian official.

The one case inside the state is older and finished. Yuri Borisov, a Russian businessman who ran the helicopter firm Avia Baltika, reportedly gave about $400,000 to Rolandas Paksas's 2002 presidential campaign and then received Lithuanian citizenship by Paksas's decree. In 2004 the Constitutional Court found Paksas had broken the constitution and his oath, and parliament removed him, the first European head of state impeached. The European Court of Human Rights later found his lifetime ban from parliament disproportionate.

Opus Dei, the Catholic traditionalist movement Tradition, Family, Property, and the Atlas Network of free-market think tanks are recorded as present, with no case against them.
Lithuania.imp: For people in Lithuania, the clearest current effect is on property: drug money from as far away as Iceland is being turned into houses and flats here, which puts estate agents, notaries and the land registry on the front line. The Paksas case showed that a citizenship decree could be traded for campaign money, and that the courts and parliament could undo it. What to watch: who buys property with money from abroad, and how campaign gifts from foreign businessmen are checked.

Luxembourg.d:
Luxembourg has no documented case of an outside force inside its government today. Its record holds two pieces of Cold War-era history that still bear on how its state and its banks are seen. The first is the Bommeleeër affair. Between May 1984 and April 1986 eighteen bombs went off across the country, many aimed at power pylons of the utility Cegedel. In 2013 two former members of the Gendarmerie's mobile brigade went on trial for them. Their defence argued the bombings were the work of NATO's Stay Behind network, the secret cells set up in Western Europe to resist a Soviet occupation, and a 2006 recording was played in court of Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, Justice Minister Luc Frieden and intelligence chief Marco Mille speculating about Stay Behind involvement. The prosecutor said 88 of 125 pieces of evidence had disappeared. The trial was suspended in 2014; eight former officers were later sent to trial for false testimony, not for the bombings.

The second is banking. BCCI, the Bank of Credit and Commerce International, was registered in Luxembourg with its operating centre in London until regulators in several countries closed it in 1991; the map lists it among the banks that carried hidden money for governments and criminals alike. Le Cercle and the Trilateral Commission, private forums where officials meet business leaders, are recorded as present, with no case. Luxembourg's scores show few outside actors embedded in the state and high resilience.
Luxembourg.imp: For people in Luxembourg, the open question from the 1980s is who set off eighteen bombs on their own power grid, and why most of the evidence went missing while in official hands. Nothing current is documented, but BCCI showed that a bank registered here can serve hidden money worldwide. What to watch: whether the Bommeleeër case is ever tried on the bombings themselves, and how banks and firms registered in Luxembourg check where their clients' money comes from.

Malta.d:
Malta's record has two parts: a power-station deal at the top of government, and Malta as a place that licenses businesses whose customers have included criminal networks. The first is in court now. Electrogas built Malta's gas power station under a state contract. One of its directors, Yorgen Fenech, was identified as owner of 17 Black, a company registered in the UAE, and leaked papers showed that Panama companies of Keith Schembri, the prime minister's chief of staff, and Konrad Mizzi, the energy minister, expected payments from it. Journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was investigating those companies when a car bomb killed her in 2017. Schembri and Mizzi resigned in 2019, the three men were charged with corruption in 2025, and Fenech's trial for complicity in her murder began in mid-2026. A 2021 public inquiry found the state had created an 'atmosphere of impunity'. None of these cases has a verdict yet.

Malta also licenses online betting, banks and crypto firms, and sells citizenship, a scheme the EU's top court ruled against in 2025. Italian prosecutors found Calabrian and Sicilian mafia groups using Malta-licensed betting firms to take bets and launder money, though some executives were acquitted. Malta's failure to act on warnings about Pilatus Bank, which lost its licence in 2018, helped put the country on the FATF grey list, the international watch list for weak anti-laundering controls, in 2021. The crypto exchanges Binance and OKX, which appear in Malta's record, pleaded guilty in the US, and Maltese brokers were designated in 2018 for smuggling Libyan oil.
Malta.imp: For people in Malta, the record shows a state energy contract, offshore companies and the prime minister's closest officials sitting in one chain, and a journalist killed while tracing it. The trials now running will decide what is proven. The licensing side matters too: a betting licence, bank licence or passport sold to the wrong buyer carries Malta's name abroad, as the grey listing did. What to watch: the Fenech, Schembri and Mizzi verdicts, and who now buys Maltese citizenship or residence.

Moldova.d:
Moldova's record is about banks, courts and parties used as routes for stolen and foreign money, and about the courts now catching up. The largest case is the 'theft of the billion'. In 2014 about $1 billion, equal to 12% of Moldova's GDP, was drained from three banks through loans repaid with new loans and moved out through UK and Hong Kong shell companies. Vlad Plahotniuc, who led the Democratic Party and was widely described as controlling the government and the parliamentary majority, fled in 2019, was extradited from Greece in 2025 and in April 2026 was sentenced to 19 years. The deputy head of the security service told parliament that President Nicolae Timofti had known of the theft since 2013.

The Șor Party of businessman Ilan Shor was declared unconstitutional in 2023 for serving a foreign state's interests. Its candidate Evghenia Guțul won the governorship of Gagauzia, an autonomous region, and in 2025 was sentenced to seven years for funding the party with undeclared Russian money; the party's former secretary was sentenced at the same hearing for handing out 9.8 million lei to pay protesters.

The older background runs through the courts. Between 2010 and 2014 Moldovan judges approved fake debts that let an estimated $20–80 billion leave Russia through Moldindconbank and on through Latvian banks, the Global Laundromat; prosecutors later charged judges. In 2018 the intelligence service sent seven Turkish teachers from schools linked to the Gülen movement, which Turkey's government pursues abroad, to Turkey; the European Court of Human Rights ruled it an illegal transfer.
Moldova.imp: For people in Moldova, the bank theft cost about 12% of a year's national output, and the record shows judges, banks and party leaders as the routes it travelled. In Gagauzia, voters chose a governor whose party was paid for with undeclared Russian money. Courts have now convicted at the top. What to watch: where party money comes from, whether the judges who approved fake debts are tried, and whether the intelligence service acts within the law, which the European Court found it did not in 2018.

Monaco.d:
Monaco's record is about a small state whose key offices are filled with the help of its larger neighbour, and about outside money courting those offices. France's hand is the steadiest. The prince still consults the French government before appointing the head of government, the Minister of State; Christophe Mirmand, a French senior civil servant, has held the post since July 2025, and until 2002 the office had to go to a French citizen. Key judicial posts are held by French magistrates proposed by Paris, the police are commanded by a French officer, and France is responsible for defence. These arrangements are set by treaty and are public.

Private money has tried to reach the same offices. Dmitry Rybolovlev, a Russian billionaire who owns AS Monaco football club, was made a formal suspect in 2018 after messages on his lawyer's phone suggested he courted Monaco officials, and a complaint named the former public prosecutor. The case was dismissed in 2023 and closed in 2025 after the courts ruled the phone data unlawfully obtained, so nothing was proven.

Monaco is also home to World Athletics, the sport's governing body, formerly the IAAF. Its president from 1999 to 2015, Lamine Diack, was convicted in Paris in 2020 of taking money to hide Russian athletes' doping. About €3.2m was extorted from at least 23 suspected dopers so they could compete at London 2012, and investigators found a $1.5m deal with Russian sports officials to fund Macky Sall's 2012 presidential campaign in Senegal. Diack died in 2021 with appeals pending.
Monaco.imp: For people in Monaco, the police, senior judges and head of government are chosen partly in Paris. That is a treaty arrangement rather than a secret, but it means the people who would investigate influence are not picked locally. The Rybolovlev case shows how hard such a probe is to finish: it ended on how the evidence was gathered, not on what it showed. What to watch: appointments to the courts and police, and how the courts treat wealthy residents.

Montenegro.d:
Montenegro's record is about drug clans reaching the people meant to stop them: prosecutors, police chiefs and the top of the courts. Most of it came to light through Sky ECC, an encrypted phone service whose messages Europol passed to Podgorica after they were decrypted. Those transcripts led to charges against a former chief special prosecutor, a former assistant police director and his son, a state security officer, for protecting the cocaine trade of the Kavac clan. Separate indictments name a former president of the Supreme Court, two former police directors and the mayor of Budva. These are charges, not verdicts.

One case has reached a verdict. Vesna Medenica headed the Supreme Court until 2020. In January 2026 the High Court in Podgorica sentenced her to 10 years for using her position to protect a cigarette and narcotics smuggling network run by her son Miloš, who received just over 10 years and fled while under house arrest. She was acquitted of creating a criminal organisation, and prosecutors are appealing for longer sentences.

The same record notes that the prime minister, Milojko Spajić, was picked in 2025 for the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses for people under about 40 run by the Davos forum. That is a selection by the Forum, not a finding of influence. Montenegro scores high on outside actors embedded in the state and below the middle on resilience.
Montenegro.imp: For people in Montenegro, the offices meant to investigate drug clans, the special prosecutor, the police command and the Supreme Court, have themselves been charged with protecting them. If a prosecutor shields a clan, cases die before they reach a courtroom; that is what these charges allege. The Medenica verdict shows the courts can now convict at the top. What to watch: the trials of the former prosecutor and police chiefs, the Medenica appeal, and whether Miloš Medenica is found.

Netherlands.d:
The Netherlands' record is large because two things meet here: Rotterdam, Europe's busiest port, and the international bodies in The Hague. At the ports, cocaine networks shipping from Ecuador buy insiders rather than force their way in. Terminal staff have supplied PIN codes from Rotterdam's release system and IT contractors have moved a container's position in the stack so extraction crews can find it; Dutch and Belgian courts have convicted several. Ecuador's Los Lobos gang ships through Rotterdam and Vlissingen, and one banana shipment in 2023 held 8,064 kg. The networks reach into the justice system too. In the Marengo trial against Ridouan Taghi's organisation a lawyer and a police employee were prosecuted for leaking information, a witness's brother, his lawyer and a journalist were murdered, and Taghi's own lawyer was convicted in 2026 of relaying his messages from prison. ING and ABN AMRO paid €775m and €480m to settle laundering failures.

Foreign states reach in through technology firms and The Hague's institutions. In 2025 the government took control of chipmaker Nexperia from its owner Wingtech, almost 30% traceable to the Chinese state, then suspended the order after China banned exports of its chips; a former ASML and NXP engineer was jailed for sending chip files to a contact in Russia. In 2018 four officers of the GRU, Russian military intelligence, were caught trying to hack the chemical weapons watchdog (OPCW), and in 2024 journalists reported Israel's Mossad spying on and pressing International Criminal Court prosecutors for nearly ten years, which Israel denies. A 2020 parliamentary inquiry found Gulf donors funding Salafi mosques and Turkey's religious directorate, Diyanet, steering Turkish-Dutch ones.

The background is a stay-behind network that ran from 1945 to 1992, and Bilderberg, founded in 1954 by the King's grandfather; the King attended in 2024 and 2025.
Netherlands.imp: For people in the Netherlands, much of the risk sits in ordinary jobs: a port worker's access code, a contractor's login, a lawyer's prison visit. Drug networks pay for these because they open doors without force, and the Marengo murders show the price paid by people who testify. Nationally, foreign states go after chip know-how and the courts in The Hague. What to watch: insider cases at the ports, the court-ordered inquiry into Nexperia, and whether individuals, not only banks, answer for laundering failures.

Norway.d:
Norway's record holds no current case of an outside force inside its government. What it has is one serious case of organised crime reaching into the police, and a piece of Cold War history. Eirik Jensen, who ran the Oslo police narcotics section for years, was convicted of aggravated corruption and of helping import around fourteen tonnes of hashish with an informant he handled, and sentenced to twenty-one years; the Supreme Court refused his appeal in 2021. It is the most senior police conviction of its kind in Scandinavia, and it sits at the point where police run informants inside the trade they are meant to stop.

The older history is the stay-behind network, the secret cells NATO countries set up to resist a Soviet occupation. In 1978 police found an arms cache and radio equipment at a mountain cabin and arrested businessman Hans Otto Meyer, who said Norwegian intelligence had supplied the weapons. Defence Minister Rolf Hansen then said the network answered neither to NATO nor to the CIA. As early as 1957 the intelligence chief, Vilhelm Evang, had protested to NATO about stay-behind activity by officers at its Kolsås headquarters.

Opus Dei, the Trilateral Commission, the Mont Pelerin Society of free-market economists and the private intelligence firm Alp Services are recorded as present, with no case. Norway's scores show very few outside actors embedded in the state and high resilience.
Norway.imp: For people in Norway, the Jensen case means that for years drugs moved under the protection of the officer in charge of stopping them in the capital. Nothing documented reaches the government now. What to watch: how police handle informants, since that is where the one serious case began, and whether Swedish criminal networks, which the map lists as likely present but undocumented here, begin to reach Norwegian officials.

Poland.d:
Poland's documented record is mostly about people moving from lawful networks into high office, along with one Chinese espionage trial and a drug route. The clearest thread is Ordo Iuris, a conservative Catholic legal institute founded in Poland. Its co-founder Aleksander Stępkowski became deputy foreign minister in the Law and Justice government in 2015, was appointed to the Supreme Court in 2019 with no prior judicial experience on the nomination of the reconstituted judicial council, and in 2020 was made acting head of that court by President Andrzej Duda. Przemysław Wipler, reported as an Opus Dei supernumerary, a member who lives an ordinary family life, sits in parliament for the Confederation and is vice-chair of the inquiry into the previous government's use of Pegasus spyware. Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski is on Bilderberg's lists for 2024 and 2025. Membership of these groups is lawful, and none of this is a finding of wrongdoing.

China's reach is in court. In 2019 Polish authorities arrested Wang Weijing, a senior Huawei employee, and Piotr Durbajło, a cybersecurity expert who had worked for the Internal Security Agency, and charged both with working for Chinese intelligence; prosecutors say Wang sought contracts that would give Huawei insight into state and local government data systems. Both pleaded not guilty, and the trial, closed to the public, opened in 2021.

Poland is also a staging point: a 2026 case describes methamphetamine moved from Western Europe through a hub at Rzeszów on to Slovakia and western Ukraine.
Poland.imp: For people in Poland, the Ordo Iuris thread shows one organisation's founder moving from drafting policy to the foreign ministry and then to the head of the Supreme Court, the court that rules on their rights. The Huawei case is about whether a foreign firm could see into government data systems. What to watch: the verdict in the Huawei trial, who is appointed to the courts and how, and the drug routes running east through Rzeszów.

Portugal.d:
Portugal's current record centres on one of its old banking families and a former prime minister, now on trial. Ricardo Salgado, nicknamed 'Dono Disto Tudo' ('owner of all this'), led Banco Espírito Santo, run by a family close to power since the Salazar era; the bank collapsed in 2014. In Operation Marquês prosecutors charge former Prime Minister José Sócrates (2005–11) with receiving undue payments, including money they link to the Espírito Santo group, and Salgado with corruption and money laundering. A judge threw out most charges in 2021, an appeal court reinstated them in 2024, and the trial began in July 2025; all defendants are presumed innocent. Salgado's separate sentence for breach of trust was raised to eight years on appeal.

Portugal's coast is also a landing point. In April 2026 a Spanish-led operation between the Canaries and the Azores seized 11 tonnes of cocaine and made 54 arrests. Mother ships carry the cargo into open ocean, where it moves to fast boats and then to small craft landing on remote Portuguese and Spanish shores, so it never passes through a watched port.

The older history is Aginter Press, set up in Lisbon in 1966 under Salazar's dictatorship and run by a former French officer. It called itself a news agency but trained members in bombing and sabotage, and an Italian magistrate later tied its instructors to Italian neo-fascist bombers. José Manuel Durão Barroso, later prime minister and European Commission president, was named a WEF 'Global Leader for Tomorrow' in 1993, a selection rather than a finding of influence.
Portugal.imp: For people in Portugal, the Marquês trial will test whether a prime minister took money linked to the country's most powerful banking family, and the court's answer will say how far that family's reach went. The Atlantic route means remote stretches of coast now see landings that would once have come through a port. What to watch: the Marquês verdict, Salgado's appeals, and how police respond to mid-ocean transfers off the Azores and the mainland.

Romania.d:
Romania has little documented on the map, and none of it has been proven in court. In September 2019 Newsweek România reported, citing anonymous Masonic sources, that Mihai Fifor, then interim interior minister and deputy prime minister, had joined Freemasonry in 2008 and later Loja Basarab, and that General Constantin Florea, head of the Gendarmerie, the militarised police, belonged to the same lodge. Neither had listed it on the interest declarations the magazine said the law required. Fifor neither confirmed nor denied; Costin Mihalache, head of the Government Chancellery and a former foreign-intelligence officer, said he had been a Mason but no longer was. The claim rests on that one outlet, and Masonic membership is lawful; the question it raised was disclosure.

The second case is about money. In February 2026 French and Romanian authorities broke up a network that laundered 306 million euros of drug and tax-evasion proceeds through front companies and real estate, using invoices for services never performed to move money between the two countries. Thirteen people were arrested; it is a charge, not a verdict.

Several groups are recorded as present with no case: Opus Dei, the Trilateral Commission, the US-funded broadcaster Radio Free Europe, and Azerbaijan's 'caviar diplomacy' network, which in Italy's record bought a parliamentary assembly leader's support. The map lists the Plahotniuc network from neighbouring Moldova, the Gülen movement and The Fellowship, a US prayer network, as likely present but undocumented.
Romania.imp: For people in Romania, the documented risks are quiet ones: whether the minister over the police and the head of the Gendarmerie declare the networks they belong to, and whether fake invoices let criminal money buy property. What to watch: interest declarations by senior police and interior officials, the outcome of the 2026 laundering case, and any sign that the Moldovan networks next door, listed as likely present, reach Romanian officials.

Russia.d:
Inside Russia today, the state and its security services reach into companies, banks and international bodies more directly than almost anywhere on the map. Under a decree President Putin signed in April 2023, the federal property agency, Rosimushchestvo, can put businesses owned by companies from "unfriendly" countries under "temporary management". It took the utilities of Fortum and Uniper that April, then Danone's Russian business and Carlsberg's Baltika Breweries in July, handing them to a Chechen minister who is Ramzan Kadyrov's nephew and to a former Putin campaign representative. The FSB, Russia's main security service, also turns up in business fights, as when it arrested the American investor Michael Calvey during a dispute over a bank. The US says the antivirus maker Kaspersky has FSB ties; the company denies it.

Money moves through the same circle. Bank Rossiya, founded by men who later shared Putin's Ozero dacha cooperative, was called "the personal bank for senior officials" by the US Treasury in 2014 and remains under US and EU sanctions. Crypto exchanges run from Russia, among them Suex, Garantex and Cryptex, have been sanctioned abroad for moving darknet and ransomware money; Garantex kept working from Moscow after Estonia pulled its licence.

Outward, Russia pays for influence and works inside international bodies. The Czech government sanctioned the Voice of Europe network in 2024 for paying European politicians. Reports for the World Anti-Doping Agency found in 2016 that the sports ministry and the FSB hid at least 643 positive doping samples. Since March 2022 Interpol, which police forces use to share wanted-person alerts, checks every Russian alert first. At home, courts have convicted a Krasnodar gang that killed 12 people after years of police protection. The claim that banker Jacob Schiff funded the Bolsheviks in 1917 is an antisemitic myth his firm's records contradict.
Russia.imp: For people in Russia, a business can be taken by the state and handed to someone close to the leadership, and a quarrel with a well-connected rival can end in an FSB arrest. A bank tied to the president's friends stays open under sanctions, and services that clean ransomware and darknet money keep working at home after being shut out abroad. How far Kaspersky shares data with the FSB is a US claim, not a proven fact. Watch which foreign-owned firms go under "temporary management" next, and who is put in charge.

San Marino.d:
San Marino's record today is the long tail of one bribery case, which ended on appeal in March 2022. In a state this small, building permits and banking licences, the permissions that decide who may build and who may run a bank, rest with a handful of politicians. Prosecutors said construction and banking entrepreneurs bought them, paying politicians with cash drawn from an account at Banca Commerciale Sammarinese held in the name of "Giuseppe Mazzini". That account gave the case its name, "Conto Mazzini".

Twenty-one former political figures, among them former state secretaries Fiorenzo Stolfi and Claudio Podeschi, went on trial in 2015 for criminal association to launder bribes, and about 200 million euros were seized. Several were convicted in 2017, and the appeal court upheld most of the convictions with lower sentences. The outside force here was local business money rather than a foreign state or a mafia, and what it got was the state's permission to build and to run banks. The network was based in San Marino itself, and the map rates its reach beyond the border as low.

The only other body listed as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order, with no case attached to it. San Marino's overall score is minimal.
San Marino.imp: For people in San Marino, the case showed that the permits and licences that shape the whole local economy could be bought, and that the courts did convict former state secretaries for it. Where a few officials decide who builds and who banks, a few payments go a long way. Watch how building permits and banking licences are granted now, and what becomes of the 200 million euros that were seized.

Serbia.d:
In Serbia the question on the record today is how far the state security service and the police work alongside violent criminal groups in Belgrade. Prosecutors charging the Belivuk-Miljković group since 2021 have produced evidence that its members carried state security identification and could enter protected facilities, and a former head of the security service was later charged in connection with them. The trial is still running, and who is to blame is fought over along party lines in Serbian politics.

The fear has a precedent everyone in Serbia knows. In 2003 Prime Minister Zoran Đinđić was shot by a serving commander of the interior ministry's special operations unit, the JSO, which had merged with the Zemun criminal clan, a group with a share of the Balkan heroin trade. Twelve people were convicted in 2007 and the unit was disbanded.

Behind that sits a longer habit of secret brotherhoods inside the army. In 1903 officers led by Dragutin Dimitrijević "Apis" killed King Alexander Obrenović and Queen Draga. In 1911 Apis and others founded Unification or Death, the Black Hand, which dominated the army; in 1913 he became chief of military intelligence, and many scholars hold he sanctioned the 1914 Sarajevo assassination. He was court-martialled and shot in 1917, and in 1953 Serbia's Supreme Court acquitted him for lack of proof. The rival White Hand put its founder, General Petar Živković, in office as prime minister in 1929. The World Economic Forum and Russia's Russkiy Mir Foundation are thought to be present but have no documented case here.
Serbia.imp: For people in Serbia, the worry is whether parts of the police and security service still protect criminal groups, as the special operations unit did when one of its commanders killed a prime minister. The Belivuk trial may answer that, but the charges are not proven yet. Until then, anyone dealing with the police cannot be sure whose side an officer is on. Watch how the case against the former security chief ends, and whether the evidence about state identification cards is tested in open court.

Slovakia.d:
Slovakia's record has no case marked as happening now, but the two it holds still shape its politics, and both are about outsiders getting close to the people who run the government. The first runs through eastern Slovakia's farmland. Journalist Ján Kuciak was shot dead with his fiancée, Martina Kušnírová, in February 2018 while finishing an article on Italian businessmen running farm companies there, among them Antonino Vadalà, who had been named in Italian investigations into the 'Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia. His unfinished article, published by OCCRP partners, showed that Mária Trošková, who had set up a company with Vadalà in 2011, had become chief state adviser to Prime Minister Robert Fico. Trošková and Security Council secretary Viliam Jasaň stepped aside, saying their names were being misused, and Fico resigned in March 2018 after mass protests. No court has found that the prime minister's office acted for the 'Ndrangheta.

The second involves a foreign government. In July 2017 Trinh Xuan Thanh, a former Vietnamese state-company executive seeking asylum, was seized in Berlin, and Germany blamed Vietnamese intelligence. In 2019 a Slovak journalist found a €17,000 interior ministry invoice to Vietnam for a flight to Moscow days later, and former president Andrej Kiska wrote that then interior minister Robert Kaliňák was behind lending the plane. Thanh was later given life in Hanoi. Other bodies listed as present, including Opus Dei, the Atlas Network and the Agrofert company group, have no documented case here.
Slovakia.imp: For people in Slovakia, these cases show two ways in: a businessman named in mafia inquiries getting a business partner into the prime minister's office, and a foreign spy service apparently borrowing a Slovak government plane. Neither has been proven in a Slovak court. Kuciak's reporting brought down a government, which shows that public pressure can work here. Watch who sits close to the prime minister, and how ministries account for the use of state aircraft.

Slovenia.d:
Slovenia has one documented case, and it ended without a valid conviction, so what it shows today is mostly how hard bribery in arms deals is to prove. Patria is a Finnish state-owned arms maker. In 2006 Slovenia signed a 278 million euro contract with it for 135 armoured vehicles. In 2008 the Finnish broadcaster YLE alleged that Patria paid bribes to win the deal, partly aimed at Prime Minister Janez Janša.

A Ljubljana court sentenced Janša to two years in prison in June 2013. The Constitutional Court annulled the verdict, and in 2016 the case lapsed. In Finland the defendants were acquitted on appeal, while in Austria one middleman was convicted. The map files Slovenia under "exposure, purge and reversal" because a court overturned the finding.

Several other bodies are listed as present: Opus Dei, the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, the Trilateral Commission, and Azerbaijan's "caviar diplomacy" network, which elsewhere on the map paid European politicians. None has a documented case in Slovenia, and Serbia's old Black Hand society is listed only as likely, without evidence. Slovenia's overall score is minimal, and its institutions score as fairly resilient.
Slovenia.imp: For people in Slovenia, the Patria case shows that arms contracts worth hundreds of millions of euros draw bribes, and that the courts struggle to say who took them: the one conviction of a prime minister was annulled. One middleman was convicted in Austria, so money did move, but no court has said who in Slovenia received it. Watch how defence purchases are tendered and who acts as go-between.

Spain.d:
In Spain today the clearest outside hand inside the state belongs to the cocaine trade, working through people paid to wave the drugs through. Around Algeciras, Spain's largest container port, eight miles from Morocco, smuggling networks recruit from the municipal police, customs and the port workforce. In 2024 a municipal officer and two national police officers were sentenced to more than seven years each for guarding a 367-kilogram load, and a 2022 operation arrested five municipal officers, a customs official and others over 6.2 tonnes. Prosecutors have also charged airport ground staff with moving drugs past security, and in January 2025 arrested 23 people running a laundering service for other criminals that handled around 100 million euros. The Galician coast, exposed in 1990 as Europe's main cocaine landing zone, is still in use.

At the top of government, Pegasus spyware, which its maker NSO sells only to governments, infected the phones of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and the defence minister in 2021. The High Court reopened the case in 2024; no state has been named. When the private Bilderberg conference met in Madrid in 2024, two ministers were on its list and King Felipe VI was reported present.

The older story is Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members follow its spiritual programme in ordinary jobs. From 1957 Franco put its members in charge of finance, trade, planning and foreign affairs; historians count eight among his 116 ministers. After the 1969 MATESA credit scandal he pardoned the charged ex-ministers before any verdict, and named a cabinet with eleven members tied to Opus Dei. Jorge Fernández Díaz, interior minister from 2011 to 2016, is reported to be a member. A 2024 book claims the failed Banco Popular sent money to Opus Dei causes; Opus Dei calls this false.
Spain.imp: For people in Spain, the most direct cost is police, customs and port staff being paid to let cocaine through, which courts have proven in Algeciras, and the money that buys them is cleaned through clubs and laundering services. Spyware on the prime minister's phone shows a foreign government may have reached the top, though none is named. Opus Dei's hold on Franco's ministries is history, and its influence now is reported, not proven. Watch the port and airport prosecutions and the reopened Pegasus case.

Sweden.d:
Sweden has strong institutions, and its main problem today is criminal networks working their way into the everyday parts of the state rather than its top. A November 2023 research review by Carina Gunnarson, published by the SNS think tank, found that criminal networks have infiltrated government agencies, run companies in the welfare sector and exploit social insurance, with incorrect welfare payments estimated at SEK 13–16.3 billion a year. Municipalities are the most exposed, because much public money is spent locally with weaker oversight. Swedish courts have convicted police employees of passing register data to the networks, and a Security Service officer of unauthorised disclosure.

Swedish banks carried other people's money. In 2020 the regulator fined Swedbank 4 billion kronor over high-risk flows through its Estonian, Latvian and Lithuanian branches, and Nordea and SEB were censured over similar Baltic flows; how much was drug money has never been separated out.

Economic power is concentrated in one family, legally and in the open. The Wallenberg foundations own about 23% of Investor AB but hold just over 50% of the votes, and through it control major stakes in Ericsson, ABB, Saab, SEB and others; one 2025 estimate puts the family's share of the Stockholm market at about 35%. When the private Bilderberg conference met in Stockholm in June 2025, Reuters reported that Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson attended though he was not on the published list. In the background is the 1973 IB affair, when journalists revealed a secret military intelligence bureau spying on the left.
Sweden.imp: For people in Sweden, the risk is in ordinary services: welfare companies, municipal contracts and police registers that criminal networks have reached, as courts and researchers have shown. Billions of kronor a year in welfare payments go wrong, and a leak from a police register hands the networks what police know about people. A single family's voting control over much of the stock market is legal and public, but it concentrates economic power. Watch how municipalities vet welfare contractors, and whether ministers' private meetings appear on published lists.

Switzerland.d:
Much of the rest of the map passes through Switzerland: the banks, traders and firms that handle other countries' money, and the international bodies other countries try to sway. In 2022 Credit Suisse became the first major Swiss bank convicted of a crime, for failing to stop laundering by a Bulgarian cocaine group, and Swiss courts have since convicted the commodity traders Glencore and Trafigura of bribery failures. In 2024 a Zug software firm running encrypted messaging apps was sanctioned by the US under its drug order, and in 2026 investigators traced a laundering service shared by the Camorra and the 'Ndrangheta through Swiss shell companies.

Foreign governments hire Swiss firms as well. From 2017 the United Arab Emirates paid the Geneva firm Alp Services at least €5.7m to build files on about 1,000 people and feed names into bank-compliance databases; criminal cases were reported open in 2025, and Alp says some files were falsified.

In Geneva, leaked documents showed Philip Morris campaigning to weaken the WHO tobacco treaty, the Gates Foundation was the WHO's second-largest funder in 2020, mostly for programmes it chose, and a pro-India network of fake NGOs lobbied the UN Human Rights Council. In Zurich, FIFA's World Cup votes brought US bribery charges and the exit of attorney general Michael Lauber over unrecorded meetings with FIFA's president. In Basel the Bank for International Settlements, owned by central banks, hosts governors' closed meetings and writes the bank-capital rules parliaments adopt; its outlines are public.

The biggest past case is Crypto AG, which sold encryption machines to over 120 governments while the CIA and West Germany's BND secretly owned it and read customers' messages; a 2020 Swiss inquiry found Swiss intelligence knew and benefited. Older still is P-26, a secret army outside government control, dissolved in 1990.
Switzerland.imp: For people in Switzerland, their banks, traders and consultants are where much of the world's dirty money and paid influence is handled, and courts have now convicted several big names. Decisions taken in Geneva and Basel on health, tobacco and bank rules reach people far beyond Swiss borders. Crypto AG showed Swiss authorities knew of foreign spying run from a Swiss firm and benefited. Watch the commodity-trader cases, the UAE-Alp prosecutions, and who pays for the WHO's work.

Ukraine.d:
Ukraine's record is mostly current, and it runs along two lines: people close to power taking money from the state companies that keep the country going in wartime, and Russia reaching in through firms and the church. In November 2025 the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) said a group led by Timur Mindich, a friend of President Zelensky, ran a $100 million kickback scheme on contractors of Energoatom, the state nuclear power company. Mindich left Ukraine hours before his home was searched; a former deputy prime minister was charged, Zelensky asked the justice and energy ministers to resign, and chief of staff Andriy Yermak later became a suspect. On the western border, customs and border officers at the Zakarpattia crossings are charged with running smuggling channels into the European Union.

Russia's hand shows in Zaporizhzhia, where the former president of the engine maker Motor Sich is on trial for treason over hidden supply channels to Russia arranged with the Russian state corporation Rostec. In August 2024 parliament banned the Russian Orthodox Church, whose patriarch backs the war, and gave linked Ukrainian bodies nine months to cut ties.

The banking story is older but still in court. Ihor Kolomoisky co-founded PrivatBank, the largest bank, and governed Dnipropetrovsk region in 2014–15. The state nationalised the bank in 2016 with a $5.6 billion bailout, and he was arrested in 2023 and charged with embezzling about $250 million. Rebuilding money is the next prize: in 2022 BlackRock agreed with Zelensky to help design a framework for public and private investment in reconstruction.
Ukraine.imp: For people in Ukraine, the money most at risk is the money that keeps the lights on and will rebuild their towns: the nuclear power company, the largest bank, and reconstruction funds. Anti-corruption bodies are charging people close to the president, which shows they can act, but most cases are charges, not verdicts. Russia's reach through companies and the church is being cut by law. Watch how the Midas and Motor Sich cases end, and who controls reconstruction money.

United Kingdom.d:
Britain is both a target for foreign states and the home of firms and lodges that reach into government. In 2022 MI5, the domestic security service, warned MPs that solicitor Christine Lee, a donor to Labour MP Barry Gardiner, was acting covertly with the United Front Work Department, the Chinese Communist Party's influence arm; a tribunal upheld the warning in 2024. On Russia's side, former MEP Nathan Gill of UKIP and the Brexit Party is serving ten and a half years for taking bribes to make pro-Russian speeches for a network the court heard led to Viktor Medvedchuk, and six Bulgarians in Britain were jailed for spying on journalists for Jan Marsalek, an ex-Wirecard executive suspected of working for Russian intelligence.

Inside Whitehall the steady pattern is industry helping write or bend its own rules. Big Four accountants were lent to the Treasury to help draft tax law they could then advise clients around. The Grenfell inquiry found in 2024 that cladding and insulation makers Arconic, Celotex and Kingspan deceived the fire-testing system before a fire that killed 72. A pandemic 'VIP lane' gave PPE Medpro £200 million of contracts, and the High Court has ordered about £122 million back. At the London-based UN shipping body, industry lobbies sit on national delegations, pressing to keep climate rules voluntary. Banks and gambling firms such as HSBC, Standard Chartered and Entain keep settling over laundering and bribery.

The Met now makes officers declare Freemason membership; 397 had by February 2026, and the High Court rejected the Grand Lodge's challenge. A leaked 2002 Met report said crime families entered the force at will, and EncroChat messages later convicted police and prison staff.

Older layer: Rothschild loans funded Britain's wars and the Suez shares; the tale of a Waterloo fortune is an antisemitic myth.
United Kingdom.imp: For people in Britain, the risk sits in who drafts the rules and who checks them. Tax law partly written by firms that sell avoidance, fire tests that cladding makers could game, and fast-track contracts handed out through MPs all reached homes, tax bills and hospitals. Foreign states have bought or cultivated MPs, and some police and prison staff have sold information to traffickers. Courts and inquiries do act here. Watch whether the Grenfell contract bans are carried out and whether outside paid roles of MPs are fully declared.

Vatican City.d:
The Holy See, the government of the Catholic Church, runs from Vatican City, and today it is both trying its own officials and governing a sovereign order abroad. Cardinal Angelo Becciu, second in command of the Secretariat of State (the papal government's main office) from 2011 to 2018, was convicted in 2023 with eight others over a €350 million London building deal that prosecutors said cost the Holy See tens of millions in fees. In March 2026 the appeals court nullified the indictment because papal decrees used in the case were never published and evidence was withheld, and ordered a retrial from June 2026. Nothing in it now stands as a verdict.

Outward, the Pope governs the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order that is recognised as sovereign, has diplomatic ties with 115 states and sits at the UN as an observer. Francis forced out its Grand Master in 2017, wrote it a new constitution in 2022 and appointed its governing council himself; the Order re-elected his choices.

The money problems run back through the Vatican Bank, the Institute for the Works of Religion. It was the main shareholder of Banco Ambrosiano, an Italian bank that collapsed in 1982, backed its loans to Panama shell companies, and paid creditors $224 million in 1984 for its 'moral involvement'. A treaty kept its president, Archbishop Paul Marcinkus, out of Italian court. In 2021 the Vatican's own tribunal convicted a later bank president, Angelo Caloia, of embezzlement. Its conditions scores are Italy's.
Vatican City.imp: Few people live in Vatican City, but the Holy See handles money given by Catholics everywhere. Its bank and its main office have each lost or misused large sums, and for decades a treaty kept the bank's chief beyond Italian courts. The Vatican now tries its own cardinals, yet the Becciu case shows that decrees issued outside public view can undo a whole trial. Watch the retrial and whether the rules it depends on are made public.

North Macedonia.d:
North Macedonia's record is thin and holds no proven case of outside capture. The one documented item is lawful: the World Economic Forum, the Davos business and government forum, picks people under about 40 each year for its Young Global Leaders programme, a five-year network of meetings and courses, and its class of 2025 includes Timčo Mucunski, the country's Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade. Membership is a selection by the Forum, not evidence that it directs his decisions.

The wider picture comes from the region. North Macedonia's conditions scores, with fairly high levels of criminal actors inside the state and middling capacity to resist, are also used as a stand-in for neighbouring Kosovo. There, the record shows former wartime commanders accused of running criminal trades from government, and Kosovo's intelligence service handing six residents to Turkey in its hunt for followers of preacher Fethullah Gülen. The Gülen movement is likely present in North Macedonia too, though nothing is documented. The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, has a recorded presence. The record does not show any of these reaching into North Macedonia's government.
North Macedonia.imp: For people in North Macedonia, the record gives no proven case to point to, but the scores suggest criminal interests have room inside the state. A foreign minister in a business forum's network is legal, though people may want to know what he is offered there. Watch Turkey's requests concerning Gülen-linked residents, as in Kosovo, and whether ministers declare outside affiliations.

Antigua and Barbuda.d:
In Antigua and Barbuda the record is about an offshore bank that grew larger than the office meant to watch it, and that story is finished but still felt. R. Allen Stanford, a Texan financier, ran Stanford International Bank from Antigua and was convicted in the US of a $7 billion fraud. A small island financial centre depends on its regulator, the body that checks what banks hold, and that is where Stanford reached. A June 2009 US indictment charges Leroy King, then head of Antigua's Financial Services Regulatory Commission, with taking more than $100,000 in bribes from Stanford to ignore the bank's real assets and help obstruct an investigation by the US Securities and Exchange Commission. Antigua extradited King to Houston in November 2019. The charge is an indictment, not a conviction.

Two other outside names are recorded as present without a case: the Order of Malta, and the Sun Kian Ip Group of the businessman Ng Lap Seng. The conditions scores are middling: few signs of outside actors embedded in the state, and moderate checks. That fits a country whose exposure comes through finance rather than through its police or courts. Antigua sits in the pattern on banks and banking families, as a case that is over but still felt, and it is the home of the Stanford group.
Antigua and Barbuda.imp: For people in Antigua and Barbuda, if the head regulator was paid, as charged, the checks meant to protect depositors and the country's standing in banking did not work. Small offshore centres live on the trust of foreign banks, and one scandal raises costs and scrutiny for every local bank and business that moves money abroad. Watch how the regulator is staffed and funded, and who oversees it.

Barbados.d: This is a best guess: no case is documented for Barbados on this map. English Freemasonry, the United Grand Lodge of England, is likely present but has no recorded case, and membership of a lodge is not wrongdoing. Barbados scores well on conditions: few signs of outside actors embedded in the state, and some of the stronger checks in the region. Neighbouring island financial centres on this map, Antigua and the Bahamas, have been reached through their banks and bank regulators rather than through cabinets or police, and global banks are cutting links with small Caribbean jurisdictions. If outside money reaches Barbados, offshore finance is the likeliest route. This is an estimate, not a finding.
Barbados.imp: For people in Barbados, the map has no case to report and conditions are better than in most countries. A blank record means nothing has been documented, not that nothing could happen. The area to watch is offshore finance: who sets up companies on the island, how the bank regulator is run, and whether foreign banks keep their links to local banks.

Belize.d:
In Belize the one documented case touches the office that decides who can hold a Belizean passport, and it ended without proof. In September 2013 Prime Minister Dean Barrow removed Elvin Penner, minister of state for immigration, after Penner was accused of selling and issuing a passport to a South Korean man, Kim Won Hong, who was then jailed in Taiwan. Penner was charged in March 2014, but the charges were dropped in July 2014 for lack of evidence. The case is marked contested.

What makes the office worth reaching is a wider trade. The citizenship-by-investment industry, the business of selling passports and residence to foreign buyers in several small countries, is recorded as present in Belize. A passport opens borders and bank accounts, so the official who signs it is a natural target for buyers abroad, whether or not any particular sale was corrupt. The Order of Malta is also recorded as present.

Belize's conditions scores are worse than those of the island financial centres nearby, such as the Bahamas and Antigua: a middling score for outside actors embedded in the state and fairly weak checks. Belize sits in the patterns on organised crime inside the state and on exposure, purge and reversal, both as a disputed case.
Belize.imp: For Belizeans, a passport is worth only as much as other countries' trust in how it is issued. If foreign buyers can get one through a minister, every Belizean faces harder questions at borders and banks. The Penner case was dropped, so nothing was proven, but the charge was never tested in a full trial. Watch how citizenship and passports are granted, and who checks the immigration department.

Colombia.d:
In Colombia, cocaine money reaches every layer of the state at once: the presidency, Congress, the high courts, prosecutors, police and town halls. The United States designated President Gustavo Petro under its illicit-drug sanctions order in October 2025, citing rising coca cultivation; it is a US executive measure, not a charge, and Colombia rejects it. In the courts, the 'Cartel de la Toga' cases closed in February 2026 with two former Supreme Court presidents, a magistrate and the national anti-corruption prosecutor convicted of taking bribes to shelve cases against members of Congress. Those cases came from the 'parapolítica' files, which since 2006 have investigated about 30% of Congress for collusion with the AUC, right-wing paramilitaries who were also big cocaine traffickers; five governors and 32 legislators were convicted by 2012. A serving prosecutor was charged in 2023 with holding property for the Gulf Clan, the largest trafficking group, and a Gulf Clan associate funded mayoral candidates in several municipalities.

The money moves through ordinary businesses. US Treasury lists show farms in Córdoba, coffee, mining, meat and property firms in Medellín, emerald mines and a football club, run as fronts; La Oficina de Envigado, a group that sells debt collection, extortion and killing to other criminals, has been hit by eight separate actions, and five of its companies shared one Medellín office. On the Pacific coast and in Nariño, mangrove boatyards build semi-submersibles, and the black market peso exchange still brings US drug dollars home as ordinary trade.

Foreign firms bought in too: Chiquita admitted paying the AUC, and Odebrecht, the Brazilian builder, paid into President Santos's 2010 campaign. The roots are Proceso 8000, which found Cali cartel money in the 1994 presidential campaign. The MIRA party, tied to a Colombian Pentecostal church, holds three Senate seats.
Colombia.imp: For Colombians, a criminal case can be bought at the appeal stage, as the Supreme Court bribery convictions show, and a mayor's campaign can be paid for by a trafficking group. A farm, a coffee firm or a building company in Medellín may be a front, and the US keeps naming replacements after earlier ones are listed. Victims' families won a civil verdict against Chiquita in Florida in 2024. Watch prosecutors who hold assets for traffickers, Gulf Clan money in local elections, and the dispute over the Petro designation.

Costa Rica.d:
Costa Rica's documented problem is new and comes with the cocaine route from Colombia: traffickers are buying advance warning from inside the security forces. On the Caribbean side, in the lowlands around Guápiles and Cariari de Pococí, investigators found regular phone contact between a trafficking group and police officers recruited to warn of raids, checkpoints and investigators' movements; five officers were charged in 2026 in the 'Caso Colorado'. Higher up, Gamboa Sánchez, a former vice-minister of public security who later sat as a judge, was arrested in June 2025 on a US extradition request. The US Treasury says he used his contacts inside the government to learn about counter-narcotics investigations while helping move cocaine worth tens of millions of dollars toward the United States and Europe. He could be sent abroad only because a constitutional change signed in May 2025 allowed Costa Ricans to be extradited for drug trafficking. Neither case has a verdict.

The other entry is open religious politics. Fabricio Alvarado, an evangelical Christian singer, reached the 2018 presidential runoff on opposition to a regional human-rights court ruling on same-sex marriage, and sat in the Legislative Assembly again from 2022 to 2026. That is a public campaign, not a hidden network.

Costa Rica scores low overall, with three documented cases, two of them from the last two years.
Costa Rica.imp: People along the Caribbean corridor live where traffickers can learn of a raid before it happens, which lets drugs be moved or hidden in time. Both cases are charges, not convictions. The new extradition rule means officials accused of helping traffickers can now face trial in the United States rather than only at home. Watch the Caso Colorado trial, the Gamboa Sánchez extradition, and whether more officials are named.

Cuba.d:
In Cuba the record shows the state reaching into private bodies rather than outsiders reaching into the state. The Grand Lodge of Cuba, the country's main Freemasons' organisation, has been under the government's hand since at least 2000. Its Grand Master from that year, José Manuel Collera Vento, took the post after government pressure, and in 2011, after WikiLeaks cables exposed him, he admitted on state television that he was a state-security officer, 'Agente Gerardo', placed at the top so the government could monitor Freemasons. A provincial assembly then gave him its highest award. Since 2024 the Ministry of Justice, which registers every association, has declined to recognise the lodge's newly elected leaders, after about $19,000 meant for a Masonic retirement home went missing and the Grand Master was expelled, the independent outlet 14ymedio reported. A former grand official who fled in 2023 said a state-security officer told him agents had watched Cuban lodges for over 40 years.

The older case is crime inside the state itself. In 1989 General Arnaldo Ochoa and an Interior Ministry colonel who ran the state's hard-currency operations were court-martialled for moving cocaine through Cuban waters and airspace, and executed by firing squad; the interior minister was dismissed and jailed in the same purge.

Cuba scores minimal overall.
Cuba.imp: For Cuban Freemasons, the government has already placed its own agent at the head of their lodge and now decides whose election counts. Members cannot know who among them reports to state security, and a dispute over missing money for a retirement home became a matter for a ministry to settle. Watch whether the Justice Ministry recognises a lodge leadership and whether other associations get the same treatment.

Dominica.d:
Dominica sells citizenship, and that trade is the one route on this map by which outside money reaches its government. A 2023 investigation by OCCRP, a network of investigative reporters, with the Government Accountability Project, counted about 7,700 people who had bought Dominican passports, among them Afghanistan's former spy chief and Russians under sanctions.

The one documented case about officials is an allegation, not a finding. Al Jazeera's investigative unit reported in November 2019 that Iranian businessman Alireza Monfared gave hundreds of thousands of dollars to Prime Minister Roosevelt Skerrit's 2014 election campaign in return for an ambassadorship and a diplomatic passport, and a witness said Skerrit handed the passport over in Kuala Lumpur. Monfared was later jailed in Iran for stealing oil revenue. Skerrit denies any trade, and no court or inquiry has ruled on the claim; the map marks it as only possible.

Dominica scores minimal overall. It sits with the citizenship-sale industry, which runs in neighbouring Grenada too, where Al Jazeera reported similar claims the same day.
Dominica.imp: When a small state sells passports and diplomatic titles, people with money from abroad can gain a citizen's papers or an envoy's standing. Dominicans cannot see the full list of who has bought citizenship, or whether any diplomatic post was paid for. The Monfared claim is denied and untested. Watch who is given diplomatic passports and whether the government ever publishes its buyer lists.

Dominican Republic.d:
In the Dominican Republic, outside money reaches officials by two routes: a foreign builder paying for public works, and drug traffickers buying the agencies meant to stop them. The builder is Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction group, which admitted to the United States in 2016 that it paid 92 million dollars in Dominican bribes to win public works. A Dominican court convicted former public works minister Víctor Díaz Rúa and businessman Ángel Rondón, named as the bribe channel, in 2021; four other defendants were acquitted, and an appeal court upheld both convictions in 2023.

The drug route runs through the ports and the security forces, on shipments heading to Puerto Rico and Spain. Senior officials of the National Drug Control Agency (DNCD) were arrested guarding traffickers who were waiting for a load bound for Puerto Rico; a navy officer in charge of port security was accused of moving 800 kilograms to Spain; and nearly twenty officials, mostly navy, were accused in 2008 of killing seven Colombian traffickers to take 1.3 tonnes. The scale shows in the purges: more than 700 DNCD staff removed since 2009, about 200 of them suspected of trafficking, and about 1,400 police officers expelled from 2010.

The country scores low overall, but its conditions score is higher, at 5.29.
Dominican Republic.imp: Dominicans paid for public works won with a foreign builder's bribes, and two people were convicted over 92 million dollars of them. In the ports, the officers checking cargo and the agents meant to raid traffickers have been recruited by the people they were meant to stop, and the dismissal figures show this was not rare. Watch how public contracts are awarded and whether the purges of the anti-drug agency and the police keep going.

Ecuador.d:
In Ecuador, cocaine gangs have reached inside the courts, the prisons and the export trade within a decade, and the country now carries more US terrorist-listed gangs than most producing states. The courts are the clearest case.
