The 'Metastasis' file began when prosecutors decrypted a trafficker's phone; in November 2024 the National Court sentenced 20 of 21 defendants, judges, prosecutors, police commanders and prison officials, for fixing cases and protecting traffickers, the former head of the Judiciary Council among them, and sent back for investigation others named at trial. In Guayas province, 'Caso Purga' charges judges and a former legislator said to be the power behind the provincial courts, over paid releases.

On the coast, cocaine leaves Guayaquil inside banana shipments, with exporters, port staff and customs officials prosecuted. In Manta, according to US sanctions of August 2026, a licensed tuna fleet meets the go-fast boats at sea with fuel, food and lookouts, using government-subsidised fuel. Los Choneros, Los Lobos and the Chone Killers are now on the US terrorist list.

President Daniel Noboa brought in a foreign private force in March 2025, announcing a deal with Erik Prince, founder of the US security firm Blackwater, to support troops and police against the gangs.

Foreign companies bought officials before the gangs did. Vice-President Jorge Glas was sentenced in 2017 for taking about $13.5 million from Odebrecht, the Brazilian builder, and the Geneva oil trader Gunvor was convicted in Switzerland in 2024 of corruption in Ecuador, paying about $661 million in US and Swiss penalties. Former president Guillermo Lasso is reported to be an Opus Dei supernumerary, a married lay member; that is membership, not wrongdoing.
Ecuador.imp: For people in Ecuador, a release order or a verdict may have been paid for, and the Metastasis convictions show that has happened at the top of the judiciary. Fishermen, banana packers and port workers on the coast are recruited into the routes, and a fuel subsidy meant for fishing ends up supplying cocaine boats. Watch the Caso Purga trial, the judges named but not charged, the extradition requests for two Metastasis fugitives, and what Prince's contractors are allowed to do.

El Salvador.d:
In El Salvador the documented question is whether the government bought its fall in murders from the gangs: MS-13, a gang that spans Central America and the United States, and its rival Barrio 18. In December 2021 the US Treasury sanctioned two of President Bukele's officials, prisons director Osiris Luna and Carlos Marroquín, head of the Social Fabric Reconstruction Unit, for negotiating with the gang leaders: privileges and money inside the prisons in return for fewer killings and electoral support. A US indictment of 13 MS-13 leaders, unsealed in New York in February 2023, says the meetings 'were organized by the government of El Salvador and prison officials', that leaders received benefits and one wanted by the US was released, and that in return the gang cut public killings and backed Bukele's Nuevas Ideas party in the 2021 election. Much of this was first reported by the newspaper El Faro from 2020.

The status matters. The indictment charges the gang leaders, not the officials; the officials face sanctions, not a trial; and Bukele's government denies any pact. No court has ruled on what the officials did.

El Salvador scores low on documented cases but high on conditions (7.12), mainly because its resilience score, a measure of the institutions that could check a deal like this, is low at 3.2.
El Salvador.imp: If the US findings are right, part of the drop in killings was bought with prison privileges, and the gangs' support counted in an election. Salvadorans have no domestic court ruling on this, only US sanctions and an indictment, and their government denies it. Watch what evidence the New York case against the MS-13 leaders puts on the record, and whether any Salvadoran body examines the officials named.

Grenada.d:
Grenada sells citizenship to foreign investors and has given ambassador titles to foreign businessmen, and that trade is the route by which outside money reaches its government on this map. The one documented case is an allegation. Al Jazeera's investigative unit reported in November 2019 that investor Eric Resteiner claimed he paid about half a million dollars to Prime Minister Keith Mitchell; Mitchell said he received only 15,000 dollars, for travel costs. In the same report, US businessman Leo Ford said a partner was offered a diplomatic post in return for kickbacks on state projects, which the government denies. No court or inquiry has ruled on any of it, and the map marks it as only possible.

Al Jazeera reported the same day on Dominica, where an Iranian donor is alleged to have bought an ambassadorship, so the two islands show the same arrangement: a small state with passports and diplomatic titles to sell, and buyers who want the head of government's attention.

Grenada scores minimal overall.
Grenada.imp: Where passports and diplomatic titles are for sale, a foreign investor can buy closeness to the prime minister and a title that carries diplomatic standing. Grenadians cannot see who has paid for these posts or what was promised on state projects in return. The claims are disputed and unproven. Watch who receives ambassador titles and whether the government publishes who has bought citizenship.

Guyana.d:
Guyana is treated by the United States as a cocaine route now, with gold smuggling running alongside, and both depend on officials paid to look away. In June 2025 the US Treasury published a chart of how traffickers use the country and designated the two men it says run Guyana's largest trafficking organisations, two Colombians managing jungle airstrips, a serving police officer accused of arranging safe passage for Mexican and Venezuelan traffickers, and a former officer wanted over the 2024 abduction of a policeman. None has been tried. In Barima-Waini, cocaine has been found buried in bunkers on airstrips, and semi-submersible boats carry loads from Guyanese and Surinamese ports across the Atlantic; in March 2025 a cargo ship out of Guyana was stopped off Trinidad with about 182 kilograms stamped with a logo the Sinaloa Cartel uses.

Gold is the second route. In 2024 the US sanctioned gold trader Nazar Mohamed, his son Azruddin and their firm for keeping over 10,000 kilograms of gold off customs declarations, saying they bribed customs officials and paid for favours in court matters and state contracts. It also sanctioned Mae Thomas, a permanent secretary in the home affairs ministry, for taking cash and gifts for contract, gun-permit and passport favours. The Mohameds deny wrongdoing.

The background is the Phantom Squad, an armed group run by trafficker Roger Khan that worked alongside the state during killings in the mid-2000s; he was convicted in New York, but the squad's link to the government was never settled in a Guyanese court.
Guyana.imp: In Guyana the police officer on a route, the customs officer at the gold declaration and the ministry official signing gun permits have each been named by the US as open to payment. Most of these findings come from US sanctions, and Guyanese courts have not ruled on them. Unpaid gold duty is money the country loses: more than 50 million dollars by the US count. Watch whether the designated officers are charged at home and how gold exports are checked.

Haiti.d:
In Haiti, armed gangs control much of Port-au-Prince, and the record shows politicians in the capital, the Artibonite and Miragoâne arming and paying them. The gangs joined in the Viv Ansanm alliance in 2023. A UN panel of experts' report released in October 2026 accuses former Kenscoff legislator Alfredo Junior Antoine of arming groups and sponsoring a 2025 attack that killed more than 100 people, and former senator Nenel Cassy of controlling a criminal group in Miragoâne. It says the long use of gangs by former senator Youri Latortue and ex-lawmaker Prophane Victor fuels violence in the Artibonite ahead of elections, that at least one member of the new Cité Soleil municipal commission is an active gang member, and that some police officers supply gangs with weapons and information. Antoine and Cassy deny it. Canada sanctioned Latortue, Senator Joseph Lambert in 2022 for financing gangs, and the US designated former president Michel Martelly in 2024 for sponsoring gangs and trafficking; he denies it and no court has heard it. The path from police to gang shows in Jimmy Chérizier, a serving officer until 2018 who went on to lead the largest gang federation in the capital.

A foreign private company is now inside the security effort. Vectus Global, run by Blackwater founder Erik Prince, took part in anti-gang raids, as Haitian authorities confirmed in January 2026, and Reuters reported Prince planned to stay ten years and help collect taxes.

Guy Philippe, a former police commander jailed in the US for laundering drug money, returned to Haitian politics in 2023.
Haiti.imp: Haitians live under gangs that some of their own politicians and police are accused of arming, so a person asking for votes may also be paying the group that attacks the neighbourhood. Most of this rests on sanctions and a UN report rather than verdicts. A foreign contractor now takes part in raids and may help collect taxes. Watch the coming elections in the Artibonite, the powers given to Vectus Global, and whether any accused politician is tried.

St. Kitts and Nevis.d:
St Kitts and Nevis has sold citizenship to foreign investors since 1984, and the industry that sells passports this way is based here. That programme is the country's one documented case, and what it shows is a state selling something to outsiders rather than outsiders sitting inside the state. A passport from a small country lets its holder travel and open bank accounts under a new nationality, which is why foreign sanctions agencies watch who buys them.

In May 2014 the US Treasury's financial crimes unit, FinCEN, warned banks that several Iranians under US sanctions had obtained Kittitian passports through the programme, which it said 'maintains lax controls', and that Iranians kept getting them even after the country suspended them in 2013. The warning made banks more cautious with anyone holding Kittitian citizenship. FinCEN withdrew it in February 2026, after the passports had expired and the programme had been reformed.

Nothing else is recorded. No organisation other than the passport industry is documented as present, and the country's overall score is minimal, 1.97, though its conditions score is middling at 4.81, with moderate signs of outside actors inside the state and moderate ability to resist them. St Kitts and Nevis sits in the map's pattern on exposure, purge and reversal: a scheme was exposed by an outside agency, the government changed the programme, and the warning was lifted.
St. Kitts and Nevis.imp: For people in St Kitts and Nevis, the record is about what the state sells: citizenship bought by outsiders, including people under US sanctions. While the warning stood, the country's own passport drew extra scrutiny from banks, which falls on ordinary Kittitians as well as buyers. Watch who buys passports now, how buyers are checked, and whether outside agencies raise new concerns.

St. Lucia.d: Nothing is documented on this map for St Lucia; this write-up is a best guess. The only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order that holds diplomatic relations with many states, and no case ties it to wrongdoing here. The conditions scores are low: 3.0 out of 10 for outside actors embedded in the state, and 5.5 for resilience. Nearby, the record for St Kitts and Nevis shows the route seen on small Caribbean islands: a state selling passports, which sanctioned buyers used. If something is going on in St Lucia, it would most likely come through money and what the state can sell.
St. Lucia.imp: For people in St Lucia, no outside group is recorded capturing any part of the government, and no official has been charged or sanctioned for working for one. That means nothing has been documented, not that nothing could happen. The neighbouring record suggests the places to watch are financial services and any scheme in which the state sells something, such as citizenship, to outsiders.

St. Vincent and the Grenadines.d: Nothing is documented on this map for St Vincent and the Grenadines; this write-up is a best guess. The only organisation recorded as present is the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order that holds diplomatic relations with many states, and no case ties it to wrongdoing here. Its conditions scores are among the lowest in the region: 2.0 out of 10 for outside actors embedded in the state, and 5.4 for resilience. On nearby islands the documented route is money, as in St Kitts and Nevis, where passport sales to sanctioned buyers drew a US warning, so that is the likeliest way in here too.
St. Vincent and the Grenadines.imp: For people in St Vincent and the Grenadines, no outside group is recorded capturing part of the government, and no official has been charged or sanctioned for working for one. That means nothing has been documented, not that nothing could happen. Neighbouring islands suggest the places to watch are financial services and anything the state sells to outsiders, such as citizenship.

Suriname.d:
Suriname's record centres on one family that held both the presidency and a security service while trafficking cocaine. The main cases are closed, but the conditions that allowed them are still scored high: 7.67 overall, with 8.5 out of 10 for outside actors embedded in the state and only 3.2 for resilience. South American cocaine networks are recorded as present.

Dési Bouterse was military head of state in the 1980s and was later elected president twice, although a Dutch court had convicted him in absentia in 1999 of trafficking almost 500 kilograms of cocaine and sentenced him to eleven years. With no extradition treaty, the sentence was never carried out. A Surinamese case over the 1982 killing of fifteen political opponents, the 'December murders', took 16 years and ended in a 20-year sentence upheld in December 2023. He did not surrender, disappeared in January 2024 and died in hiding that December, having served no time for either conviction.

While his father was president, Dino Bouterse ran Suriname's Counter-Terrorism Unit. In 2013 the US Drug Enforcement Administration lured him to Panama and arrested him. He pleaded guilty in New York to cocaine trafficking, weapons offences and offering a base in Suriname to people he believed were from Hezbollah, the Lebanese armed movement; they were in fact DEA informants. He was sentenced in 2015 to about 16 years. The US-funded National Endowment for Democracy and the Order of Malta are also recorded as present, with no wrongdoing found.
Suriname.imp: For people in Suriname, voters twice elected a president who had already been convicted abroad of cocaine trafficking, and the unit meant to protect them from armed groups was run by his son as a trafficking business. Courts at home convicted the father of murder but could not make him serve. The weak checks the scores describe remain. Watch who controls the security services and whether courts can enforce rulings against powerful people.

Argentina.d:
In Argentina the reach of outside money is being argued out in the courts now, and it runs through public works, the drug trade and the economy ministry. Former President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner faces two trials. In the 'Notebooks' case, opened in November 2025 with 87 defendants, prosecutors allege construction, energy and transport firms paid officials of the Federal Planning Ministry in cash for public-works contracts from 2003 to 2015; several executives testified for leniency, and she denies the charges. Separately, the Supreme Court ruled in December 2024 that she must stand trial for covering up for Iran over the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish centre, through a 2013 pact. These are charges, not verdicts.

Drug money has reached provincial police and federal judges around Rosario and in Salta province. Santa Fe's police chief, Hugo Tognoli, was convicted in 2016 of protecting a trafficking network around Rosario; a federal judge in Orán was convicted in 2019 of selling rulings to traffickers, after another judge bought by the same trafficker was convicted in 2007; and a judge in Mendoza was charged.

At the top of the economy are people from foreign banks and think-tank networks. Economy Minister Luis Caputo and Central Bank president Santiago Bausili both came from JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank. President Javier Milei won a prize from an Atlas Network think tank in 2018, and the US-based Atlas Network says its partners helped push his reforms; that is its own claim, and holding these posts is not wrongdoing.

The older background is the P2 lodge, a secret Italian Masonic lodge whose 1981 lists named an interim president, ministers and junta commanders, and Operation Condor, the joint repression of the region's dictatorships, for which 15 officers were convicted in 2016.
Argentina.imp: For Argentines, money meant for roads, power and transport has been at the centre of bribery charges, and provincial police and judges in trafficking areas have been bought, so a case in Rosario or Salta can be decided before it reaches court. The economy and central bank are run by people from banks Argentina borrows from, which shapes how debt is handled. Watch the Notebooks and Iran-pact trials, how Atlas-linked groups shape new laws, and whether trafficking cases reach officials.

Bahamas.d:
In the Bahamas the record is about banking, and the live part of it is decided in other countries. Correspondent banks are the big foreign banks that let a small country's banks send and receive money abroad. Global banks have been cutting these links with small Caribbean jurisdictions faster than anywhere else, citing the cost of checking for criminal money. The IMF, the World Bank and the Caribbean Financial Action Task Force report the effect: legitimate remittances and trade move to less visible channels, while trafficking money, which never depended on those links, finds other routes. The map rates this as possible, not proven, and it is a pattern across the region rather than a Bahamian scandal.

The older case shows why the region is watched. Banco Ambrosiano Overseas in Nassau was a subsidiary of Calvi's Banco Ambrosiano, and Archbishop Paul Marcinkus, president of the Vatican Bank, had sat on its board. When Ambrosiano collapsed in 1982, Bahamian authorities suspended the Nassau unit, which with the Luxembourg unit owed about half of the $1.2–1.4 billion lent to shell companies in Panama.

The Order of Malta and the Vatican Bank are recorded as present; English Freemasonry and the collapsed bank BCCI are likely but undocumented. The conditions scores are good: few signs of outside actors embedded in the state and fairly strong checks. The Bahamas sits in the patterns on banks and banking families and banks that carried hidden money, as a booking centre.
Bahamas.imp: For people in the Bahamas, rules made in foreign head offices decide whether families can send and receive money cheaply and whether local firms can pay suppliers abroad. When foreign banks pull out, ordinary customers are pushed to costlier or less visible channels, while criminal money moves on regardless. The Ambrosiano case shows how an offshore unit can hold a large share of hidden debt for someone else. Watch for further bank withdrawals and how the regulator responds.

Bolivia.d:
In Bolivia, the police meant to fight the cocaine trade have been led by men working for it. Two heads of the FELCN, the national anti-narcotics force, were convicted in US courts. Maximiliano Dávila, who led it until 2019, was convicted in Manhattan in October 2025 and sentenced in March 2026 to 25 years; prosecutors showed he steered investigations away from allied traffickers and sent armed FELCN officers to guard cocaine loads. René Sanabria, an earlier commander, pleaded guilty in Miami in 2011 after a sting and got 14 years. Both cases were proven abroad, none at home.

The money side is now on an international watch list. In June 2025 the Financial Action Task Force, the global anti-money-laundering body, added Bolivia to its list of countries under increased monitoring, at the same session as the British Virgin Islands: a cocaine-producing country and an offshore company registry at the two ends of one chain. Brazil's police also trace a trafficking route from Bolivia through Paraguay into Minas Gerais, where a judge was convicted of ruling for traffickers.

The background is the 1980 'cocaine coup' of General Luis García Meza. His interior minister, Luis Arce Gómez, was given a life sentence by a Rome appeals court in 2019 in the Operation Condor case. Journalist Robert Parry reported that the Unification Church of Sun Myung Moon backed the coup with about $4 million; that rests on one author's account. Bolivia sits in the patterns on organised crime inside the state and the anticommunist web.
Bolivia.imp: For Bolivians, the anti-drug police, the force meant to protect them from traffickers, was twice led by men later convicted of serving them, and both convictions came from US courts, not Bolivian ones. That leaves people unsure whether a raid or a dropped case at home is genuine. Being on the international watch list makes banking with the outside world slower and costlier for ordinary businesses. Watch who is appointed to lead the FELCN and whether cases are brought in Bolivia.

Brazil.d:
In Brazil, organised crime has moved into ordinary businesses and the money system. The PCC (Primeiro Comando da Capital), the country's largest criminal organisation, is accused of owning two São Paulo bus companies that received more than R$800 million of city money in a single year, and which the city took over in 2024. Operation Carbono Oculto has since traced PCC money through about forty investment funds in São Paulo's financial district, fintechs moving some 26 billion reais, and more than a thousand petrol stations across ten states selling adulterated fuel. Named firms deny wrongdoing, and most of this is still under investigation. The same groups reach officials: São Paulo police are charged with shielding PCC members, and in February 2026 the Supreme Court convicted a federal deputy and an audit-court counsellor of ordering the 2018 murder of councillor Marielle Franco, over land in militia-held west Rio.

Companies have bought officials at the state oil company, Petrobras: the trader Trafigura pleaded guilty in the US in 2024. Operation Car Wash charged 429 people, though former President Lula's convictions were annulled in 2021 because the court lacked jurisdiction.

Churches and agribusiness are organised inside Congress openly and lawfully. The Evangelical Parliamentary Front registers 213 of 513 deputies, the Republicanos party was founded by Universal Church pastors and is led by a bishop, and a Presbyterian pastor sits on the Supreme Court. The farm caucus's agenda is drafted by a think tank funded by groups including Bayer, Cargill and JBS.

The older background includes a CIA-linked institute funding 1962 candidates, the 1964 coup, US NSA spying on President Rousseff in 2013, and the 2005 'mensalão' vote-buying scheme run through Banco Rural.
Brazil.imp: For Brazilians, criminal money now runs through things they use every day: city buses, petrol stations and investment funds. Adulterated fuel cheats drivers twice, on volume and on quality. Firms have paid officials at Petrobras, and several politicians accused have seen cases annulled or blocked. Churches and agribusiness shape laws openly through their caucuses. Watch the Carbono Oculto prosecutions, the São Paulo police case, and how fintechs are regulated now.

Canada.d:
Canada has two kinds of outsider working inside it: foreign governments reaching into elections and diaspora communities, and drug and money-laundering networks reaching into police, border posts and casinos. A federal public inquiry led by Marie-Josée Hogue reported in January 2025 that China is the most active state interfering in Canada, working through diplomats, proxies and the United Front Work Department, the Chinese Communist Party body that builds influence over overseas Chinese communities and foreign elites. It named India second, citing intelligence that India's proxies may still be giving illicit money to Canadian politicians. A parliamentary security committee said in 2024 that some unnamed MPs and senators took part knowingly; Hogue found no 'traitors' but 'some concerning conduct'. In British Columbia, after activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar was shot dead in Surrey in 2023, Canada expelled six Indian diplomats, saying they passed targets to the Lawrence Bishnoi gang, now listed in Canada as a terrorist entity. The Chinese cases in Toronto and Montreal have mostly ended without charges, and an ex-RCMP officer was acquitted in May 2026 (prosecutors are appealing). China and India reject the findings.

Crime has reached the security services. Cameron Ortis, an RCMP intelligence director, was convicted of offering police material to the head of the encrypted-phone firm Phantom Secure, and border officers at Windsor and on the Pacific Highway have been convicted of waving drug loads through. Inquiries found the Rizzuto Mafia taking a cut of Montreal public works and bags of cash accepted at BC casinos. In 2019 the ethics commissioner found Prime Minister Trudeau broke conflict law by pressing his attorney general to help SNC-Lavalin, the Montreal engineering firm.

The older background is the lodges: the Orange Order, a Protestant fraternity, counted four prime ministers and ran Toronto city hall for a century.
Canada.imp: Chinese and Sikh Canadians are the first targets of foreign states: watched, pressured, and in one case an activist shot dead in Surrey, a killing Canada links to agents of India's government, which India denies. Voters cannot see whether a nomination race was steered by a foreign mission, because the inquiries name no parliamentarians. Police secrets have been offered for sale and border posts opened to drug loads. Watch whether Hogue's 51 recommendations are carried out, the Majcher appeal, and the US case against Bishnoi.

Chile.d:
Chile's documented picture today has three parts: Catholic lay movements close to the new government, a mining company that paid politicians, and police drawn into the drug trade. President José Antonio Kast, in office since March 2026, is reported by BBC Mundo and El Mercurio to belong to the Schoenstatt Movement, a Catholic lay movement founded in Germany in 1914 with many shrines in Chile. His under-secretary of justice, Luis Silva, is reported to be a numerary, a celibate member, of Opus Dei, the Catholic organisation that urges lay members to excel in public life; Joaquín Lavín, an Opus Dei supernumerary, ran education under President Piñera. Membership is lawful, and nothing on the map shows either group directing policy. Money is the proven route. From 2015 prosecutors traced fake invoices that SQM, the lithium and fertiliser miner whose main shareholder is Pinochet's former son-in-law, paid to politicians, advisers and relatives across the spectrum; SQM settled US bribery charges in 2017 and now partners the state copper company Codelco on lithium. Think tanks feed the cabinet too: Cristián Larroulet went from Libertad y Desarrollo, an Atlas Network partner, into Piñera's government. In Santiago and the northern border region, prosecutors are charging Carabineros police officers with reselling seized drugs and protecting dealers, as Chile turns from drug market into transit route.

What the dictatorship left is still close. DINA, Pinochet's intelligence service, convened Operation Condor, the joint campaign of South American military regimes against their opponents, in Santiago in 1975, and held prisoners at Colonia Dignidad, a German sect compound near Parral. Economists trained in a US-funded Chicago-Catholic University programme ran the economy ministries and the central bank, among them Miguel Kast, the president's brother.
Chile.imp: Chileans are governed partly by people from lay movements whose internal guidance the public does not see, though the record shows membership, not direction. The proven harms are concrete: campaigns paid through a miner's fake invoices, and police in Santiago and the north charged with selling seized drugs and shielding dealers. Pinochet died without being convicted of the Condor crimes he was indicted for. Watch the Carabineros cases, the SQM-Codelco lithium deal, and whom Kast appoints.

Guatemala.d:
In Guatemala, drug traffickers have reached town halls, Congress, the regional parliament and the police, and since 2019 the cases against them are heard mostly in US courts. On the Mexican border, the 'Los Pochos' organisation, which supplies the Sinaloa Cartel, was designated in 2019 together with the serving mayor it is named after; when the US relisted it in 2024 its members were still in local politics, and its nine companies are the part that survives a change of leader. The Huistas organisation, also on the border, is led according to US prosecutors by a sitting deputy of the Central American Parliament, whose 2017 cocaine indictment is untried. In Escuintla, the mayor of Santa Lucía pleaded guilty in July 2026 to using his office, and municipal letterhead, to pass a cocaine shipment off as cement. A congressman pleaded guilty in 2024, and the head of the anti-drug police and his deputy did so in 2006. In Guatemala City, import firms broker fentanyl chemicals from India for the Sinaloa Cartel.

The cases go abroad because of what happened to CICIG, an international commission set up with the UN in 2006 to help Guatemalan prosecutors take apart criminal networks in the state. In 2015 it exposed 'La Línea', a customs-bribery ring that brought down President Otto Pérez Molina and Vice-President Roxana Baldetti, both sentenced in 2022. When it turned to President Jimmy Morales's campaign money he ended the agreement, and by 2023 more than thirty judges and prosecutors who had worked such cases had left the country under threat of arrest.

The older background is the Cold War: Mario Sandoval Alarcón, a leader of the World Anti-Communist League, was vice-president in 1974–78.
Guatemala.imp: Guatemalans live with mayors and legislators who have worked for traffickers, and with fewer prosecutors at home to pursue them, since many who did have fled. Cases end in Washington or Texas, far from the towns they concern, and along the border Treasury says Los Pochos members are still in local politics. Watch the Salazar Flores case, the fentanyl precursor route through Guatemala City firms, and whether exiled prosecutors can return.

Honduras.d:
Honduras is where traffickers' reach into the state has been proven at every level in US courts: the presidency, Congress, the police command and a bank. Juan Orlando Hernández, president from 2014 to 2022, was convicted in New York and sentenced to 45 years in 2024; he received a full US presidential pardon on 1 December 2025 and went free the same day, and Honduras then asked Interpol to act on an arrest order written in 2023 for exactly that event. His brother Tony, a congressman, is serving life, with trial testimony that drug money funded the National Party's campaigns. Juan Carlos 'El Tigre' Bonilla, police chief in 2012–13, pleaded guilty to taking payments to give armed protection to loads crossing the country. Under the previous president, Porfirio Lobo, his son Fabio arranged police escorts for shipments he believed belonged to the Cachiros trafficking group; Porfirio Lobo himself was named by witnesses and put on a US corruption list, but never charged.

The money ran through respectable firms. In 2014–15 the US designated Honduran networks with legitimate business faces, among them Los Valles and the Rosenthal family, whose members included a former vice-president and a congressman and whose Banco Continental laundered for the Cachiros; regulators liquidated the bank within days. Former president Rafael Callejas, later head of the football federation, pleaded guilty in the US FIFA bribery case.

The older background is the 1980s army: a group led by armed forces commander Gustavo Álvarez Martínez took $50,000 from a front for the Unification Church, the Korean-founded religious movement, and took control of university, labour and peasant bodies before officers ousted him in 1984.
Honduras.imp: For Hondurans, the police who were supposed to stop cocaine were escorting it, and the governing party was funded by it, according to US verdicts. The pardon means the most senior convicted figure is free, and Hondurans are relying on their own arrest order to bring him back. Banco Continental's depositors were paid out over a year after its liquidation. Watch whether Hernández is arrested, whether Honduran courts try any of these cases, and how campaign money is checked.

Jamaica.d:
Jamaica's two documented cases are finished, but between them they show a gang and a foreign bank each sitting close to the head of government. The recent one is Christopher 'Dudus' Coke, leader of the Shower Posse, a gang based in Tivoli Gardens, West Kingston. When the United States asked for his extradition, the government resisted for nine months and retained a Washington law firm to lobby against the request. The security operation that finally went in killed at least 69 people. Coke pleaded guilty in New York in 2011; the prime minister had already resigned over the affair, and a 2016 commission of enquiry found the operation unjustified in its conduct.

The older case is BCCI, the Bank of Credit and Commerce International, which collapsed in 1991 amid fraud and money laundering. A 1992 US Senate report found that under Prime Minister Edward Seaga the bank handled Jamaica's US commodity financing and most government foreign-currency accounts, lending $33.9 million to the Bank of Jamaica, the central bank, and $45.4 million to the state oil firm Petrojam. A BCCI officer told the Senate the bank 'handled every penny' of Jamaica's foreign currency.

Jamaica scores low overall (3.18), though its conditions score is higher, at 6.08.
Jamaica.imp: In West Kingston, a gang leader's protection reached the prime minister's office, and residents paid for it when the operation to take him killed at least 69 people. Decades earlier, the state's foreign money sat in a bank later shut down for fraud. Watch how future extradition requests are handled, whether gang leaders keep that kind of shelter, and who holds the government's banking business.

Mexico.d:
Mexico is the map's central case of organised crime working from inside a state. In Sinaloa, Tabasco and Nayarit the heads of state law enforcement are accused or proven to have worked for cartels. In April 2026 US prosecutors in Manhattan charged Sinaloa's sitting governor, Rubén Rocha Moya, and nine others, including the mayor of Culiacán, a senator and police commanders, with protecting the Chapitos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, saying cartel members stole ballot boxes for him in 2021. He denies it and resigned in May; none of the ten is in custody, and Mexico has opened its own inquiry. Tabasco's former security chief is held accused of running a gang tied to the CJNG, the Jalisco cartel, from his office. In Michoacán, Guerrero and Tamaulipas whole town police forces have been disbanded for working for traffickers.

The cartels also run ordinary businesses. In Jalisco, Nayarit, Michoacán and Zacatecas the US Treasury lists tequila distilleries, agave growers and gas stations as CJNG fronts; a Puerto Vallarta resort fed timeshare scams that cost about 6,000 Americans roughly $300 million. Casinos and restaurants in Sinaloa and Sonora wash Sinaloa Cartel money. Michoacán avocado and lime growers pay a fee per hectare and per shipment.

Most proof comes from US courts: Genaro García Luna, federal security minister from 2006 to 2012, was convicted in New York of taking Sinaloa Cartel money, and two former governors admitted guilt there. Mexican cases often collapse: all 30-plus officials arrested in Michoacán in 2009 were freed. A journalist and a former mayor claimed El Yunque, a secret Catholic group, had members in Vicente Fox's cabinet; those named deny it. The older foreign hand was American: from 1927 a J.P. Morgan partner, as US ambassador, advised President Calles and helped delay oil nationalisation.
Mexico.imp: For people in Mexico, the police, prosecutors and judges meant to protect them have in proven cases worked for the groups they were supposed to stop, from Iguala's town police, who handed 43 students to a gang in 2014, up to a federal minister. Ordinary purchases, petrol, tequila, a holiday, can feed cartel revenue, and farmers in Michoacán pay a levy on every crate. Most cases are settled in US courts, not Mexican ones. Watch whether the Sinaloa indictment reaches a courtroom and whether Mexico's own inquiry charges anyone.

Nicaragua.d:
Nicaragua's documented case today is a foreign government training its police. Since October 2017 Russia's Interior Ministry, which runs Russia's own police, has operated a training centre in the Las Colinas district of Managua, set up as an affiliate of the ministry. Laureano Ortega Murillo, the president's son, attended the opening with Russia's ambassador. The centre teaches Nicaraguan police and, later, officers from elsewhere in Central America and the Caribbean. In May 2024 the US Treasury sanctioned it, saying it trains officials of the Ortega-Murillo government in the Russian government's 'playbook of oppression' and is a key actor in repressing civil society. Nicaragua's conditions score is among the map's highest, 8.50, because power is concentrated and few checks remain, so other arrangements could exist unrecorded.

The older record shows foreign money working on more than one side of Nicaraguan politics. Banco Ambrosiano, Roberto Calvi's Italian bank, had a Managua unit from 1977–78 that funded both the Somoza dictatorship and the Sandinista opposition; Daniel Ortega's government cancelled its licence in 1985. In the 1980s the US-funded National Endowment for Democracy (NED) put about $2 million into the civic opposition, half of it to La Prensa, the paper run by Violeta Chamorro, and in 1989 the US Congress approved $9 million more before the 1990 election, which Chamorro won. NED says its grants are public and nonpartisan. Opus Dei, the Order of Malta and the Unification Church are also recorded as present, without any wrongdoing found here.
Nicaragua.imp: For people in Nicaragua, the record is about their own police: officers who stop, question and arrest them are trained at a centre run as an arm of a foreign interior ministry, which the US says helps repress civil society. The president's family has been part of it from the start. With courts and other checks weak, Nicaraguans have little route to find out what else is going on. Watch who trains and equips the police, and where political money comes from on every side.

Panama.d:
Panama's part on the map is twofold: officials paid by a foreign builder, and a country whose banks, law firms and free zone others use to move and hide money. The first is in court now. Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction group, admitted in 2016 paying $788 million in bribes across Latin America and Africa and says $59 million went to Panamanian officials under President Ricardo Martinelli (2009–2014). The main laundering trial opened in January 2026 with more than 20 defendants; Martinelli, living under asylum in Colombia, takes part by video and pleads innocent. Two of his sons and former president Juan Carlos Varela face separate Supreme Court trials.

The second runs through Colón and Panama City. The Colón Free Zone, the largest in the Americas, lets goods pass without entering Panamanian customs, and laundering studies and several US sanctions run through it; Panama has tightened rules on who owns companies, but the volume has not fallen. In 2016 the US named a free-zone trading group and its bank, Balboa Bank & Trust, as a laundering network, and Panama's regulator seized the bank. Two Panama City law firms that set up offshore companies sit on the record: Mossack Fonseca, at the centre of the Panama Papers, whose founders and 26 others were acquitted of laundering in 2024 on weak and improperly gathered evidence, and Alcogal, which formed thousands of companies without checking who owned them; it says it followed the law and has not been charged.

The roots lie with General Manuel Noriega, who in 1982 opened an account at BCCI, a bank later shut for fraud worldwide, in the name of Panama's Defense Forces, and had it pay the mortgage of his chosen presidential candidate. A Miami court convicted him of trafficking for the Medellín Cartel in 1992.
Panama.imp: For people in Panama, the country's banks, law firms and free zone are tools other people use to move money, and the cost lands on Panama's name and its courts. Cases end in acquittals or no charges as often as convictions, and a former president faces trial from abroad. Officials who signed public contracts are accused of selling them. Watch the Odebrecht verdicts, the Supreme Court cases against Varela and Martinelli's sons, and whether ownership rules ever shrink what passes through Colón.

Paraguay.d:
In Paraguay the cocaine trade moving down the Hidrovía has reached into the police, the prosecution service, the courts and Congress. A Ultranza Py, a case prosecutors opened in February 2022, has charged police officers, a serving prosecutor, court officials and a sitting member of the Chamber of Deputies. Several principals fled before arrest, and one of the case's own prosecutors was later removed.

The second thread runs through the Tri-Border Area, where Paraguay meets Argentina and Brazil around Ciudad del Este. Hezbollah, the Lebanese armed movement and party the US lists as a terrorist group, has long had money networks there. In January 2023 the US Treasury sanctioned former president Horacio Cartes and the sitting vice-president, Hugo Velázquez, for corruption, saying both had ties to Hezbollah members and that their representatives collected bribes at Hezbollah events in Paraguay. The sanctions on Cartes and several of his companies were lifted in 2025. In Ciudad del Este's free zone, Argentina froze a trading network's assets in 2018 and the US designated its principals.

The roots go back to Alfredo Stroessner's dictatorship. In 1992 the 'Archives of Terror', his secret police files, were found in a police station in Lambaré outside Asunción; they proved Operation Condor, the joint campaign of South American military regimes against their opponents, and helped a truth commission document 9,923 victims. A US Senate report records a $5 million central bank deposit at BCCI in 1989. In 2005 the Senate voted to take back land around Puerto Casado that the Unification Church had bought.
Paraguay.imp: For people in Paraguay, the river trade has bought the police officers, prosecutors and judges who would handle a complaint about it, and a lawmaker as well. The US accused the presidency of ties to an armed group, then lifted the sanctions on Cartes, so the question was never tested in a court. Principals often leave before arrest. Watch how A Ultranza Py ends, whether prosecutors who pursue it keep their jobs, and what the Ciudad del Este trade is used for.

Peru.d:
Peru's record today centres on money from one foreign company and on networks inside its courts and regional governments. Odebrecht, a Brazilian construction group, admitted in 2016 paying $788 million in bribes in a dozen countries. Peru's courts have sentenced two former presidents over it: Alejandro Toledo to 20 years in 2024 for taking about $35 million for the Interoceanic Highway contract, and Ollanta Humala and his wife Nadine Heredia to 15 years each in 2025 for laundering Odebrecht money; Heredia left for Brazil under asylum and both deny the charges.

Inside the state, the problems sit in Callao and Junín. In Callao wiretaps on a trafficking group in 2018 caught a supreme court judge, the president of the local superior court and members of the judicial appointments council trading sentence cuts and promotions; the first trial conviction came only in November 2025. In Junín, prosecutors say a network in the regional transport office has sold driving licences since 2012, and argued in 2021 that the money helped fund Perú Libre, the party that won that year's presidential election. Its leader Vladimir Cerrón is a fugitive in a separate case. ENACO, the state coca buyer, pays growers less than traffickers do, so most legal coca leaves its channel.

Religious and lodge ties reach the top. Opus Dei, a Catholic organisation whose lay members are encouraged to excel in public life, has had a defence minister and a Lima mayor, Rafael López Aliaga, now a senator; membership is lawful. In 2025 a TV programme reported Prime Minister Eduardo Arana was a senior Freemason who hired a lodge member; he denied any favour, and it remains a report.

The background is Vladimiro Montesinos, Fujimori's intelligence chief, who ran much of the military, courts and press and was convicted of drug trafficking.
Peru.imp: For people in Peru, two presidents have been sentenced over money from one foreign company, meaning roads and contracts were priced around bribes. In Callao, people facing trial could not trust that sentences were decided on the evidence, and a verdict on the judges took seven years. A driving licence in Junín could be bought, with the money allegedly going into national politics. Watch whether the Junín case reaches trial, whether the Arana report leads to any inquiry, and whether sentences handed down are served.

Trinidad and Tobago.d: No case of capture of Trinidad and Tobago's own government is documented on this map, so this write-up is a best guess. The nearest case is filed under FIFA, world football's governing body. Jack Warner, a FIFA vice-president until 2011, sat in the cabinet from 2010 to 2013, latterly as national security minister. US prosecutors indicted him in 2015 for fraud, racketeering and laundering, including a $10 million payment tied to South Africa's World Cup bid; FIFA banned him for life, and in 2025 Trinidad's High Court blocked his extradition. Opus Dei is present and English Freemasonry likely, with no wrongdoing found. Conditions scores are middling, so sport and international bodies look like the likeliest route in.
Trinidad and Tobago.imp: For people in Trinidad and Tobago, a man US prosecutors charge with taking bribes as a football official was the minister in charge of national security, overseeing police and border control. The charges have not been tested in court, and he will not be sent to the US to face them. Watch how officials who also hold posts in international bodies are vetted before they join the cabinet.

United States.d:
China's reach runs from US phone lines to city hall. A hacking group widely attributed to its Ministry of State Security (its spy service) sat inside at least nine US phone companies and their wiretap systems; Google and GE engineers have been convicted of carrying designs to China; and the mayor of Arcadia, California, has pleaded guilty to acting as Beijing's agent. North Korea slips its programmers onto more than 300 US payrolls under stolen identities, and the wages fund its weapons. Other governments work through officials in both parties: Senator Bob Menendez is imprisoned for acting for Egypt, while a Republican fundraiser who pleaded guilty as a foreign agent and a congressman charged over Azerbaijani money were both pardoned.

At home, private networks supply people and drafts. Authors of Project 2025, a plan organised by the conservative Heritage Foundation, now run the budget office, FCC and CIA; nearly 70 staff of its Democratic counterpart, the Center for American Progress, joined the Biden administration. In statehouses the corporate-funded American Legislative Exchange Council writes model bills with lawmakers; a study found 10,000 near-copies introduced and 2,100 passed. Membership in these groups is lawful. Power companies paid off the House Speakers of Ohio and Illinois, both convicted, and Boeing staff do much of the FAA's safety checking of Boeing planes. Cartels reach in through border officers (over 200 corruption convictions in a decade), banks and Chinese brokers buying their cash; TD Bank pleaded guilty in 2024, yet in 2025 no US bank faced a major penalty.

Behind this lies a long record: the 1920s Klan elected governors in three states, and the CIA hid money in foundation grants. The claim that the Rothschilds own the Federal Reserve is an antisemitic myth; the Fed's governors are chosen by the President and the Senate.
United States.imp: People here live under rules that outsiders helped write or check: a state law copied from a model bill, a plane certified partly by its maker's own staff, a $1 billion nuclear-plant rescue in Ohio that a power company paid to pass. Their call records sat open to a foreign spy service. Cartel money moving through banks and through anonymous Delaware, Wyoming and Nevada companies rarely brings a penalty now; some foreign-agent cases end in a pardon or a dismissal rather than a verdict. In Chicago, more than 200 convictions built on one police team's word have been thrown out.

Uruguay.d:
Uruguay shows no outside force inside its government today. Its record is about military rule and the foreign networks that worked with it, and mostly Uruguay's own courts and parliament did the exposing.

The first thread is Operation Condor, the pact through which South America's military governments hunted each other's opponents across borders. Gregorio Álvarez, the army commander who became Uruguay's last de facto president, was sentenced to 25 years for 37 homicides, among them people moved to Argentina under the Condor plan. A Rome appeals court gave life terms to 24 people in its own Condor case, including the former foreign minister Juan Carlos Blanco; most were tried in absentia and the verdict can still go to Italy's highest court.

The second thread is outsiders who settled in Montevideo under the generals. The Unification Church, the movement founded by Sun Myung Moon, bought 49% of Banco de Crédito, one of the oldest banks, and started a daily paper that called itself 'fully identified' with the military 'process'. When the bank closed in 2002 a parliamentary commission found about US$100 million of its roughly US$600 million in loans had gone to Moon-linked companies. Licio Gelli, head of the Italian lodge P2, hid in Montevideo from an Italian arrest warrant in 1981, and police there seized his files; what became of them rests on press reports.

The one present-day case ran the other way. Philip Morris International sued Uruguay over health warnings covering 80% of cigarette packs, and the World Bank's investment tribunal ruled for Uruguay in 2016.
Uruguay.imp: For people in Uruguay, the record shows institutions that worked: a former de facto president and a foreign minister convicted over disappearances, a parliamentary commission tracing where a failed bank's loans went, and a health law defended against a tobacco company. The quieter risks are the ones that came through in the 1980s: foreign groups buying a stake in a bank or a newspaper. Watch who owns the banks and the press, and whether companies use investment treaties against new health or environmental rules.

Venezuela.d:
Venezuela is in transition after a foreign government removed its head of state. On 3 January 2026 US forces seized President Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores in Caracas and flew them to New York; Vice-President Delcy Rodríguez became interim president. Three outside forces run through the record.

The first is the drug trade, which US prosecutors say runs through the officer corps and the ministries meant to police it. They call it the 'Cartel de los Soles', and the men they name have held the anti-drug office (Néstor Reverol, later interior minister), the vice-presidency (Tareck El Aissami), the National Assembly and, since 2024, the interior ministry (Diosdado Cabello), and military intelligence (Hugo Carvajal). Most of this is indictment and sanction, never tested at trial; analysts dispute that it is a real cartel while agreeing officials are in the trade. Smaller parts have been tested in court: the first lady's two nephews were convicted in New York of offering 800 kilograms of cocaine, and Carvajal pleaded guilty in 2025. The US also says the Tren de Aragua gang acts on government orders, which its own intelligence council doubted.

The second is Cuba. Under 2008 agreements Cuba oversaw the rebuilding of Venezuela's military intelligence, which turned to watching Venezuela's own soldiers and grew to at least 1,500 agents.

The third is the United States, which now sells Venezuelan oil into US-controlled accounts, after months of CIA covert action and strikes on boats that left no seizure or court file behind.

Odebrecht's local chief told Brazilian prosecutors the firm gave $35 million to Maduro's 2013 campaign, which the government denies. In 2002 the director of Cedice, a Caracas think tank funded through the US National Endowment for Democracy, signed the coup decree dissolving the National Assembly and Supreme Court.
Venezuela.imp: For Venezuelans, the people accused of running the drug trade have held the very posts meant to stop it: the anti-drug office, the interior ministry and military intelligence. Few of those accusations have reached a courtroom, and the evidence is not public. Now a foreign power has taken the head of state and controls the accounts that oil money flows into, which is most of what the state earns. Watch who holds the interior ministry, military intelligence and the oil accounts during the transition, and whether any charge reaches a trial.

Kosovo.d:
In Kosovo, outside hands reach the state from two directions: wartime commanders whose networks followed them into government, and Turkey's pursuit of its opponents through Kosovo's own security services. The first goes back to the 1999 war. In 2010 Swiss senator Dick Marty told the Council of Europe, a human-rights body of European states, that a 'Drenica Group' of former Kosovo Liberation Army commanders, which he said was led by then Prime Minister Hashim Thaçi, controlled criminal trades including heroin, and he found 'credible, convergent indications' of organ trafficking from captives. Thaçi denied it. An EU task force later reported compelling indications of war crimes, and Thaçi has been on trial at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers since 2023. The organised-crime claims have never been tested in court.

The second is Turkey, whose government calls the movement of preacher Fethullah Gülen a terrorist group and has hunted its members abroad since 2016. In March 2018 Kosovo police and intelligence seized five teachers and a doctor that Ankara accused of Gülen links and flew them to Turkey on a private plane. The prime minister said he had not been told and sacked the interior minister and the intelligence chief, and in 2023 a Pristina court jailed former intelligence chief Driton Gashi for abuse of office. Kosovo's conditions scores borrow North Macedonia's figures.
Kosovo.imp: For people in Kosovo, the record points to two risks: men who ran a war carrying their networks into public office, and a foreign government able to get local officers to hand over residents without the prime minister's knowledge. Courts have acted on both. Watch the outcome of the Thaçi trial and whether the intelligence service stays answerable to elected leaders.
